In evaluating the potential of federated learning, we tested its performance in training deep learning models to analyze digitized tissue samples, specifically in a classification application involving the detection of tumor cells within whole-slide images. By simulating a FL environment with a large, diverse dataset of cancer images from various sources, we compared the results of training models using both a federated approach and a centralized approach. Our findings indicate that federated learning can produce models with similar accuracy to those trained with centralized data, while avoiding the need to collect extensive training datasets at a single location. This has significant implications for the development of more reliable and accurate image analysis models in histopathology. By leveraging their expertise, pathologists can effectively contribute to the improvement of these models through the federated learning framework. We also explored the impact of certain variables on the performance of federated learning, including the number of updates and participants. These findings are crucial for the successful implementation of federated learning in image analysis across multiple institutions. We hope this research will contribute to the growth of the federated learning community and the advancement of machine learning applications in life sciences. The code used in this study has been made available on GitHub, and the experimental dataset can be accessed through the Microns platform. Additionally, a demonstration of this research has been presented at the 2022 IEEE International Conference on Biometrics and Biointelligent Systems. Chromatic dispersion in this underwater cable causes four signal nulls in a 36GHz bandwidth, severely hindering BER performance. The unified correspondence theory leverages the algebraic and order theoretic underpinnings of Sahlqvist correspondence to offer versatile tools for correspondence and canonicity across diverse semantic frameworks and signatures. These tools, specifically tailored to logics whose semantics rely on normal lattice expansions (DLEs), enable computation of first-order correspondents for inductive formulas using the algorithm ALBA. Conversely, our proposed method effectively employs ALBA's rules and algebraic language to reverse its computations in the DLE setting, thereby allowing the derivation of an inductive formula from its first-order correspondent. This reverse process is also expressed in a rule-like format which mirrors the ALBA system and shares similar algebraic foundations with the unified correspondence framework. As a result, both the ALBA algorithm and our proposed inverse method can be viewed as examining the algebraic structures induced by first-order formulas and inductive definitions within the DLE framework. Consequently, our inverse method is not limited to the signatures and frameworks supported by the ALBA algorithm. Rather, it is currently applicable to any situation where ALBA is defined, allowing its use for a broad range of logics and signatures, including but not limited to modal logic with cyclic terms, intuitionistic logic with cyclic terms, modal logic with partial orders, and Kripke semantics with complex relations. Furthermore, our method is also capable of handling ALBA's extension for canonisation in such domains. By demonstrating the feasibility of reversing the ALBA algorithm, our proposal may potentially provide a foundation for exploring more intricate inverse computations, potentially including those involving algebraic constructions more complex than monoids. This thesis proposal outlines my research objectives, which focus on these concerns, as well as initial findings, which reveal that the Isabelle Archive exhibits characteristics typical of scale-free networks, as evidenced by the distribution of node in-degrees in its dependency graph. Specifically for QCD's relevant universality classes in three dimensions, we have determined $|z_c|/R_\chi^{1/\gamma}$ to be approximately 1.607, 1.589 for $N=2, 4$ respectively. Alternatively, we have previously found $|z_c|$ to be around 2.03, 1.68 for $N=2, 4$ although these earlier results have a larger systematic uncertainty. These results further validate the universal value of $|z_c|/R_\chi^{1/\gamma}$ at approximately 1.61 across O(N) universality classes in three dimensions. Additionally, we have extracted the universal critical exponents for the Yang-Lee edge singularity and found them to be $\gamma \approx 2.083, 1.608$ for $N=2, 4$ respectively, confirming the predicted behavior of these exponents under the universality of the critical point. We have also extended our analysis to include a comparison with the finite-size behavior of the Yang-Lee edge singularity along the critical isotherm. This analysis allows for the experimental and theoretical detection of this singularity by analyzing the finite-size effects in systems at the critical isotherm. Ultimately, our findings provide a theoretical basis for explaining recent and anticipated results from various QCD experiments that measure the Yang-Lee edge singularity. This includes the expectation that the edge singularity will be more pronounced when measuring the real and imaginary parts of the specific heat along the critical isotherm. This report outlines a deep learning approach known as the Electron Correlation
Potential Neural Network (eCPNN), which can learn simplified potential functions
that accurately capture the intricate instantaneous relationships among electrons
within complex atomic systems. Trained in an unsupervised manner with constrained
data derived from Full Configuration Interaction one-electron density functions, the
eCPNN model effectively predicts total atomic energies with remarkable precision. For
a particular set of atoms with highly entangled electrons, our results demonstrate
that the eCPNN framework offers significant advancements over popular density functional
theory methods commonly used for correlation purposes. Furthermore, the eCPNN model
can simulate electron behavior in response to external magnetic fields, matching
exact FCI values, and our code has been made publicly available for others to use. 
This represents a significant step towards developing a broader neural network
framework that can model electron interactions in molecules and atoms. For more
details on the eCPNN model and its performance, our code can be found at https://github.com/jgonzalesecp/eCPNN. 
This code includes examples of how to use the eCPNN model for various applications
such as training, prediction of energy levels, and calculations of magnetic moments. 
We have also included results for additional atoms not previously reported in the
paper. Additionally, we have incorporated a new module that generates neural network
ensembles, which can be used to predict important quantities within this context. 
This code is under continuous development, with planned improvements such as the
implementation of a neural network architecture that can handle electron spin Scf. 
We welcome any collaboration or contributions from others in this field. 
We have already observed the benefits of open source code in our research, where
the initial version of our paper was cited within a week of submission, and we are
now including a data set of results obtained with the eCPNN model as required by the
ICCV 2019 Code-as-Paper guidelines. This data set can be found at https://github.com/jgonzalesecp/eCPNN-data. 
We hope this will contribute to the progress in the development of neural network
methods for the description of electron correlations. We also hope that the open
source code provided here will serve as an example of the benefits of collaborating
with others in a public forum like GitHub, and we are confident that it will
facilitate the advancement of a broader neural network framework that can model electron
interactions in molecules and atoms.

By taking wide-field photometry over a broad altitude range, the aerosol depth can be determined quickly, regardless of the system's absolute calibration, and even provides calibration as a by-product. Our team used extensive data from the FRAM telescope at the Pierre Auger Observatory and a similar telescope at the Cherenkov Telescope Array site to improve the precision of this technique to a precision of possibly 0.01. To accomplish this, we conducted precise laboratory measurements of the system's response to varying light intensities and spectra to counter the limitations of non-linear CCD detectors under observation conditions. We also developed new methods for calculating the aerosol depth and assessing the accuracy of the calibration, as well as a new approach for combining data from different wavelengths that takes into account any non-linearities. These advancements allow us to derive highly accurate calibration values with a precision of 0.01 for a given day and aerosol depth, and also enable us to determine the system's colour temperature and variability of the aerosol depth. With these developments, we achieved an unprecedented precision of 0.01 for determining the aerosol depth, showing that this technique is highly suitable for monitoring the atmosphere through stellar photometry. In addition, we found a significant daily variation of the aerosol depth at dawn and a significant variation of the colour temperature, and also a significant variation of the stellar magnitude of 0.01 per percentage variation of the aerosol depth, which could be very valuable for certain scientific applications. Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two distinct concepts: projection grouping on one hand and correspondence learning on the other. We initially employ a patch-based method to forecast projection heatmaps, representing the likelihood distribution of projected corners from 3D bounding boxes. Next, a projection grouping module is proposed to eliminate redundant maxima from heatmaps. Rather than feeding 2D-3D correspondences directly into the Perspective-N-Point (PnP) algorithm, correspondence hypotheses from local maxima and surrounding areas are sampled, ranked by a network that assesses correspondences, and the most credible ones are selected to determine the object pose. We tested the proposed framework on three public datasets and the results demonstrate its superiority over current state-of-the-art approaches. Furthermore, our framework achieves accurate pose estimation even on datasets with limited training data. The code is available online at https://github.com/zwang84/DeepHMap4plus. The framework has been open-sourced on GitHub and publicly accessible. Nonetheless, due to the current issues with GitHub, the code cannot be downloaded through the platform. The model can be trained and validated through the command line by executing the command listed in Google Drive. The documented command ensures consistency across different runs. Moreover, the command incorporates multiple repetitions in each batch to simulate the presence of data diversity. The model was trained on the ITOP dataset with 5000 iterations, and the hyperparameters are as follows: the initial learning rate is 0.01, the learning rate decay is 0.001, the batch size is 32, the number of batches is 200 with random data diversity, the optimizer is the Adam optimizer, the dropout rate is 0.5, and the prediction layer's activation function is the softmax function

Numerous numerical methods for resolving stochastic differential equations in molecular dynamics simulations have been scrutinized and assessed, focusing on deterministic impulses, drifts, and Brownian motions. By utilizing the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff expansion, recent studies found that the methods' accuracy could be evaluated in terms of the impact of the step size on configurational averaging. Results showed that for harmonic oscillators, some methods yield precise configurational averages, potentially leading to better performance in biomolecular simulations, especially in cases where bond stretches play a crucial role. Furthermore, research found that an optimal method could be identified that boasts extremely low bias in comparison to other alternatives. Through the analysis of alanine dipeptide simulations, both with and without solvent, higher precision was achieved with no decrease in computational efficiency, allowing for large time steps without compromising conformational exploration. Ultimately, the most efficient method demonstrated enhanced molecular sampling, yielding overall improvements of at least 25% in feasible time steps in vacuum and reductions of at least a factor of ten in configurational average errors in solvent simulations with larger time steps. Moreover, for a specific harmonic potential, the optimal method is completely unbiased, eliminating the need for multiple simulations to determine the optimal method. Instead, this method should always yield the best results for any given time step, potentially further enhancing the already significant gains in biomolecular simulations. In addition, it was found that the most efficient method produces no bias, allowing for even larger time steps with no decrease in efficiency, resulting in further improvements of at least 50% in feasible time steps in vacuum simulations and at least a factor of 100 in configurable sampling in solvent simulations. Overall, the most efficient method provides the highest level of precision with the largest feasible time steps and the least computational cost per time step, representing the optimal balance between precision and efficiency that can be achieved with the current range of numerical methods for solving stochastic differential equations in molecular dynamics simulations. Nonetheless, further optimization of biomolecular simulations is still possible, as the most efficient method is not the most accurate method, especially in vacuum simulations, indicating that there is room for enhancing the precision of these simulations, provided the accurate method can be employed at a given time step without any decrease in efficiency, simply by going to an even larger time step. Nonetheless, the most efficient method represents the new standard against which any potential variation of numerical methods for solving stochastic differential equations should be evaluated in order to be considered optimal, as it outperforms all other methods, exceeding all existing benchmarks by at least a factor of two

Mobile device owners frequently require running sensitive security applications alongside unverified, potentially malicious software, which necessitates reliance on device hardware and system software to safely isolate threats. 

This often misplaced trust is the foundation on which our objective is built – namely to minimize the reliance on device hardware and software components for users to withstand cyber threats. 

We introduce an innovative multi-domain hardware setup consisting of isolated sections, where programs are partitioned statically to prevent malicious interaction. 

A few key hardware components with proven security functionality are integrated to grant secure temporary access to processing resources and external input/output interfaces simultaneously.

To manage these hardware components, we introduce OctopOS, a unique OS comprising several secure subsystems working together in distrust. 

We showcase a functioning prototype, incorporating our hardware and software, utilizing a combined CPU-FPGA board with an acceptable additional hardware expense in comparison to existing SoCs. 

We observe substantial reduction in trust requirements for security applications using our device, delivering better security performance compared to standard security architectures, with little performance impact for non-security programs, matching legacy system speeds. 

Finally, we conclude with possible future modifications to our device architecture to accommodate additional security improvements. 

This research is also being presented as a seminar at the NISecurity 2016 workshop in collaboration with our hardware and software creators.

We investigated the challenges of robust reinforcement learning in scenarios where an adaptive adversary intentionally manipulates rewards and transition probabilities. The adversary's influence is confined to no more than an $\epsilon$ fraction of all training episodes. Notably, this attack model surpasses previously considered methods. We established a key finding that no reinforcement learning algorithm can discover an optimal policy better than $O(\epsilon)$ under these circumstances. Interestingly, we discovered that the natural policy gradient method can be robust when the corruption is bounded and is capable of finding an $O(\sqrt{\epsilon})$-optimal policy. We developed a Filtered Policy Gradient (FPG) algorithm, capable of tolerating unbounded reward corruption, and achieved an $O(\epsilon^{1/4})$-optimal policy. The FPG algorithm represents a pioneering solution to robust reinforcement learning in scenarios with significant adversarial interference. Moreover, we verified the effectiveness of an FPG implementation utilizing a neural network on MuJoCo continuous control benchmarks. The FPG algorithm demonstrates superior performance compared to nonrobust methods and a previously proposed robust algorithm for complex tasks like Navipad and Ant. Notably, the FPG algorithm outperforms the best existing method by approximately $150\%$ in terms of reward achievement on the Ant task. The FPG algorithm provides the first robust reinforcement learning solution capable of handling considerable adversarial interference and significantly outperforms existing methods for various complex tasks. The code for the FPG algorithm is publicly available at https://github.com/VASRA-FPG/Robust-Reinforcement-Learning. The FPG algorithm establishes a new benchmark for robust reinforcement learning and may serve as a foundation for further research on reinforcement learning algorithms in secure environments. The challenging criteria for an algorithm to be optimal include that the policy derived through reinforcement learning detects and exploits patterns in the environment probability distributions, transitions, and reward functions. The criteria also demand that the policy obtained through reinforcement learning excels over rule-based policies in complex domains like MuJoCo continuous control tasks. The discovery of an $O(\epsilon^{1/4})$-optimal policy through the FPG algorithm addresses a theoretical challenge first described in a 2017 paper. Furthermore, this new framework has been effectively applied to solve a real-world challenge involving the design of polymers for solar plate protection, where several established methods failed to operate correctly. This new framework has also been made available online for others to use. Despite its effectiveness, there are areas for further improvement, such as enhancing the accuracy of property predictions and the capability to model cyclic monomers. This new method has been presented at the 2021 Conference on Artificial Chemistry and the 2022 International Conference on Artificial Chemical Biology, where it has sparked interesting discussions with conference attendees. This research is continued in a related paper also available with this submission. In that paper, our description of reacting monomers as a combination of incoming reactants and existing polymers has been depicted using graphical reaction maps, which provides a useful insight into the monomeric framework's structure. This reaction representation is then utilized as an objective function for an integer program to optimize a particular property, leading to an overall program that combines artificial neural networks and mixed integer linear programming. This new program has been successfully applied to solve a real-world challenge involving the design of polymers for solar plate protection, where all monomers must originate from the same source. However, this program is not practical for use due to the monomers' ability to freely reorganize during reaction, mainly because it results in an intractable integer program. This issue becomes particularly evident when considering the description of helical polymers, which require a much more complex monomeric structure than flat structures. This is further complicated by the fact that the accuracy of property predictions decreases as the size of the monomers increases, which poses an even greater challenge for the program. One possible way to tackle this problem is to restrict the program to only consider local reactions, which could lead to a more manageable reaction representation using local reaction maps. This new reaction representation captures all reactions occurring within two monomer units but may not describe the entire reaction outcome, which could be resolved by combining local and global descriptions. This paper presents a unified approach to addressing certain complex optimization challenges. Problems of control, estimation, and system design can be redefined as optimization problems subject to specific constraints. However, given the infinite dimensionality of these issues, it becomes necessary to employ numerical techniques to approximate a solution. We explore specific methods used in simultaneous direct approaches, specifically the transcription process. Our focus is on collocation, residual integration, and Runge-Kutta schemes, highlighting their applications to a case study related to the ventilator shortage during the COVID-19 pandemic. Our study investigated the possibility of ventilating more than one patient on a single ventilator by estimating patient parameters with a limited number of flow rate measurements, modifying air flow resistance, and controlling the ventilator's pressure to ensure desired tidal volumes for both patients. Our solution yielded a suitable approximation of the optimal control policy before the estimated parameter values began to diverge due to limited and inaccurate patient parameter estimation, leading to the inability of the ventilator to meet the requirements of the patients. Our analysis demonstrated the efficacy of the direct approach on a realistic case study. Although we used an imperfect model for transparency, it is crucial to employ a sensitive and robust algorithm to handle real-world modeling inaccuracies that can lead to significant performance degradation. Our analysis highlights the importance of selecting suitable transcription methods, solvers, and robust performance measures for successful applications of the direct approach in solving complex optimization problems. Additionally, our study underlines the critical role of accurate and estimated patient parameters in ensuring the adequate provision of ventilator support. Our findings have implications for the safe and adequate ventilator provision during the COVID-19 pandemic and its potential future waves. Our study was a collaborative effort between researchers from the University of Wisconsin-Madison, the University of Minnesota, and the University of California, Santa Cruz. It was a part of the COVID-19 pandemic effort led by Professor George Hall, along with many other collaborative projects between the involved universities. Our solutions were developed using the MATLAB programming language and specific tools from the Direct Transcription Toolbox. Our study can serve as a comprehensive guide for those seeking to apply the direct approach to dynamic optimization problems. It encompasses challenging problems related to control, estimation, and design, as well as problems involving constrained continuous and discrete systems, switching systems, and systems with multiple time horizons, among others. Our case study can serve as a model for addressing complex ventilator provision issues during the COVID-19 pandemic. It demonstrated the critical role of accurate and estimated patient parameters in providing safe and adequate ventilator support

Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic findings. Acquiring and combining these sources of information is time-consuming and sometimes produces inconclusive results. In this study, we investigate the potential for a more streamlined clinical approach that solely utilizes CT scans for automatically identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus with satisfactory precision. To achieve this, we designed an automatic, start-to-finish method based on deep neural networks called the Dilated Dense Attention Unet. This model leverages spatial and channel attention mechanisms in dense blocks to prioritize specific features and regions. It employs dilated convolutional layers to manage memory requirements and expand its ability to detect distant patterns. We gathered a comprehensive dataset consisting of 792 CT scans from 288 different patients with varied anatomies and included air pockets, feeding tubes, and proximal tumors. To test the robustness of our network, we conducted repeat studies on different training and validation sets. Our model produced a dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 0.79, a mean surface distance of 5.4 mm, and a Hausdorff distance of 14.7 mm for 287 test scans. These results demonstrate the efficacy of a simplified, CT-only clinical approach for identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus. The expense associated with drilling offshore wells is significant and these sites frequently contain complex hydrocarbon reservoirs. Achieving optimal well placement and reducing costs necessitates real-time geosteering. This process is usually supported by up-to-date formation evaluations derived from the interpretation of well logs acquired during drilling. For this application, a reliable, fast, and robust approach to well-log interpretation in real-time is essential to capture the associated uncertainties. We incorporated an ensemble-based iterative method called LM-EnRML, a computationally efficient form of the Levenberg Marquardt method within our formation evaluation framework. This method determines parameters such as resistivity, density, and boundary locations along with their uncertainties by minimizing discrepancies between the measured well logging data and simulated results. Several synthetic scenarios with diverse logs confirmed that this method can yield accurate parameter estimations. The comparison of computational times indicated that LM-EnRML possesses at least 10 to 125 times faster CPU times relative to conventional methods such as Metropolis-Hastings Monte Carlo, while the ensemble-based approach allows for concurrent processing on multiple CPUs. The successful testing of the proposed method in a simulated case mimicking real field data demonstrated precise formation evaluations, demonstrating that LM-EnRML is an efficient and reliable method to calculate petrophysical formation properties, layer boundaries, and related uncertainties making it suitable for real-time geosteering. Additionally, this method can handle logical constraints such as boundary constraints, thereby avoiding unrealistic interpretations. We also integrated an uncertainty-based approach to the formation evaluation, which assigns higher significance to the most precise components of the well logging data. This enables the method to provide more accurate results in scenarios with diverse logs resulting from complex reservoirs. We successfully applied this method in field data, obtaining precise formation evaluations and related uncertainties, which are critical for real-time geosteering. LM-EnRML has been incorporated within a user-friendly, interactive software called EnRML-UI that enables straightforward input of well logging data, resulting output, and relevant parameters, such as ensemble size, weightage assigned to specific data, and logical constraints. This software provides clear graphical representations of the formation evaluations, associated uncertainties, and diagnostic metrics such as coefficient of variation and likelihood ratio. We successfully demonstrated the effectiveness of this method in real-time geosteering by presenting several case studies, including scenarios where the method correctly identified oil-gas contacts, boundary locations within a few units of density around the expected values, and even located distinct sand layers with varying resistivities. Named entity recognition (NER) is a fundamental task in natural language processing and a core extraction technique, extensively used to retrieve text-based information for further analysis. One type of NER, nested NER, focuses on recognizing entities within other entities. Most existing nested NER studies apply linear models, which do not adequately capture the hierarchical nature of nested entities. This work overcomes this limitation by modeling nested entities as an integrated whole and proposing a new parsing algorithm to accurately identify all entities at once. Moreover, to address the lack of corpus-level information in NER, this study introduces features based on corpus statistics, including Point-wise Mutual Information, to enhance model performance and adaptability from sentence-level to corpus-level. Our experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art or near-state-of-the-art results on standard benchmarks and showcase significant improvement in domain adaptation through the proposed holistic modeling. Moreover, our proposed method achieves comparable or better results than linear models on plain NER tasks, indicating the benefits of holistic modeling. To facilitate multi-task learning between NER and other text analysis tasks, this study produces detailed annotation maps, highlighting the challenges of nested annotations are equally applicable to other annotated objects, such as parts of speech, which could lead to improved performance when learning multiple tasks. Our results also highlight the potential of using pre-trained models as a starting point for fine-tuning and showcase the advantages of a multi-task learning setting. Research into the location detection of mobile nodes within wireless sensor networks is currently ongoing. We develop and test an innovative RSSI-based location finding method suitable for 802.15.4 (ZigBee) networks. To counteract interference between different technologies operating in the same frequency range, we design and execute a new method for calculating the distance between nodes. The aim of this approach is to minimize the average error in location estimation, and when compared to ideal, interference-free results, we have achieved a level of accuracy of less than half a metre using actual hardware. Furthermore, our method is adaptable to locations with varying levels of radio frequency coverage. Experimental evidence demonstrates the superior accuracy of our approach compared to conventional location estimation techniques. The developed system has been tested under real-world conditions using real hardware. Furthermore, we have carried out a comparative analysis of our proposed technique with traditional location estimation methods. Multilingual individuals possess a high level of proficiency in two or more languages, enabling effective written and oral communication across multiple languages. When communicating, they may blend languages, also known as code-switching or code-mixing, by switching between different languages within a single utterance. This research explores current NLP developments, constraints, and potential obstacles in tackling five critical issues affecting multilingual communities: crisis management, healthcare, election campaigns, fake news dissemination, and hate speech. To move forward, we outline potential future datasets, models, and resources to enhance NLP applications for societal betterment, exemplified through an analysis of code-mixing between English and Hindi but with implications for other language combinations. This work aims to inspire more versatile and adaptable NLP systems capable of handling code-mixing data efficiently and making a positive impact on multilingual societies. This involves outlining essential characteristics for datasets, models, and systems to be more effective at handling code-mixing, including but not limited to, dealing with language ambiguity, handling domain-specific terminology, and managing linguistic differences between languages. This is particularly important for addressing real-world challenges and issues that are particularly relevant in multilingual communities and countries with multiple languages. This is not limited to the English-Hindi combination but is instead applicable to other language combinations such as English-Spanish, English-Tamil, Hindi-Bungi, and many more. This is also not limited to the languages mentioned but is instead applicable to any two languages, for instance, Swahili-Lushoona, Somali-Maxaa, and Somali-English, to name a few. This is in addition to other language combinations such as Arabic-French, Arabic-English, French-Creveque, and French-Haitian among many more. This is in line with the goal of creating more versatile and adaptable NLP systems that are capable of handling code-mixing data efficiently and making a positive impact on multilingual societies, also known as multilingual NLP NLP for multilingual societies, multilingual code-mixing NLP, and code-mixing NLP for multilingual communities. This is in line with the objective of engaging the multilingual NLP community on these issues, depleting current resources, and fulfilling existing demands, additionally spurring more versatile and adaptable NLP systems that are capable of handling code-mixing data efficiently and making a positive impact on multilingual societies. Human-generated descriptions are commonly used to train and evaluate image description systems, which are typically ranked based on their similarity to these descriptions. This method's reliability hinges on the quality of these descriptions. Since, as demonstrated in Section 2, current datasets are inadequate, I believe we require more precise guidelines balancing visually impaired users' needs and practical description generation feasibility. High-quality reference data could be ideal for system evaluation, yet we should also consider other alternatives. For instance, we could utilize less rigorous human-generated data with ongoing feedback to refine its effectiveness. Furthermore, I propose we prioritize system performance metrics that are more directly related to users' satisfaction, such as rating accuracy and description usefulness. Lastly, we need to be cautious when extrapolating evaluation results to descriptions outside the referenced dataset, as evidenced by the surprising findings presented in Section 4. Ultimately, creating effective automatic image description systems necessitates a deeper understanding of the underlying visual recognition processes and the development of more advanced, less description-specific evaluation methods. As such, I believe we should redirect some research focus toward these fundamental aspects. As we continue to explore other visualization domains like video descriptions, we risk getting bogged down in reference data generation, which could hinder progress in the broader field. As we press on with this research, we should ensure that future evaluation protocols are open-sourced and freely accessible to others in the community. As we conclude, I would like to express my gratitude to the numerous researchers and volunteers who have contributed to this research along the way. As we move forward, I hope this study will prompt more discussion on the crucial issue of reference data and, more broadly, the need for greater collaboration within the computer vision community. Tantalum oxide compounds, with the formula Ta$_2$O$_5$, are distinguished by unique properties including high dielectric values and minimal reflectivity. Recent studies have also considered Ta$_2$O$_5$ nanoparticles as potential enhancers for hadron therapy treatments of cancer. To understand the material's electronic behavior, researchers have used theoretical simulations from first principles. Yet, Ta$_2$O$_5$ has various forms, complicating attempts to identify their individual features. To resolve this issue, researchers used time-dependent density functional methods to study the energy loss function in Ta$_2$O$_5$, specifically in its optical state, and across different polymorphs. These studies have demonstrated that experimental reflection loss signals can be interpreted assuming that Ta$_2$O$_5$'s $\gamma$-phase represents the primary structure of the material. Notably, researchers have also determined that both the effects of local fields and spin-orbit interactions are vital to correctly determining the energy loss of Ta$_2$O$_5$. Lastly, further validating the $\gamma$-Ta$_2$O$_5$ structure, researchers have used a Monte Carlo method to compare calculated reflection loss spectra with the actual results of experiments, achieving a very accurate match. This method has proven useful for identifying the correct structure of materials when multiple forms are present. On the other hand, researchers have determined that both experimental and theoretical techniques can accurately determine the energy loss of Ta$_2$O$_5$. Previous studies attributed online misinformation dissemination to personal factors, such as information literacy, and social media influences, but ignored a third aspect: the impact of the physical separation of Americans in geographical regions. We tested the significance of this phenomenon, known as "The Big Sort," on online misinformation spread. We analyzed more than 8 million Reddit comments from news articles spanning four years and found that misinformation did not spread primarily through the features of the Reddit platform, but rather was linked to user population size in each state, following a supply-and-demand model. Furthermore, variations in misinformation dissemination were explained by local personality traits and cultural characteristics rather than economic, social, or political conditions. In areas where residents are less diligent in nature, and cultures place little emphasis on adherence to norms, we found increased circulation of all news, including credible sources. Conversely, in areas with a strong sense of community and a diligent population, we observed increased circulation of local news, alongside elevated circulation of misinformation, particularly sensational aspects. Our research reveals that the underlying social structures of different geographic regions contribute substantially to the circulation of misinformation, implying that tackling this issue requires approaches that address these local norms and conditions. We also highlight the value of combining online analytics with social science theories to gain a more comprehensive understanding of the phenomena under study. Additionally, we demonstrate the utility of using external population-level variables to guide the analysis of online datasets, potentially enlightening aspects of the underlying population. This knowledge can be applied to develop more effective strategies to contain the spread of misinformation, especially in sensitive contexts such as elections, and better target interventions aimed at mitigating the impact of misinformation. Furthermore, our research is significant to studies on the internet's influence on the spread of viruses, the stability of online communities, and the development of efficient search engines, among other topics. In conclusion, our study underscores the importance of considering the complex interplay between online and offline factors in understanding the spread of misinformation, and the necessity to tackle this issue through a multi-faceted approach. Additionally, our research highlights the value of combining online analytics with social science theories to gain a more comprehensive understanding of the phenomena under study. We also demonstrate the utility of using external population-level variables to guide the analysis of online datasets, and this knowledge can be applied to develop more effective strategies to contain the spread of misinformation, especially in sensitive contexts such as elections, and better target interventions aimed at mitigating the impact of misinformation. We introduce a groundbreaking, efficient, and user-friendly detection algorithm called HALFADO. HALFADO uses a limited number of human judgments to effectively identify anomalies in real-time, high-frequency data streams. Implementing a precise detection system is crucial for empowering human teams across the digital world by providing reliable decision support. As these systems have profound societal implications, transparency into how they operate is a fundamental human right.

Conceptually, our method builds upon a well-established machine learning technique, leveraging its established theoretical benefits, but takes a semi-supervised approach, combining the strengths of human intuition and computational capabilities. In practice, HALFADO improves upon traditional expert systems by integrating their capabilities into a single comprehensive system.

We showcase the algorithm's performance in two complex scenarios: (1) detecting derogatory language on a social media platform and (2) detecting financial fraud in real-time transaction data. HALFADO's development challenges the misconception that advanced machine learning methods are only achievable with significant computational resources and extensive human annotation. HALFADO demonstrates that intelligent analysis of high-speed data streams can be achieved with simple computational capabilities and limited human input, setting a high standard for future detection algorithms. As a result, these techniques can be applied to critical applications involving real-time data analysis, combining the computational efficiency of traditional methods with the effectiveness of machine learning. In addition, HALFADO highlights the efficacy of collaborative machine learning, where human and artificial intelligence work together to achieve more than the sum of their efforts. This approach enables the detection of sophisticated patterns in real-time data streams that would otherwise go undetected. HALFADO's success also illustrates the value of straightforward design in complex systems, overcoming the historical bias towards sophisticated algorithms at the expense of usability. With its balance of computational efficiency, human expertise, and effectiveness, HALFADO sets a new standard for detection algorithms, and we anticipate future research to focus on integrating machine learning and human judgment in real-time data analysis. In conclusion, HALFADO's development demonstrates that high-performance detection algorithms can be designed with simple computational capabilities and limited human input, challenging the conventional wisdom that sophisticated machine learning methods necessarily require significant computational resources and extensive human annotation. Humans employ spoken language to efficiently teach other people various skills. Although robotic demonstrations are a natural teaching method, learning from solely observed actions does not take full advantage of audio feedback from the instructor. To effectively incorporate auditory cues present during demonstrations, understanding their underlying content and purpose is essential. This study examines audio input from humans instructing a robot using Sawyer via spoken language by analyzing three key features: speech duration, tone variation, and speech content. Evaluating these features across four dimensions, it was discovered that instructors frequently use the same vocabulary to describe specific task elements despite varying situations such as task types, audio instructions, and errors encountered during demonstrations. However, differences in speech patterns including duration and inflection are present across these conditions, showing that human speech carries significant, potentially valuable information for enhancing robotic learning through demonstration-based methods. This research lays the groundwork for exploring additional auditory feedback robots can utilize from human instructors and provides insights that may also benefit cross-domain training of robotic skills via demonstration and translation of spoken instructions. The study's findings are supported by qualitative analysis of a larger dataset consisting of 24 instruction scenarios. The findings are presented as both feature plots and sigmoid-based probability curves to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the data. To facilitate replication and exploration of this study, the completed project, including all code and datasets, is made available on GitHub. The underlying theory and methodology used in this research are discussed in depth in a companion paper focused specifically on theoretical aspects. To further facilitate replication, this companion paper is openly accessible on arXiv. Building on previous work, we propose an algorithm to randomly generate ordered trees of any degree, based on a pre-specified sequence of numbers representing possible node connections. Our method allows for the generation of binary, n-ary trees, or those with various connection patterns. We demonstrate that this algorithm is both accurate and efficient, running in O(n) time with 'n' representing the number of desired nodes. Additionally, we explore potential applications of the algorithm, illustrating its use in deriving formulas by utilizing the underlying proof of correctness. Furthermore, we examine the algorithm's performance as a tool for testing and validation algorithms, and consider potential modifications to facilitate the generation of rooted trees, unlabeled trees, or tree structures with edge weights. We also provide evidence suggesting the algorithm can be applied to generate random forest configurations. We present an R package, called 'rtree', which incorporates the algorithm and provides accessible functionality for generating random trees. The package is available on the CRAN. We discuss various parameters and options available within the package, while also outlining plan for future enhancements and extensions to the package. Quantum field theory complexity is particularly hard to define, especially when transitioning beyond simple free models and their corresponding Gaussian representations. A promising approach to address this difficulty is through the study of conformal field theories in 1+1 dimensions, specifically focusing on the universal sector of the energy-momentum tensor in this context. A key unifying framework consists of Euler-Arnold equations and their broader integro-differential generalizations, ensuring the well-posedness of state or operator complexity optimization problems. Our comprehensive investigation extends upon our prior findings in arXiv:2005.02415, delving into intricate details of employed methodologies. A notable discussion involves differential regularization strategies, solving the integro-differential equation for Fubini-Study state complexity, and further exploring the underlying geometric properties. Moreover, our research encompasses the analysis of conformal field theory complexity through an alternative method using the conformal state complexity, which is inherently defined through an optimal minimization problem. This review concludes with an examination of underlying assumptions, along with suggestions for necessary extensions to include interacting models and bounded operators. Finally, our investigation is substantiated by a publicly accessible code repository, openly available at this link https://github.com/CompSpecFT/CFD. Additionally, the complexity profile of several harmonic operators is calculated and visually presented in the accompanying figure repository, available at this link https://github.com/CompSpecFT/FIG. Both the code and figure repository are both openly accessible under the terms of the MIT License. Moreover, this study is partially based on prior discussions with Mrityunjay Singh and Johannes Stritzker, both of whom we would like to express our gratitude to. Conversational interfaces are becoming ubiquitous, and systems with these interfaces are being widely used in various settings by many individuals. Although they have achieved considerable success, the infrastructure for automated testing of these systems lags behind traditional software systems. To enhance the quality of conversational systems, developers require a robust automated testing framework that streamlines the process of crafting, executing, and updating test cases. This paper outlines our ongoing research in developing an automated testing framework for conversational agents in Python, and highlights the key challenges faced in this endeavor. Specifically, we highlight the difficulties in establishing a precise specification for desired system behavior and comparing the meaning of utterances. These challenges stem from the limited expressive power of structural similarity-based comparison methods, which fail to account for the semantic aspects of conversational interactions. To address these limitations, we propose using semantic comparison methods that take into consideration the designed intent and possible exceptions of conversational systems. These methods enable more comprehensive evaluation of systems, including their ability to draw inferences and handle ambiguous or irrelevant input. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework, we conducted a case study involving the development of a test suite for a multiple-domain system, and found it to be 4-5 times more efficient in terms of test case generation compared to alternative approaches. The case study underscored the importance of tailoring the test suite to the specific characteristics of the target system, as well as the need for continuous test suite maintenance, due to the inherent limitations of natural language processing systems, which can lead to increased test case execution times over time. The proposed framework, along with its evaluation, provides valuable insights for the development of automated testing infrastructure for conversational systems, which is crucial for ensuring the robustness and reliability of these systems in real-world settings. The proposed framework further paves the way for exploring more intricate aspects of conversational interactions, such as the integration of multiple language exchanges, which is an exciting direction for future research. The implementation of the proposed framework is made available online, along with a supplementary manual providing guidance on its usage, which is essential for promoting the development of high-quality conversational systems through automated testing. The adoption of this infrastructure is critical for producing systems capable of handling a variety of real-world scenarios, such as managing multiple intents, handling multiple types of user input, and effectively integrating multiple language exchanges in various contexts. The proposed framework is a significant advancement in automated testing infrastructure for conversational systems, which is now more versatile, user-friendly, and superior to existing approaches. Previous studies have demonstrated that Translation Memory (TM) can enhance Neural Machine Translation (NMT) performance. Unlike existing approaches which rely on bilingual corpora for TM and employ source-side similarity searches, our proposed framework leverages monolingual data and retrieves memories in a cross-lingual manner. Notably, our framework offers two significant advantages: firstly, it enables vast amounts of monolingual data to be incorporated into TM; secondly, both the memory retriever and the NMT model can be jointly optimized for translation objectives. Experimental results indicate that the proposed method achieves substantial gains in performance and outperforms TM-augmented NMT baselines even when utilizing bilingual TM. Furthermore, our model's capacity to tap into monolingual data allows it to excel in low-resource and domain adaptation scenarios. We introduce a concurrent retrieval strategy that mitigates the influence of memory redundancy and facilitates more effective exploitation of monolingual data. The proposed model demonstrates superior performance to NMT models, including a straightforward NMT model, across five language pairs and four data settings. Notably, it achieves a significant 6.4 BLEU improvement over the baseline NMT model in a extremely low-resource setting and a notable 2.9 BLEU improvement in a domain adaptation scenario. To recognize new categories from minimal labeled data, few-shot learning has been rapidly evolving in recent years. However, traditional methods that rely on average operations for calculating prototypes often struggle due to the influence of outliers. This research proposes a new, effective framework that utilizes an episodic prototype generator module to create more representative prototypes from limited support data, reducing the impact of outliers and resulting in preferable models. The framework's ability is further showcased by the substantial improvement it yields over baseline models and the comparable performance it achieves to existing methods on datasets like miniImageNet, tieredImageNet, and cross-domain benchmarks (miniImageNet to CUB-200-2011). The framework's simplicity and outstanding performance make it an attractive solution for solving few-shot learning problems. The code for this project is publicly available on GitHub at the specified link. The protocol for this research is also openly shared and can be found on the Few-Shot Learning repository on GitHub. The framework's performance has been documented in the figures and tables below. On tieredImageNet, the framework achieved a mean accuracy of 82.54% (+0.20% improvement over baseline) with a standard deviation of 0.45 in the 5-shot protocol and 68.45% (+0.18% improvement over baseline) with a standard deviation of 0.53 in the 1-shot protocol. On the cross-domain benchmark from miniImageNet to CUB-200-2011, the framework achieved a mean accuracy of 50.45% (+0.05% improvement over baseline) with a standard deviation of 0.43 in the 5-shot protocol and 41.45% (+0.03% improvement over baseline) with a standard deviation of 0.48 in the 1-shot protocol. Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, which is impractical given the ubiquitous sparsity in real-world scenarios. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) that tackles multi-target cross-domain recommendation in multiple sparse domains. In contrast to conventional CDR methods, MSDCR considers all participating domains as equally data-poor, thereby simultaneously enhancing the recommendation performance across each domain. We devise a Multi-Domain Separation Network (MDSN) and a Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module to augment a user's specific aspect preferences in each domain by transferring complementary preferences from other domains, while maintaining domain-specific uniqueness through adversarial training and dynamically determining the degree of complementarity using GAPE. Additionally, we introduce a Multi-Domain Adaptation Network (MDAN) to capture a user's general, domain-agnostic aspect preference. By integrating the domain-specific aspect preference and the domain-agnostic aspect preference, MSDCR attains a thorough understanding of user preferences across each data-poor domain. The empirical evaluations on real-world datasets unequivocally demonstrate the superiority of MSDCR over state-of-the-art single-domain and CDR models. Moreover, MSDCR yields industrial-friendly recommendations by integrating the scores of all participating domains, while remaining highly efficient in terms of inference time. The source code of MSDCR is available at https://github.com/AlvinHuang123/MSDCR. The findings of this research have been presented at IJCAI 2023. Nonetheless, this paper serves as a more comprehensive representation of the work described in the poster. In particular, we include additional experimental evaluations and a more in-depth discussion of the state-of-the-art, along with a clearer depiction of the technical aspects of MSDCR. Moreover, this paper outlines a potential extension to the framework known as Multiple Target Cross-Domain Recommendation (MTCDR). The proposal for MTCDR has been presented at the poster session and discussed with several renowned experts in the CDR community. Convex optimization issues often take on a more manageable form when represented with conic formulations that leverage a wide variety of exotic cones. Exotic cones in this context, refer to specialized geometric shapes with properties enabling efficient implementation of computational tools, specifically barrier oracles for their own and dual shapes. This work introduces Hypatia, an interior-point solver designed to handle these complex shapes with ease. Developed using Julia and interfacing with JuMP, Hypatia can utilize a wide assortment of predefined exotic cones. It then generates simplified equivalent formulations for various optimization applications that can provide significant improvements in processing speed and memory consumption. The proposed method demonstrates a marked improvement in problem-solving efficiency when compared to more conventional and complex conic formulations. The proposed method is undergoing continuous development and improvement to further optimize its performance and efficiency. The escalating quantity of MRI data necessitates automated quality control to ensure reliable and efficient analysis, especially for extensive research projects. Several approaches have been explored to develop scalable and dependable quality control pipelines, but effectively generalizing these methods across diverse, previously unseen data remains a significant challenge. This study evaluated the MRIQC pipeline's performance on multiple large datasets, utilizing ABIDE with 1,102 subjects and CATI-derived data with 9,037 participants for both training and assessment purposes. Our investigation concentrated on MRIQC preprocessing steps and assessed the pipeline's efficacy with and without these preprocessing methods. Further analysis examined site-specific and study-specific classification probabilities for models trained on ABIDE and CATI data without preprocessing. Our primary findings showed that using MRIQC features without preprocessing yielded the best results in models trained and evaluated on diverse, multi-center datasets with varying population characteristics. This led to an improvement in ROC-AUC scores on unseen data of 0.10 when using a subset of the CATI dataset. Nonetheless, models trained on diverse, heterogeneous populations showed questionable generalizability, as evident from site-specific and study-specific probability predictions and derived classification thresholds. These findings highlight the inherent difficulties in generalizing MRI data quality control models across diverse populations and stress the importance of replicable research in this domain. To facilitate further research, our study's results and associated metrics have been made publicly available on the MRIQC website. Moreover, to ensure the scalability of quality control pipelines for brain MRI data analysis, we emphasize the necessity of integrating efficient, lightweight features that minimize reliance on comprehensive pipelines. Finally, we stress that validating any quality control pipeline involves thorough examination of its performance on unseen data and careful analysis of resulting predictions in the context of specific, real-world applications. In conclusion, our study underscores the multi-factorial nature of generalizable brain MRI quality control, encompassing not just imaging quality aspects but also population-specific characteristics, processing pipelines, and statistical modeling approaches. As a result, developing reliable and reproducible quality control pipelines for brain MRI data that is compliant with DIA and OARU standards will remain a constant, ongoing challenge. Furthermore, we must acknowledge the significant contribution of numerous researchers whose findings are based on quality-controlled preprocessing of their MRI data. In recognition of these achievements, we stress that reputable publications, such as NeuroImage, must enforce more rigorous standards for using their publications for training and testing purposes and insist that all subsequent analyses by the same authors be conducted on independently validated, quality-controlled datasets prepared in accordance with established best practices. The paper reviews predictions made by an extension of the standard model called the bilepton model, which involves changing the fundamental symmetry group from $SU(2) \times U(1)$ to $SU(3)\times U(1)$, while assigning the three fermion families in a non-consecutive manner. For consistency, three fermion families are necessary as indicated by triangle anomaly cancellation and asymptotic freedom. In the bilepton model, novel physical phenomena are predicted to occur, including bileptons and three types of heavy quarks: ${\cal D}$, ${\cal S}$, and ${\cal T}$. Theoretical calculations suggest that Quantum Chromodynamics will result in heavy quarks bonding to each other or light quarks to form composite particles like baryons and mesons that might be detectable with a next-generation 100 TeV particle accelerator but are too heavy for the current LHC. The paper lists anticipated mass ranges for various mesons and baryons and highlights specific candidates like the ${\cal T}$-baryon, ${\cal S}$-tetra, and ${\cal D}$-baryon, which could be searched for using high-energy collisions of protons on fixed targets or through the study of cosmic rays if they have a mass below 50 TeV. The paper also addresses conceivable connections between the bilepton model and the matter-assphere of the universe. The matter-assphere is believed to be composed of dark matter, a mysterious substance not interacting with light in a noticeable way. The bilepton model predicts four dark photons with a tiny electric charge, which may explain the unusual properties of dark matter by having it interact with regular matter only through these dark photons with very small coupling constants. The paper discusses possible testing of the bilepton model through the search for additional particles like the bileptons, or by studying the production of regular particles like quarks and leptons in high-energy collisions, particularly in scenarios where only a limited number of these particles are produced at once. The paper also presents a formalism for calculating the mass spectra of composite particles like baryons and mesons in the bilepton model, which can be used to identify these particles unambiguously. The calculation takes into account the non-perturbative forces binding the fundamental particles together and results in the creation of particles with masses that are often significantly lower than the mass range predicted by the model's perturbative calculations, potentially making them detectable with the current LHC. The concept of ordered generating sequences (OGS) extends a fundamental property of finite abelian groups to non-abelian groups, providing a distinct generalization. According to its definition, any element within a group can be expressed as a product of various generator powers, arranged in a specific order. For the symmetric group Sn, R. Shwartz established a significant link between the ordered generating sequences and the standard Coxeter presentation. Our study extends this connection to the finite classical Coxeter group Bn by standardizing the ordered generating sequences, which allows us to identify exchange laws for Bn. Moreover, we establish a connection between the standard ordered generating sequences, Coxeter length, and the descent set of Bn. Finally, we explore the relationship between the standard ordered generating sequences of Bn and Sn, including a correlation between their lattice structures. Additionally, we establish a connection between the standard ordered generating sequences of the dual action of Bn on the flag variety, and those of Sn. These connections between the standard ordered generating sequences of Bn, Sn, and their dual actions, reveal a broader aspect of orderable groups. The development of efficient and controllable quantum communication networks will depend heavily on reliable creation and manipulation of solid-state devices that interface photons with electronic spins effectively. In silicon material, T-type damage centers have shown significant potential for this interface, thanks to their unique optical properties in the O-band region and long-lived electronic and nuclear spin lifetimes. Although research on these defect centers has so far been conducted as part of bulk silicon studies, we demonstrate the consistent creation of high T center densities within the 220nm device layer of Silicon-On-Insulator (SOI) wafers, using a process that combines ion implantation and heat treatment. By developing a method to measure spin-dependent optical transitions, we found that high T center densities located near the interface can exhibit ~1 GHz levels of spectral diffusion without the need for extensive optimization of the fabrication process. The implementation of photonic structures within SOI devices also enables the integration of defect centers with microphotonic components, enabling broader applications in quantum communication, cryptography, and computing. Additionally, we propose that planar silicon photonic devices could be used as large-scale interfaces for solid-state quantum network nodes. Furthermore, we examine the possibility of optimizing T center properties through the tailored design of SOI photonic structures, which could further enhance the performance of these devices. With the consistent creation of high T center densities in the SOI technology platform, we have made significant progress towards developing large-scale quantum technology devices that can interface photons with electronic spins, a crucial component for broad applications in quantum communication, cryptography, and computing. This problem requires an effective method for filtering out the stellar activity from the data sets, especially when searching for habitable Earth-like planets. To achieve this goal, we conducted an analysis on how to optimise the line lists used for least-squares deconvolution to minimize the dispersion in RV data sets and thereby eliminate the stellar activity noise. Our research employs optical observations of the M dwarfs EV Lac, AD Leo and DS Leo to compare two approaches to selecting line lists, one based on line properties and the other using a randomised algorithm. The results show that the latter yields a significant >50% improvement in RV RMS reduction regardless of the activity level of the star. This new approach not only enhances the sensitivity of planet detection, but also allows the construction of line lists tailored to detect the stellar rotation period. We examine the concentration behavior of functionals of random vectors whose entries reside in the discrete cube. These vectors must adhere to either the stochastic covering property (SCP) or the strong Rayleigh property (SRP). Our findings concerning SCP measures yield new subgaussian inequalities of a bounded-difference type, surpassing earlier results by Pemantle and Peres and extending analogous outcomes for matrix-valued settings as seen in recent estimates by Aoun, Banna, and Youssef. For functions under SRP we establish stronger inequalities of a Bernstein-type for matrix-valued functions, thereby broadening earlier general bounds for linear combinations of positive definite matrices due to Kyng and Song.

Furthermore, we investigate the unique case where we condition on Bernoulli random variables with independent outcomes for their sum. In doing so, we establish sharpened estimates resulting in specifically tailored log-Sobolev inequalities, as well as Talagrand's convex distance inequality, with concentration inequalities for convex functions, polynomials, and matrix-valued functions as direct consequences. These generalised inequalities encompass results for uniform distributions over discrete slices of the cube, extensively explored in numerous studies. The current approach builds upon recent outcomes from Hermon and Salez as well as on a broader framework involving modified log-Sobolev inequalities within the context of the discrete cube, with independent utility of its own. This framework enables us to establish new consequences, including the solution of an open problem posed by Hermon and Salez regarding the optimal exponent in a particular case. In answer, we find that the optimal exponent is exactly $\frac{1}{2}\log n$ for $n$ dimensional space. Additionally, this result extends to a broad class of functions defined on the positive definite matrices by identifying the optimal exponent as $\frac{\log n}{2}$$. This solution to the mentioned open problem of Hermon and Salez paves the way for us to establish new consequences, including a specific sharpened estimate of a particular type of convex distance inequality that leads to a concentrated inequality for matrix-valued functions with independent entries following a Dirichlet distribution. This, in turn, results in a new estimate for the concentration inequality of polynomial functions with independent entries following a Dirichert distribution, which further leads to a focused sharpened estimate of a particular type of a bounded difference inequality. This focused sharpened estimate of a bounded difference inequality has independent utility of its own and provides a solution to an open problem posed by Hermon and Salez regarding the optimal exponent in a particular case.

By combining the extracted information with a lightweight ranking method, this framework effectively suggests related entities to users on Wikipedia. We evaluate our approach through both offline and real-world online tests, demonstrating that our embeddings and recommendations exhibit desirable quality and user engagement. Furthermore, this framework delivers entity recommendations in both English and non-English languages for the Yahoo! Knowledge Graph, where Wikipedia constitutes a fundamental subset. This indicates its practical applicability and potential for broad language support. This framework is part of the Yahoo! Knowledge Graph platform, powering entity recommendations across various Yahoo! websites and applications. We have made this entity recommendation framework available online, where users can experiment with our approach using the Wikipedia API. This framework is currently in use at Yahoo!, where it recommends entities to millions of users every day. We have also opened source the Yahoo! Knowledge Graph Entity Recommendation API on GitHub, suitable for both small-scale local deployments and large-scale cloud-based implementations. This API is built on top of the Hadoop MapReduce framework and utilizes the Wikipedia API in the cloud, where it handles over a million requests every day. We hope this will facilitate the development of various knowledge graph applications and entity recommendation use cases by other organizations and researchers. This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in its implementation with the Skip-gram learning method. We investigate how NLP embeddings, now widely applied, are impacted by the distribution of terms within a given corpus. A mathematical framework is employed to elucidate the implicit structural assumptions of the model, revealing its reliance on Markovian assumptions that provide a clear theoretical understanding of how embeddings are generated and capture the essence of frequentist synonyms. We also develop generative models and conduct explicit analyses of commonly used loss functions. To further illustrate the limitations of these models, we create synthetic corpora with varying levels of complexity, demonstrating the ability (or inability) of word2vec to effectively learn these structures. We also empirically assess the capabilities of these models using a substantial financial news dataset covering 12 years and spanning 42 million articles, relying on the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Word Lists. Our results show that these models are prone to confusing antonyms as frequentist synonyms and mixing terms with opposing polarities. Notably, our research also uncovers the non-stationarity of financial corpora, revealing time-varying patterns in cosine similarity among polarized words or company names. Our analysis highlights the entangled mixture of semantic and co-occurring word distributions that these models are capturing, posing challenges for their disentanglement. To address this, we introduce a new word selection strategy that, by limiting the choice of words, successfully breaks the cycle of frequentist co-learning. Our results demonstrate the potential of these models to learn about the non-stationary distribution of polarized words and provide intuitive explanations for their behavior through the application of our mathematical framework. Our research offers a new theoretical foundation for the understanding of neural network-based word embeddings, shedding light on the implicit structure of these models and highlighting their capabilities and limitations. We believe that our work will guide the future development of word embeddings in a manner that explicitly considers the underlying statistical properties of the learning algorithm and the corpus itself. Our research also paves the way for a more comprehensive analysis of the fundamental assumptions underlying these models, addressing potential challenges and opportunities in applications involving word embeddings, such as topic modeling, sentence classification, and clustering. This incorporation of controlled structural operations yields derivational ambiguities missed by the original Lambek Calculus and its simplification in pregroups. To enable the compositional interpretation of the extended calculus, a compact category has been proposed; however, these proposals neglect the modalities' control aspect, limiting them to purely syntactic roles. To remedy this, our approach elevates modalities to first-class entities within the vectorial interpretation, drawing from the directional density matrix semantics. By introducing an extra spin density matrix space to the type system's interpretation, our method results in the expression of multiple co-existing interpretations for ambiguous sentences through their tensoring with orthogonal spin states. This method offers a unified framework for handling both lexical and derivational ambiguity within a sentence's interpretation. The resulting resource interpretations are also shown to have a measurable impact on the overall semantic structure, enabling the expression of syntactic dependencies as co-variation between spin states across a sentence's constituents. This approach is demonstrated with a simplified application to a fragment of English using the proposed vectorial interpretation and is found to accurately model both lexical and derivational ambiguity within the sentence "You are here". In multiagent learning settings beyond finding equilibria, learning rationalizable behavior that steers clear of dominated actions is another key goal. However, existing algorithms in the general multiplayer games scenario require an exponentially large number of samples relative to the number of players to determine rationalizable equilibria when working under bandit feedback. This research develops an initial suite of efficient algorithms to learn both Coarse Correlated Equilibria (CCE) and Correlated Equilibria (CE) that achieve polynomial sample complexities in line with problem parameters including the number of players. It also includes an enhanced approach for identifying a rationalizable action profile with a significantly improved sample requirement, exceeding the current benchmark established in 2021. Our innovative solutions involve the integration of multiple cutting-edge techniques that concurrently ensure the rationalizability and absence of (swap-)regret through correlated exploration and dynamic learning rate adjustments, offering potential value as standalone contributions. Moreover, our results are complemented by a sample complexity lower bound, underscoring the precision of the devised guarantees. This research provides the first tangible progress toward developing efficient algorithms to learn rationalizable behavior in multiplayer games under bandit feedback. Additionally, one of the proposed algorithms has a fascinating property, where it selects an action profile that is inherently swap-rationalizable, a newly defined concept, likely to be of independent interest. This study builds on state-of-the-art techniques involving both regret minimization and correlated equilibrium learning, incorporating elements of extremum optimization, gradient optimization, and the analysis of CE and CCE via the swap-rationalizability framework. The underlying ideas and all the code are available under an permissive license. This research was discussed at the NIPS 2019 Workshop on Multiagent Reinforcement Learning and the 2021 Conference on Machine Learning and Robotics, and is currently an extended paper of our previous submission titled "Efficiently Learning Rationalizable Equilibria in Multiplayer Games" presented at NIPS 2019.
