Initial findings from a measurement of the spin asymmetry of the top quark, 
relevant to the top quark's polarization, have been reported for events 
resulting from $t$-channel single top quark production. The data, derived from 
proton-proton collisions at 8 TeV and with a total luminosity of 19.7 fb^-1, 
included events characterized by an isolated muon. By comparing experimental 
data to theoretical models, the signal and background components were quantified, 
enabling a measurement of the differential cross-section of an angular observable 
correlated with the top quark's polarization, taking into account detection biases. 
The results revealed a spin asymmetry value of 0.26, with a 95% confidence interval, 
which does not differ significantly from the standard model's predicted value of 0.44. 
This value is relevant to studying the top quark's polarization. 
Moreover, this study set a precedent for analyzing top quark and Higgs boson 
interactions. The research also facilitated the development of methods 
to measure the top quark's polarization and that of the W boson in other processes. 
These methods may be applied to 13 TeV and higher energy collisions. 
The results of this study have been published in the journal Physical Review Letters

Miller and Sheffield introduced the concept of an imaginary surface as a pairing of subdomains of the complex plane and associated Gaussian free fields under conformal equivalence. Specifically, they considered the relationship between these pairings and chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution. This paper develops Gaussian free field-valued processes in the upper half-plane and the first orthant of the complex plane, establishing their connection to multiple SLE evolving in time on these domains. We demonstrate that such connections can be made locally by driving multiple SLE with the Dyson model on the real line and the Bru-Wishart process on the positive reals, respectively. Ultimately, these pairings yield domains that evolve in time and associated Gaussian free fields. We also establish the relationship between these implementations and the original idea of imaginary surfaces, confirming that our domains and Gaussian free fields correspond to Miller and Sheffield's framework. Additionally, we derive statistics for the growth rates of these domains and estimate their conformal equivalence classes. Finally, we observe that our implementations provide a new means of generating conformal growth processes directly, without requiring the use of Riemann surfaces or Loewner equations. Instead, our approach is rooted in the underlying stochastic processes that define these systems. We anticipate that this new perspective will be valuable in studying and analyzing these systems. Lastly, we discuss potential extensions of our findings to multiple SLE driven by more comprehensive Dyson models and the Wickita-MacBrien process. Ultimately, we anticipate that such extensions will significantly advance our understanding of the underlying physics and mathematics of these systems. In particular, we expect that multiple SLE driven by the Dyson model on the full real line will result in domains that are conformally equivalent to the upper half-plane and associated Gaussian free fields that are harmonic in the upper half-plane. Similarly, we expect that multiple SLE driven by the Bru-Wishart process on the positive reals will result in domains that are conformally equivalent to the first orthant of the complex plane and associated Gaussian free fields that are harmonic in the first orthant. We present a novel universal method for detecting multiple types of dynamic behavior,
including stable and traveling chimera states using a dynamically adjusted measure of
coherence. This method automatically identifies and differentiates between synchronized
clusters, traveling wave patterns, chimera states, and asynchronous states. Additionally,
it is capable of determining the number of clusters present in cluster synchronization
situations. To further enhance our method, we developed a new technique for measuring the
speed of traveling chimera states. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method using a
specific example of a ring network composed of type II Morris-Lecar neurons with asymmetric
nonlocal inhibitory connections, where a diverse range of coherent and wave states are
identified. Notably, we propose that our method is robust for networks of phase oscillators and
generalizable to a broader class of relaxation oscillator networks. We outline the theoretical
justification for this proposal. The proposed method is executed using a user-friendly Python
package available at https://github.com/RKumar-Physics/Coherence-method. The code can be
easily adapted for application to other network connectivity configurations. The package includes
a main function for identifying coherent and wave states in the specific Morris-Lecar network
mentioned in this study, as well as two other main functions for (i) determining the number of
clusters in cluster synchronization scenarios and (ii) measuring the speed of traveling chimera
states. The proposed method provides a valuable solution for the complex problem of identifying
multi-cluster coherent and wave states in network dynamics. The executive summary of this study
has been presented at the 2019 EPS Conference on Physics of Complex Systems in Budapest, Hungary.

The proposed method relies on simulations of interactions between high-energy photons and the Sun's magnetic field, utilizing the PRESHOWER program with significant modifications. Distributed storage systems rely on replication to enhance both performance and reliability, but ensuring low latency data access requires handling updates without prior coordination. Asynchronous updates inevitably lead to conflict resolution issues with concurrent changes. A specific technique addressing this challenge is the Conflict-free Replicated Data Type (CRDT). Despite existing CRDT designs' complexity and difficulty to adapt to other data types, there's a clear need for a design framework to facilitate creating new CRDTs with consistency. We propose the RWF, a Remove-Win design framework that utilizes a conflict-resolution approach to update conflicts, allowing its use across various data types. Through two practical applications using Redis, RWF showcases its effectiveness and performance in developing new CRDTs that can handle conflicts efficiently. Furthermore, RWF's design provides a solid foundation for adapting existing CRDTs, making it a valuable framework for building high-performance distributed storage systems. With increasing interest in distributed systems and CRDTs, RWF is poised to become a valuable resource for developers working on distributed storage platforms. Understanding how genomic elements affect specific traits through genome-wide association studies remains complex due to the sheer number of available annotations. We've developed a statistical approach to pinpoint relevant genomic elements, based on associations across the entire genome, by identifying patterns of influence in trait-associated SNPs. This approach can incorporate multiple annotation types and has been successfully applied to eighteen human traits such as blood, platelet counts, metabolism-related disorders, height, obesity and a bowel disease, by examining 450 distinct genomic features across one hundred plus tissues and cells types. Our results show that protein-coding regions influence traits to a degree of up to twenty percent, in comparison with two percent, in a wide range of cases and demonstrate specific patterns of depleted and enriched regions associated with different traits and SNPs that target repressed or accessible regions specifically within certain cell types. Deep neural network approaches have achieved great success in various AI tasks, particularly in image recognition tasks, yet some challenges remain unresolved. The issue of processing continuous visual data streams and dealing with unbalanced datasets in the learning process continues to persist. Past research has tackled these issues independently, despite their concurrent presence in real-world applications. In this work, we address the challenge of learning incrementally from datasets that are not only unbalanced but also grow over time. We examine algorithms that rely on fixed deep neural network architectures and employ bounded memory to retain examples from previously encountered classes throughout the learning process. It can be demonstrated that any knot diagram can be converted into a trivial unknot through a sequence of unknotting operations, combined with some variations in the diagram configuration, which are referred to as Reidemeister moves. In this context, we explore a privacy-preserving approach called federated learning that enables several entities to train a robust machine learning model jointly, without exchanging sensitive information about their data. Based on how entities cooperate, FL can be categorized into two primary forms - horizontal and vertical FL. The former involves participants who collaborate using identical data attributes, while in the latter, entities with overlapping sample IDs collaborate using different features. Given its versatility, vertical FL is deemed particularly suitable for collaborative training by major enterprises. Here we concentrate on FL and delve into possible privacy breaches in actual VFL implementations. Two applicable attacks were created by us - one is called a reverse multiplication attack designed to circumvent logistic regression, while the other, known as a reverse sum attack, targets XGBoost protocols. Our empirical study validates that both attacks are successful, effective, evasive, and straightforward - they do not diverge from the predefined protocol, nor do they lower the model's accuracy; even with data encrypted. Additionally, we found out the stolen information can train a new machine learning classifier which is just as accurate as the one trained using actual data, without knowing beforehand much about the target user. Our analysis highlights potential preventive strategies, while revealing challenges that might give rise to several exciting research opportunities. Despite initial intuition that a simple 3-band d-only model would suffice, our study shows that this assumption can lead to inaccuracies. For instance, a more complex spectral structure is revealed when the model incorporates additional correlated orbitals, a phenomenon not seen in the simpler model. Utilizing the Fork Tensor Product State impurity solver allows us to resolve high-frequency differences and obtain more precise results. Our results indicate that using this solver for full 5-band DMFT calculations yields spectral structures consistent with experiments, showcasing the solver's ability to perform such complex calculations directly on the real-frequency axis. Nonetheless, the DMFT-Linux package still demonstrates speed advantages when using the Zuber algorithm. Nonetheless, the additional computational resources required for the Fork Tensor Product State solver may limit its widespread adoption. Our study suggests that further optimization of this solver is still necessary. Our research was carried out at the Max-Planck Institute for Physics, where our lead author is currently affiliated. This research focuses on creating resilient Molmer-Sorensen gates using trapped ions arranged in a line, incorporating Gaussian amplitude modulation and a consistent laser frequency. We chose a frequency that maintains balanced entanglement accumulation across all motion modes to provide a significant degree of protection against frequency errors, particularly for long chains of ions. A demonstration of this method is performed on a chain of three ions, achieving an average reduction of under one percent from peak precision within a twenty kilohertz range of frequency deviation, and the efficiency of this gate design is examined through numerical simulations on chains consisting of two to thirty-three ions. This efficient frequency robustness is crucial for combining Molmer-Sorensen gates with controlled motional state preparations, a vital resource for fault-tolerant quantum computing. Additionally, this work offers an understanding of balanced entanglement generation across multiple motion modes within trapped ion systems. Furthermore, this research can be used to develop frequency-robust lattice gauge gates, a novel application. This innovation was found to be applicable to both nitrogen and calcium-based quantum computing setups. Finally, this work demonstrates the potential for robust quantum processing using trapped ions by addressing the long-standing challenge of efficient, fault-tolerant quantum computing through a combination of controlled motional state preparations, Molmer-Sorensen gates, and parity checks, specifically highlighting the critical role of resilient gate operations in this process. Specifically, this implementation can serve as a prototype for a surface code quantum computing system. Moreover, this work includes a discussion on further optimization strategies for this type of gate in addition to thorough numerical simulations of quantum processing workflows. Ultimately, this research confirms that frequency-robust Molmer-Sorensen gates are essential for building robust quantum processors and highlights the value of balanced entanglement generation across all motion modes within trapped ion systems. Furthermore, this work has been pending discussion and agreement among the co-authors for an extended period. We've developed families of three-dimensional $\mathbb{Q}$-factorial, non-toric terminal Fano varieties of considerable depth, corresponding to 54 distinct mutation classes in the realm of Laurent polynomials. From the perspective of mirror symmetry, these high-dimensional non-toric varieties establish the Fano/Landau-Ginzburg connection for our current knowledge limits. Building upon this foundation, 46 more $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano threefolds have been constructed, with their depth spanning between 10 and 19. Among these, certain examples will be expressed as toric complete intersections and others as Pfaffian varieties. Through the lens of the Gross-Hacking Keel Nakai theorem, we determine the complete set of symplectic and effective divisors for 17 of these three-dimensional $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano varieties. Moreover, several of these non-toric three-dimensional $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano varieties exhibit super Rural properties, meaning their volume exceeds the maximum value achievable by rationally connected varieties within the same dimension. As a side discovery, we identify two specific $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano threefolds whose complete intersection as variety pairs mirrors that of a certain pair of Calabi-Yau fourfolds. This, in turn, yields 55 distinct 3D $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano varieties in total, with 41 of them being uniquely identified. We've further extended these constructions to $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano varieties of higher dimensions, specifically dim 4 and 5, though the number of defined mutation classes remains too great for a comprehensive list in these dimensions. From the provided examples, it's evident that both rational and non-rational $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano varieties can arise through these constructions. Moreover, our work paves the way for further research in the field of Fano/Landau-Ginzburg physics. Reconstructing three-dimensional faces in complex real-world scenarios poses significant difficulties due to frequently missing or occluded facial details, particularly in images depicting large head orientations. This challenging problem is compounded by the extensive variability of head poses, which significantly expands the potential solution space and complicates modeling efforts. To break down this complex task into more manageable components, our approach focuses on modeling both pose and occlusion. In this regard, we introduce an end-to-end framework called SADRNet, which produces a face that varies based on the orientation and another face that remains invariant, then fuses these faces via a self-alignment mechanism informed by occlusion. Exhaustive testing of our proposed technique on the widely used AFLW2000-3D and Florence datasets shows substantial performance enhancements over existing top-ranking methods. Furthermore, our method exhibits superior robustness in handling real-world images. The code for our method has been made publicly available online. Despite achieving exceptional results, there is room for further improvement, as demonstrated by the stagnation of evaluation metrics on previously achieved highs. To facilitate continued progress, we release additional challenging datasets constructed from the Florence dataset, which includes 8000 face images characterized by extensive pose ranges and varying occlusions. Furthermore, we highlight the critical need for more robust vote counting methods, as well as provide data showcasing the limitations of OCR techniques, and make available the iOCR system alongside its source code for public use. Additionally, we invite stakeholders to collaborate with us in refining the iOCR system. 

In the United States, the accuracy of electoral ballot counting is paramount, as even the smallest margins can determine the outcome of an election. Unfortunately, traditional Optical Character Recognition techniques have inherent flaws that can lead to critical errors in vote tallying. These shortcomings stem from the typical testing used to validate OCR performance, which only identifies corrections for obvious spelling errors, neglecting more subtle misconversions such as incorrect character selection, missing digits, and misalignment due to inadequate font support. As a result, OCR's inadequacy in processing ballot counts has significant implications, especially considering the increasing reliance on automated vote counting systems and the difficulty of verifying the integrity of electronically tabulated votes. For instance, a renowned voting system's failure to accurately count presidential election votes in a particular state resulted in a recount, demonstrating the critical need for more reliable vote counting methods. Moreover, data analysis has revealed disturbing statistics on the frequency of scanning errors, further emphasizing the necessity for precise vote counting. Given these concerns, we believe that using the latest spell-checking technologies to enhance Optical Character Recognition can significantly enhance the accuracy of ballot count tabulation. Furthermore, we contend that such an approach not only addresses the specific challenges faced in vote counting but also provides a model for improving the precision of OCR in other domains. To that end, we have developed an Informed OCR system that incorporates these advanced spell-checking features, and through comprehensive testing have validated its superiority over traditional OCR methods. Additionally, we have made the iOCR system's source code publicly available, and we invite collaboration with other researchers and stakeholders to refine the system further. The iOCR system's code can be found at the provided repository link. The data analysis and evidence presented in this research are based on the development of an Informed OCR system for accurate ballot count tabulation, and we hope that it will contribute positively to the discussion on the importance of accurate vote counting. In recent years, significant progress made by large-scale models has underscored the relevance of statistical models featuring multiple parameters. Research has been conducted to evaluate linear models with numerous parameters in high-dimensional environments characterized by non-sparse data. These studies typically assume the independence of data samples, but the current research extends beyond this limitation by exploring a linear regression model with time series data under conditions of over-parameterization, where data samples are inherently interdependent. The study develops an interpolation-based estimator and associated risk theory that accommodates varying levels of data interdependence, infinite data dimensions lacking sparsity, and both short and long-memory processes. The theoretical risk analysis leverages the concept of integrated covariance along with non-degeneracy properties of autocorrelation matrices. The results demonstrate comparable risk convergence rates to those in independent settings for short-memory processes and significantly slower convergence rates for long-memory processes. The research also illustrates specific, applicable examples of dependent processes. The study's findings are complementary to those in independent settings, providing valuable insights into the behavior of linear models that leverage time series data. The research suggests that, despite potential difficulties in optimizer convergence, linear models can achieve interpolation-based risk minimization with time series data. The study's results are relevant to a broad range of applications that leverage linear models, including forecasting, exponential smoothing, and structural time series models. The research's findings on dependent processes enable the development of more accurate forecasts and model specifications. It then uses these corrected examples to update its model through transfer learning. In x-ray image analysis, identifying prohibited items contributes to maintaining public safety. However, the difficulty lies in detecting low-contrast, color-less objects which can result in unsatisfactory performance. Until now, there have been limited studies in this field due to the absence of high-quality specialized datasets. To bridge this gap, we introduce a novel dataset named High-quality X-ray (HiXray), which contains a comprehensive collection of 8 prohibited item categories and comprises 102,928 high-quality images. These images are extracted from real-world airport security inspections and annotated by experienced security personnel. Moreover, to enhance the accuracy of prohibited item detection, we introduce a Lateral Inhibition Module, which emulates the human ability to disregard irrelevant information and focus on distinguishing characteristics. By incorporating a flexible module and leveraging Bidirectional Propagation and Boundary Activation modules, LIM successfully minimizes noise and accentuates identifiable features from multiple directions. Experimental results on HiXray and OPIXray demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to existing detection approaches. Additionally, our research showcases the versatility of HiXray as a general-purpose dataset, yielding outstanding results in each prohibited item category. HiXray is currently the largest and highest-quality dataset specific to x-ray prohibited item detection, and our proposed LIM model provides compelling evidence that with advanced modules and proper data representation, it is possible to Accurately and Reliably Detect prohibited items. A newly defined polynomial, referred to as the nth toroidal colored Jones polynomial, is established for links in a thickened torus. Dubbed $J_n^T$, this polynomial demonstrates numerous properties similar to the original colored Jones polynomial, and notably displays volume conjecture behavior. By applying $J_n^T$, we prove the volume conjecture holds true for a specific link, and provide computational data suggesting it holds for additional links. Moreover, $J_n^T$ can be represented through two distinct constructions, a pseudo-operator invariant, and a construction rooted in the Kauffman bracket skein module of the torus. Notably, $J_n^T$ yields invariants for virtual and biperiodic links, providing an instance of volume conjecture behavior in a virtual link. Finally, we explore connections between $J_n^T$ and other invariants, including the toroidal Kauffman polynomial, and propose future research avenues for this new invariant. Additionally, we include an open problem related to the toroidal whitegraph conjecture.

Recent advancements in wireless communications research have led to increasing interest in the Intelligent Reflecting Surface (IRS) technology. Comprised of passive reflective components that can modulate the characteristics of incoming waveforms, such as phase, amplitude, frequency, and polarization, an IRS offers a means to actively control the characteristics of wireless channels. Given its promising properties, researchers are looking into the potential of incorporating IRS technology into radar systems to optimize target parameter estimation. This paper provides a theoretical basis for implementing IRS technology in radar systems, with a particular focus on scenarios where the line-of-sight (LOS) link between the radar and target is obstructed or weak. We investigate the potential of utilizing IRS technology to create a virtual non-line-of-sight (NLOS) link, enhancing radar performance and target parameter estimation. Through numerical simulations and comparative analyses under both optimized and non-optimized scenarios, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the IRS-provided virtual link in target parameter estimation when the LOS link strength is lower than a relative strength of $~10^{-1}$ in comparison to the NLOS link. Additionally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the development of optimized IRS protocols to achieve optimal target parameter estimation. Furthermore, we introduce the concept of dynamic polarization targeting, an area that provides opportunities for further research and advancement. With the former, we explore how selecting appropriate polarization targets on both the radar and the reflective surface can further enhance the efficacy of the virtual link, thereby improving target parameter estimation in scenarios where the LOS link strength is lower than a relative strength of $~10^{-1}$ in comparison to the NLOS link. On the other hand, we establish that selecting the same polarization target on both the radar and the reflective surface is optimal for target parameter estimation when the LOS link strength is higher than a relative strength of $10^{-1}$ in comparison to the NLOS link. Moreover, we investigate how the choice of radar wave form affects the accuracy of target parameter estimation in the presence of the strong LOS link, and demonstrate the effectiveness of both linearly independent waveforms such as BPSIN and Chirp in target parameter estimation. With the latter, we examine how the target parameter estimation performance in the presence of the weak LOS link can be enhanced by optimizing the phase shift matrix of the IRS, and validate the efficacy of both non-federated and federated learning approaches in achieving this optimization. We also explore the potential of utilizing both weak LOS and virtual NLOS links, and demonstrate the effectiveness of targets with high differential reflectivity in target parameter estimation

Yet, due to the random partitioning inherent in CV, estimated model performance exhibits significant variability. This unpredictability makes effective parameter tuning challenging, as it introduces substantial uncertainty into the choice of parameters. Moreover, our study reveals that the optimal parameters obtained are excessively sensitive to the manner in which the data is divided, often resulting in suboptimal solutions and significant difficulties in achieving reproducibility. In contrast, our research suggests employing the reduced variance j-k fold CV method, which involves conducting multiple independent assessments across K subgroups within the training set J times. The aim is to mitigate performance estimation's intrinsic instability and facilitate effective parameter tuning by prioritizing variance minimization over bias. In line with this principle, our study advocates for a smaller K than typically adopted and instead invests computational resources in increasing the value of J, as demonstrated across diverse NLP tasks including sentiment analysis, part-of-speech tagging and text classification. The introduced efficient variance-reduced 5-2 fold CV method has been made available as an open-source repository alongside this paper. Experimental results show models tuned using the proposed j-k fold CV method outperform those tuned using standard k-fold CV across all evaluated settings. Furthermore, model tuning using the proposed method achieves superior performance to individual optimal results obtained through an exhaustive search, reflecting the practical outcome of combining high quality parameters with low variance. Graph neural networks have excelled in multiple applications by leveraging relational data. These models combine node features with the graph structure, creating flexible and effective models, but they can be challenging to interpret due to their implicit representation of node interactions and graph connectivity. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach called Kedge, which involves explicitly reducing unnecessary graph edges by selectively removing neighboring nodes. By utilizing the Hard Kumaraswamy distribution for edge sparsification, Kedge enables a flexible integration with existing GNN models through gradient-based optimization. Experiments demonstrate that Kedge effectively prunes a substantial proportion of graph edges with minimal accuracy degradation. Notably, Kedge achieved a reduction of over 80% of edges on the PubMed dataset with only a 2% decrease in accuracy, indicating that node features have a more significant impact than graph connectivity. Furthermore, Kedge effectively mitigates the over-smoothing issue prevalent in deep GNNs by maintaining robust task performance even with multiple GNN layers. The code for Kedge is publicly available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/ghrua/Kedge. The framework is described in the paper, which has been accepted for presentation at the 28th ACM Joint Conference on Research in Computer Science, https://jpc.cs.tufts.edu/index.php/jpc/index/article/view/119. Additionally, the paper has been nominated for the Best Paper Award at the conference. The paper is also published in the Proceedings of the 28th ACM Joint Conference on Research in Computer Science, https://doi.org/10.1145/4501545.4501550. The research received support from the National Science Foundation through Grant IIS-1734254 and the University of Florida's Research Opportunity Fund. The authors are currently exploring extensions of the Kedge framework in the domains of computer vision and machine learning for natural language processing. The name Kedge is derived from the marine term 'to keed,' which means to trim or adjust sails in response to changing wind conditions. The name accurately reflects the action of a node feature distribution being adjusted in response to the Hard Kumaraswamy distribution's dependence on the graph's edge matrix. Under such circumstances, the classic estimator can be compromised by a relatively low number of inferences, essentially making it vulnerable to manipulation. A more resilient estimator was proposed, which, albeit requiring quadratically more queries in proportion to the sketch size, significantly enhances the safety by a factor of k (with k being the number of key components) when compared to prior studies on CountSketch sketches. Moreover, this enhanced estimator's performance aligns closely with that of traditional CountSketch when the vectors undergo random transformations. Notably, a new and efficient variant of the sketch was also introduced, which, while losing only a factor of two in proportion to the original dimension, still provides similar robustness. Furthermore, both designs can be applied to a broader category of moduli functions, thereby establishing a more general framework for searching the top elements of a given vector. The proposed solutions can also be applied to the problem of identifying the top columns of a matrix, for which a corresponding estimator was developed. Analytical properties of MEF are examined, and it is shown that MEF can be approximated through reinforcement learning and utilized as a penalty term in the penalized predictive control (PPC) algorithm, an adaptation of model predictive control (MPC). Key benefits of our approach include (1) reduced communication demands for operators, requiring only MEF information, (2) faster computational processing due to lower variable counts, and (3) lower operational costs, with certain assumptions indicating optimal performance. The proposed PPC is evaluated on an adaptive electric vehicle charging dataset, yielding superior outcomes compared to traditional MPC methods. The code for this study can be found at https://github.com/babonanni/realtime-aggregation. The investigation is further expanded to a multi-agent setting in Section 7 of the paper, where policies are shared across agents with minimal modification, leading to even greater efficiency gains. This modification, however, introduces an assumption of shared variability across individual MEF components, which may not hold in all cases. The proposed approach is ultimately applied to a practical context of EV charging in California, with the fully abstraced results shown in Figure 1 of the paper. One of the most intriguing phenomena in astrophysics is the common envelope (CE) phase of binary star evolution, where two stars are enveloped in the shedding material from one of them. This process triggers a shrinking of the orbit as the stars interact with the envelope. Ultimately, it can result in either mergers or further complex interactions, which can involve a mix of compact objects and stars. Certain CE scenarios, particularly those involving white dwarfs, can produce supernovae, while neutron star mergers can result in gamma-ray bursts, and all types of compact object mergers can produce gravitational waves. Predicting the end states of these CEs is challenging due to their diverse origins and the intricate processes involved, which are compounded by the need to consider many systems at once in population synthesis calculations. This difficulty often prompts the use of conservation principles such as angular momentum conservation to simplify complex scenarios, such as in the case of multiple star systems. This method allows for a simpler, more intuitive approach to understanding the behavior of these binary star systems, particularly in the study of higher order multiples which are increasingly being recognized as significant in the potential mergers of these stars. This particular work focuses specifically on the common envelope phase of binary stars, while an accompanying paper will explore the broader implications of this research for multiple star systems that undergo CE phases. This research introduces a new conservation principle based on the total specific angular momentum of all stars within a common envelope, which garners support from various studies of binary star interactions. This model distinguishes between the angular momentum contributed by the stars' internal processes and their orbital motion, with the total specific angular momentum remaining constant throughout the common envelope phase. This particular approach ensures that conservation of angular momentum holds true, even in the face of angular momentum being released from the envelope during the envelope ejection phase, which is governed by the conservation of energy. This research also introduces a new equation that describes the evolution of the orbital angular momentum, as well as a new equation that describes the evolution of the total specific angular momentum of all stars within a common envelope. This work also explores various potential outcomes of common envelope phases, particularly in the case of white dwarf companions, where the discovery of dozens of dead binary stars with white dwarfs provides valuable constraints, with these dead binary stars often exhibiting mass ratios that favor equality. These constraints, combined with considerations of conservation principles and the properties of compact objects, allow for the prediction of the outcomes of these common envelope phases, including both mergers and binary systems. This research investigates double Higgs boson production at future electron-positron colliders CLIC and ILC with TeV-scale energies within the framework of Effective Field Theories (EFTs), focusing on beyond-Standard Model Higgs physics. Initially, we consider the Higgs Effective Field Theory (HEFT) and then compare the predictions with the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT). Our primary analysis concerns the double Higgs production process in the two EFTs through the dominant subprocess $WW \to HH$. We calculate the cross-section of this subprocess for all polarization channels and relevant effective operators at various energies, and demonstrate how in the HEFT case, the cross-section primarily depends on two leading coefficients at these TeV scales. We then establish the equivalence between the dominant coefficients of the HEFT and SMEFT at the level of the scattering amplitude for this subprocess. In the subsequent analysis, we explore the detectability of the two leading HEFT coefficients at the two planned colliders CLIC (operating at 3 TeV, 5 ab$^{-1}$) and ILC (operating at 1 TeV, 8 ab$^{-1}$), and identify the accessible parameter regions by studying the predicted rates for the characteristic four bottom jet signatures with missing energy in the $b \bar b b \bar b \nu \bar \nu$ final state. In addition, we examine the effective operator sensitivity to the Higgs sector of a generic extra scalar field and validate the detectability of a specific mass scale $\Lambda$ associated with the HEFT at the two colliders for the relevant parameter regions. Finally, we highlight the importance of precise threshold corrections in the prediction of double Higgs production at these colliders, and the necessity of accounting for the interactions of heavy particles beyond the weak top quark approximation, particularly top quark pair production in the double Higgs decay channel which leads to $t \bar t HH$. We find that in the HEFT case, the dominant coefficient $|\kappa_{WW}|$ has a distinct impact on the cross-section of the subprocess $WW \to HH$ across various mass scales, whereas the influence of the second leading coefficient $C_H$ is notable solely at heavy particle thresholds. Using observations from KCWI and NOEMA, we studied a distant starburst galaxy, examining how star formation-driven gas outflows are linked to other properties of the galaxy. Our data show a nearly linear relationship between outflow mass and star formation rates, as well as a significant correlation between outflow mass and gas usage times. In regions of high star formation rates within the galaxy, the mass ejected through outflows actually exceeds the amount of gas converted into new stars, indicating a limit on how quickly gas can be turned into stars due to outflows. Our findings support the idea that outflows play a critical role in regulating the conversion of gas into stars, highlighting the need for further studies of outflows in galaxies across the universe. This research utilized observations from KCWI and NOEMA and includes data that can be accessed through the VLA Archive Library (VAL) and the National Radio Astronomy Archive (NRAO).

Current auto-tuning frameworks for computer systems face challenges due to their large configuration spaces and the difficulties associated with evaluating their performance. Recently, researchers have made progress in this area using probabilistic models in Structured Bayesian Optimization (SBO), a technique that rapidly converges to optimal configurations by exploiting expert-provided contextual information about the system's structure. Despite its effectiveness, the SBO approach has limited adoption due to the complexity involved in building probabilistic models. To address this issue, we introduce BoAnon, an SBO framework that enables the discovery of system structures from logs, allowing for the incorporation of expert knowledge. By combining this learned structure with expert-provided performance models and dependency information, BoAnon generates a probabilistic graph model. This model accelerates the optimization process, allowing BoAnon to identify efficient configurations significantly faster than existing methods. Through evaluation of a hardware architecture search problem, BoAnon demonstrates a notable improvement in energy-latency objectives, achieving a 5-7x factor improvement over the default architecture. The innovative approach of BoAnon, based on its contextual structure learning pipeline, now makes SBO applicable to various computer systems, such as databases and stream processors. Furthermore, BoAnon's expertise accumulation via contextual learning enables the discovery of valuable insights from performance logs, revealing that expert-tuned configurations often overlook structurally significant factors and instead focus on superficially important ones. By building on top of BoAnon's learned structure, future SBO studies can explore more efficient configurations and reduce the search space complexity. Additionally, BoAnon's expertise accumulation provides a foundation for addressing real-world challenges like system downtime, through the development of robust performance models capable of handling structural changes and anomalies. These models can be used to create adaptive configuration policies that balance efficiency and risk, taking into account the potential costs and benefits of switching configurations. As a result, systems engineers can rely on BoAnon to efficiently identify optimal configurations that minimize energy latency, reduce the risk of downtime, and provide a fair balance of performance and stability. Furthermore, BoAnon's expertise accumulation enables the discovery of valuable insights from performance logs, revealing that expert-tuned configurations often focus on structurally significant factors, such as system stability and adaptability, in addition to efficiency. This understanding propels the field forward, making it even more appealing for top researchers to participate and contribute to the advancement of auto-tuning technologies. Over the years, the availability of Linked Data has surged exponentially with more than 10,000 online datasets now available and formatted according to Linked Data standards, enabling seamless machine readability and interconnectivity.  While such datasets provide numerous opportunities, numerous applications remain hindered due to data of poor quality, significantly affecting tasks such as data integration, search, and interlinking.  Existing quality assessment techniques for Linked Data, although limited, suffer from decreased effectiveness with rising data sizes and become unmanageable for single-machine operations.  To address these challenges, our proposed DistQualityAssessment is an open-source, cluster-enabled implementation designed for comprehensive quality evaluation of large-scale RDF datasets, leveraging the processing capabilities of Apache Spark to distribute quality metrics computation.  This innovative, distributed in-memory approach allows for flexible metric extension via a provided quality assessment pattern and, through seamless integration with the SANSA framework, has been successfully applied in at least three external use cases, showcasing its superiority over existing methodologies.  With its source code available on GitHub, this project provides a crucial solution for the robust assessment of large-scale Linked Data.  In this research, we delve into the design choices made and the technical details of this highly scalable quality assessment framework. When working with data generated by random processes, an appropriate model is often employed for subsequent statistical analysis, but the standard method of maximum likelihood estimation is vulnerable to model imperfections and data contamination. As alternative methods without assumptions about a specific model typically lose efficiency, this paper introduces a robust procedure for estimating parameters in discrete data sets based on a well-known distance measure. Specifically, this method defines and evaluates minimum density power divergence estimators for independent increments and Markov processes, proving its consistency and providing distributional results in the context of dependent stochastic processes, ultimately showing the method's advantages in comparison to traditional maximum likelihood estimation for common processes like Poisson processes, Brownian motion with a drift and autoregressive models. The findings are illustrated through empirical examples and simulation data, revealing the method's efficiency and robustness to model errors and outliers. The research extends established results from the field, focusing on discrete data sets and dependent processes. The implementation of the technique is made available in an R package called MDPDE, enabling easy access to the method for general use. The package can be obtained from the CRAN website. The paper also introduces a new estimation procedure for generating models that can be extended to various statistical models, including regression models, time series and counting processes, enabling robust parameter estimation in these contexts. The package has an adaptable structure, allowing the easy inclusion of additional estimation methods for different models. This study presents temperature maps for electrons within one kiloparsec of three high-brightness Seyfert galaxies. The findings from Gemini's GMOS-IFU data, acquired at a spatial resolution of 110-280 parsecs, reveal temperature variations between 8000 to >30000 Kelvin. We discovered temperature ranges in these galaxies are significantly influenced by gas outflows producing shocks, particularly in Mrk 79 and Mrk 348, while photoionization processes fit the results for Mrk 607. The orientation of these shocks in Mrk 79 and Mrk 348 appears to be perpendicular to the axis of ionization, suggesting the potential for shock ionization to be observed more easily when obscured by a dusty torus. This implies that narrow ionization cones can coexist with wider shock patterns. These findings have implications for modeling gas dynamics and ionization processes in active galactic nuclei. We also propose a method to identify shocks using electron temperature maps, particularly in situations where other signatures of shocks are absent. This method can help researchers better understand gas processes in active galactic nuclei across various scales. Additionally, we observed a gas stream or spiral pattern in Mrk 79 and Mrk 348, which can contribute to the formation of narrow ionization cones and larger shock patterns. Further studies are needed to analyze these features over longer scales and at higher spectral resolution. This study is the fifth in a series examining the ionized gas distribution and chemistry in Seyfert galaxies, and it sets the stage for investigating these processes in broader samples of active galaxies through integral field unit observations. To address these shortcomings, we have developed Frisbee, a framework for the automated testing of IoT applications. By utilizing Kubernetes and virtual testbeds, Frisbee speeds up the testing process by streamlining the setup of distributed virtual environments and enabling complex 'what-if' scenario simulations. The creation of realistic traffic scenarios through automation is the primary focus.
Currently used approaches insert virtual characters into the environment using predefined rules but struggle to capture the intricate nature of actual traffic conditions, ultimately resulting in a gap between artificially generated scenes and real ones. As a consequence, these simulation tools lack the required level of accuracy necessary to train self-driving vehicles. Detecting three-dimensional objects at great distances, or far-field detection, is a crucial capability for autonomous vehicles operating at highway speeds. They need to be able to spot obstacles from afar in order to allow enough time for the vehicle to stop. Unfortunately, the majority of existing evaluation benchmarks, like nuScenes, don't emphasize this challenge because they only assess performance within a certain range. There are a couple of key reasons for this - firstly, annotating distant objects can be difficult because lidar sensors typically only return a limited number of data points at such great distances, with almost 50% of objects more than 50m away from the sensor containing zero data points. Secondly, the commonly used metrics for evaluating three-dimensional detection tasks apply the same tolerance thresholds to near and far objects, which isn't aligned with either human vision or the disparities seen in stereo images. As a result, the task of far-field three-dimensional detection has not been given the attention it deserves. For instance, it has long been believed that high-resolution RGB sensors are key to detecting distant objects, but a more in-depth analysis shows that lidar-based approaches outperform RGB counterparts on the existing leaderboards. To better assess this challenge, we created a new evaluation protocol and a far-field validation dataset based on the well-annotated scenes from the nuScenes dataset. We compared a variety of three-dimensional detection methods with this protocol and the results verify the widely-held assumption that high-resolution RGB does enhance detection in the far-field. We've also proposed an innovative fusion approach for detecting distant objects, which combines the capabilities of RGB and lidar sensors using non-maximum suppression, yielding significant improvements over state-of-the-art 3D detectors in far-field scenarios. Our approach has great potential for detecting distant objects in other applications that rely on the evaluation of nuScenes-val-far. In order to allow other researchers to build upon these findings, we've released our code and the detailed protocol for this task on Far3Det, the benchmark used for evaluating far-field detection on nuScenes-val-far. Unlike typical three-dimensional detection benchmarks, nuScenes-val-far requires the evaluation of multiple objects in a single scene, as well as the detection of distant objects with small data points. Determining scene flow involves calculating the three-dimensional motion trajectories for specific points within an animated three-dimensional environment. Motion trajectory data has been found beneficial for downstream tasks like activity classification and obstacle detection. Nonetheless, obtaining precise data through LiDAR sensors and stereo cameras is laborious due to its computationally intensive annotation process. We address this issue by presenting a 3D scene flow benchmark alongside a novel self-supervised training framework for estimating scene flow. The benchmark comprises progressively complex datasets to study the estimation process, beginning from a singular object in motion to complex real-world environments. We introduce a unique method, Adversarial Metric Learning, for self-supervised flow estimation where two models work in tandem: one performs flow estimation and another derives a latent metric to differentiate the altered points from the target point cloud, achieved through a Multi-Scale Triplet loss calculation using intermediate feature vectors. We leverage our benchmark to gain insight into various models and our proposed framework, finding that our method successfully preserves spatial coherence and detailed geometric structures, whereas many self-supervised baselines fail in this aspect. Nonetheless, overcoming occlusions remains a significant challenge. We anticipate our benchmark to contribute significantly to the development of robust scene flow estimation algorithms. This property is equivalent to even-2-factorability (E2F), which means all the graph's 2-factors are even cycles. We can disregard bipartite cubic graphs, as they automatically satisfy the E2F condition, thus our focus shifts to non-bipartite cubic graphs. A non-bipartite cubic graph with the PMH-property will satisfy the E2F condition, even though it is not a necessary condition. We then determine the parameters under which the papillon graph exhibits the PMH-property or E2F condition, as well as proving no two distinct papillon graphs have identical structure. This paper introduces a new method called Timeloops for automating system call filtering policies in containerized applications. During operation, Timeloops can automatically determine the system calls a program should be permitted to make and prevent unauthorized system calls from being made. In addition, Timeloops rectifies various shortcomings of static analysis-based techniques, such as the creation of highly precise filters for programs in languages like JavaScript, PHP, and Python. Developed using standard, reliable technologies, Timeloops features a simple and efficient design comprising less than 500 lines of code. Our research showcases the capabilities of Timeloops by implementing system call learning for individual services and a couple of benchmark applications employing Python Flask, Apache Thrift, and Memcached, among other technologies. Furthermore, we show that Timeloops' performance, despite generating a more limited system call filter, is comparable to that of an unsecured system. The project's code has been made open-source and is available on GitHub under the Permissive Public License. In practical terms, this means that while the code can be used for free, the developers who use it do not have to make any contributions in return. We have also introduced a new concept called path-based learning, which combines elements from both static and dynamic analysis to create system call filters. This new approach results in the generation of more comprehensive system call filters, even for programs written in languages like JavaScript, PHP, and Python. This technique's efficiency, however, is inferior to that of Timeloops. Nevertheless, we believe that path-based learning represents a significant step in the automatic creation of system call filters for containerized applications and could potentially serve as a foundation for future research aimed at enhancing the security of cloud and on-premise computing platforms. The dynamics of soccer games mean even small moments can greatly impact the outcome, making players, coaches, and scouts intensely curious about how to act effectively in pivotal situations. In such moments, teams may lose possession of the ball or score, leading to a desire for an optimal course of action. To address this need, we propose a novel way to describe the game's state and a batch reinforcement learning method to train a strategic policy network. By analyzing the contextual aspects of situations, the network can provide the best action to increase the team's chances of scoring, drawing on real soccer data from InStat. In a large-scale experiment with 104 European soccer matches, we found our optimized strategy consistently outperformed the standard policy, and it even mimicked the behavior observed in real games. Notably, we observed situations where actions like committing a foul or kicking the ball out of bounds might be preferable to shooting, showcasing the importance of nuanced decision-making. The optimized network also exhibited an interesting mix of consistency and variability, producing similar actions for similar situations while also discovering unique solutions. To facilitate further research, we've released the optimized model and the code for the policy network at https://github.com/hjdw/StrategicSoccer. By achieving better results with deep reinforcement learning, we've taken a significant step towards creating a more realistic soccer simulation, which can be used to explore other aspects of the game. This work has significant implications for the soccer community, particularly in areas like match analysis, player evaluation, and coaching. In addition, the techniques we've developed could be applied to other team sports, such as basketball, football, and hockey, where the outcome depends on multiple players and the action of one can greatly impact the game's trajectory. This has important implications for the sports statistics community, with new opportunities for collaborative research on the application of machine learning in soccer. A Quasi Periodic Oscillation was observed at a frequency of 0.032 Hz and an RMS amplitude of 18%. Ancient sundials served as primary timekeepers before the invention of mechanical clocks, with the classical Islamic civilization utilizing the Sun's daily movement to determine prayer times, often relying on sundials for this purpose. This knowledge eventually spread to Indonesia through Islamic cultural influences. Indonesian sundials developed as a reflection of local advancements in astronomy, technology, art, and architecture, with historical examples warranting detailed documentation and study, though often overlooked in existing literature. To collect necessary spatial and temporal information on these sundials, a citizen science initiative could be implemented, addressing research inquiries while promoting science education among the general public. This concept has been proposed as a framework, referred to as the Suryakala-Nusantara program, to explore sundials through citizen science methods. By examining sundials through this approach, researchers aim to gain insights into historical timekeeping, the transfer of knowledge, and the development of astronomy in Indonesia. Furthermore, analyzing sundial documentation will provide valuable information on the country's cultural and technological evolution. The Suryakala-Nusantara program could also contribute to the development of a citizen science platform focused on astronomy and physics, encompassing various research areas such as astronomical documentation, field observations, and participatory research. To execute this project, collaboration is key, requiring partnerships between research institutions, museums, cultural organizations, and the general public to ensure its success. By doing so, the Suryakala-Nusantara program will have a lasting impact, as it will not only produce valuable scientific outcomes but also leave a lasting legacy of science promotion and education in Indonesia. To facilitate this partnership, we propose establishing the Suryakala-Nusantara Working Group, to coordinate efforts and direct the project's progression. This document outlines the program's framework, which can be adapted to accommodate various cultural timekeepers known as clocks, while maintaining the core concept's essence. We believe that the Suryakala-Nusantara program will serve as a model for uncovering the history of sundials and other ancient clocks throughout the world. Additionally, this project has the potential to inspire further research into the developmental processes of ancient technologies and the transfer of knowledge and astronomy across different cultures. The success of data-driven dialogue models heavily relies on their ability to accurately encode user input to generate relevant and effective responses. While it is common to evaluate the generated text for its semantic and syntactic quality, the underlying representation of this encoding is often overlooked, which can hinder the model's performance in anticipating the next utterance. This work argues that merely assessing text generation metrics from human or automated sources is insufficient in gauging a model's understanding of dialogue language, prompting the proposal of a set of evaluation tasks to scrutinize the encoder representations used in these models. In experiments, our findings suggest that certain evaluation tasks prove more manageable for certain sophisticated architectures to grasp than others and, interestingly, that RNN-based architectures outperform Transformer models in these evaluation tasks despite underperforming them in standard text generation metrics. Moreover, our study reveals that models' performance in these evaluation tasks often correlates with their performance in human evaluation but struggles to match the standards set by human users. To mitigate these limitations, the proposed architecture incorporating a dialogue-specific encoder is explored, along with various dialogue-specific evaluation tasks designed to assess the encoder representations used in these models. Our research uses 81.4 million annotated data points from the ConvAI2 dataset to train and test these models. Ultimately, our study is a call to action for the development of more robust data-driven dialogue models that can accurately encode the information provided in user input. In addition to opening the code and model selections used in this study, our work also introduces six newly created annotation tools for the ConvAI2 dataset that can be found at https://github.com/Ashtitus/ConvAI2-Eval-tools. This work is a precursor to exploring more sophisticated tasks that can evaluate the capabilities of advanced dialogue models in greater depth. Nonetheless, establishing reliable metrics for assessing the encoder representations used in these models is a critical step in creating more effective and engaging dialogue models. Continuous speech leads to consistent prosody patterns, yet current speech synthesis models often disregard context. These systems fall short when it comes to producing high-quality paragraphs, necessitating a system that integrates contextual elements. MaskedSpeech is a context-aware synthesis system addressing this limitation. By building upon a masking strategy, MaskedSpeech incorporates contextual acoustic features into each sentence, enabling a more detailed understanding of semantic relationships. Additionally, cross-sentence coarse-grained semantic features aid in the development of a natural prosody. Through augmenting masked acoustic features with contextual elements during training, MaskedSpeech outperformed baseline systems in expressiveness and naturalness. Experimental results indicate that incorporating contextual semantic features through masking yields a more versatile and efficient integration of context than traditional attention-based mechanisms. Furthermore, MaskedSpeech's flexibility enables the easy incorporation of additional context-related features via masking, likely to benefit other natural language processing tasks. Evaluations with both objective and subjective methods demonstrate the superior performance of MaskedSpeech. The model's code and demo are available at https://github.com/XiaofengRu/MaskedSpeech. earlier contextualized approaches and apply it to investigate the levels of
semantic change in English vocabulary over the course of 5 decades. Our
results show that contextualized methods may inaccurately predict significant
change in words with little to no actual semantic evolution, or whose
status remains unclear. These difficult cases are scrutinized, along with
suggested categorizations, to better understand the challenges faced. We
conclude that pre-trained contextual language models frequently confuse shifts
in word meanings and contextual fluctuations due to their reliance on
distributional properties. Moreover, they often blend the grammatical and

Optimizing hyperparameters in the private version of the stochastic gradient descent algorithm is a critical issue due to limited access to private datasets for hyperparameter tuning. The development of algorithms that efficiently find optimal hyperparameters for a favorable balance between privacy and performance within a predetermined search space is, therefore, crucial. In this paper, a generalized framework is established to determine an optimal balance between privacy and performance, and three cost-effective algorithms are systematically examined within this framework: evolutionary optimization, Bayesian methods, and reinforcement learning. The results of our experiments, conducted using MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets for hyperparameter tuning in private deep learning, show significant improvements over the conventional grid search method. The paper addresses existing challenges and potential research directions in the field, and provides an open-source code for hyperparameter tuning in private deep learning. The code is available on GitHub at the specified URL. The paper also presents a novel algorithm, called the private deep learning hyperparameter tuner, which achieves notable gains in performance on the CIFAR-10 dataset, and underscores the importance of conducting thorough experiments before the proposed algorithms can be widely adopted. The paper further highlights the need for simpler and less expensive private datasets, as well as the incorporation of prior knowledge in the hyperparameter tuning process. For a Coxeter system denoted by (W,S), we develop the concept of a boolean complex consisting of involutions within W, mirroring Ragnarsson and Tenner's previous work. By applying discrete Morse theory, we identify the homotopy type of this boolean complex for a significant subset of Coxeter groups, including finite groups, revealing that its homotopy type is equivalent to that of a collection of spheres with dimension |S|-1. Moreover, we derive straightforward, recursive formulas to compute the number of spheres within this collection. Additionally, we establish connections between these spheres and various geometric structures within the corresponding reflection poset, particularly highlighting the relationship between certain antichains in this poset and the spheres present in the boolean complex. Moreover, this association allows us to identify the spheres within the boolean complex more efficiently than through discrete Morse theory alone. Finally, we explore the statistical properties of the dimensions and numbers of these spheres for a broad ensemble of Coxeter groups, including those derived from the Grassmannian and the orthognal group. Furthermore, we make available an interactive tool that enables users to generate and explore boolean complexes for a wide variety of Coxeter groups. Finally, we anticipate that future research will further establish the relationship between boolean complexes and the geometry of reflection posets. The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020 and caused severe consequences in China, also exacerbating public health anxiety fueled by rampant online rumors. To address this pressing issue, we examined the dynamics of rumor propagation and proposed a method to measure the impact of a rumor by tracking the speed of its new adopters. Utilizing search frequency as a proxy for this metric, we identified the peak and attenuation coefficients which conform to an exponential distribution. Subsequently, we developed and evaluated machine learning models, discovering that decision trees effectively forecast the peak coefficient and linear regression accurately predicts the attenuation coefficient. Our analysis indicated that certain precursor characteristics are crucial for predicting a rumor's peak influence, whereas location and entity information are more significant in determining its attenuation. Intriguingly, features that accelerate a rumor's initial spread are often detrimental to its continued dissemination. Moreover, anxiety proved to be a critical factor in promoting the propagation of a rumor. To further minimize forecasting losses, we proposed integrating the BERT model, leveraging deep learning techniques to enhance predictive accuracy. Our study provides insights into the dynamics of online rumor propagation and useful metrics for evaluating the influence of rumors, which can be applied to other epidemic models. Furthermore, our results have implications for COVID-19 pandemic management and the development of more effective counter-fighting strategies. Additionally, we explored the possibility of applying our influence measurement model to other information diffusion processes. To this end, we defined the general form of an exponential distribution model and established a connection with the Poincaré inequality. By analyzing the variational inequality, we derived an algorithm for optimizing model parameters, which was subsequently evaluated through simulations. Our proposed method outperformed alternative strategies, demonstrating the benefits of explicit feature engineering in machine learning models. Our study provides a theoretical foundation for studying complex diffusion processes and can be adapted to address other pressing issues in online social networks. To facilitate reproducibility, we made our data and implementation publicly available. Our study can serve as a benchmark for future research involving the development of more sophisticated prediction models. Additionally, we explored potential applications of our model to predict the spread of malicious software and identified the peak influence coefficient to be a critical factor. Our analysis revealed that the attenuation coefficient is essential in determining the long-term impact of a rumor. Our results showed that anxiety plays a crucial role in promoting the propagation of a rumor and should be addressed in counter-fighting strategies. Furthermore, we found that features accelerating a rumor's initial spread can hinder its continued dissemination. Our study provides insights into the dynamics of online rumor propagation

Determining the precise distances to galaxies through planetary nebulae analysis depends on collecting comprehensive data sets, and the observed frequency of these nebulae directly correlates with the galaxies' overall mass. Therefore, researchers must either utilize wide-field observations or focus on the central areas of galaxies. The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making it crucial to carefully select one. Despite its significance, research on the topic often omits explicit justification for loss function selection. We contend that this lack of justification reflects an untested assumption prevalent within the deep learning community. In this research, we investigate how loss function impacts performance in a supervised classification context. Our findings reveal that certain, previously underappreciated loss functions, including the KL divergence, can yield superior outcomes compared to established methods, underscoring the need to view loss function choice as a parameter amenable to optimization, rather than a fixed constant. To demonstrate this, we introduce a novel, adaptive loss function mechanism designed to optimize network performance by dynamically switching between relevant loss functions in accordance with training progress and classification accuracy. This dynamic loss function approach can lead to substantial gains over standard loss functions, as evidenced by our results showing it yields superior performance in multiple scenarios, including challenging datasets and dataset fusion experiments. The proposed dynamic loss function can be viewed as a neural module interpreter, providing valuable insights into the behavior of individual networks and uncovering previously hidden patterns in the data, such as the discovery of implicit classes, by incorporating auxiliary classifiers that serve as detectors for data patterns, network anomalies, and overfitting. To further examine the role of loss functions in deep learning, we conducted a comprehensive survey covering all aspects of loss function research, along with an open-source implementation of our dynamic loss function approach, available online at https://github.com/author/dynamic-loss-function. The open issue associated with this repository has been approved and can be found at https://issues.hub://dynamic-loss-function/1. The achievements of this research have been presented in the form of a demo at the Deep Learning Conference 2023 in Berlin, Germany. This research aims to advance the understanding of thermomechanical behavior in polymer crystallization. Strain-induced crystallization plays a significant role in polymer mechanical and thermal properties and must be accounted for during production and final product application design. To effectively capture its mechanical and thermal impacts, the proposed model utilizes a unique decomposition approach to the deformation gradient and applies the Coleman--Noll procedure and minimum dissipation potential principle to material modeling. The resulting model includes suitable Helmholtz free energy and dissipation potential assumptions, which enables simulation of crystalline region formation, degradation, and temperature changes during cyclic loading tests. Numerical implementation based on the finite element method provides the basis for numerical solutions, which include simulations of material sample microstructure and temperature evolution. This proposed model offers a more comprehensive representation of material behavior and can be adapted for application to other crystalline polymers. Numerical results validate the model's effectiveness in predicting material behavior, strain-induced crystallization, and temperature changes, making it a valuable asset for polymer materials science and engineering. The model's ability to accurately capture crystallization, temperature, and material microstructure within the finite element framework provides a solid foundation for its application in various industrial settings. The model is demonstrated through the simulation of actual polymer materials with strain-induced crystallization properties. It is also adapted to model the thermomechanical behavior of polyethylene, a commonly used polymer in medical devices and implant applications. The paper presents the model's application to the simulation of a range of polymer materials, including poly(ethylene terephthalate) (PET), poly(cyclohexylene dimethylene) (PCHD), and polyethylene (PE), and explores its potential to be used in the analysis of medical devices that rely on these polymers. The model is currently being developed to include new features such as crack growth simulation, material nonlinearity, and multiple stage crystallizations, which will enable a more comprehensive understanding of material behavior and improve the design of medical devices that rely on polymers. The paper also presents the model's results for the simulation of a range of medical device applications, including catheters, guidewires, stents, and implantable devices, and explores its potential to be used in the analysis of these devices. The model is a groundbreaking development in the field of polymer materials science and engineering, and its results demonstrate its effectiveness in predicting material behavior, strain-induced crystallization, and temperature changes. The paper provides a comprehensive overview of the model's development, its features, and its application to polymer materials science

To analyze the impact of external magnetization on doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$ with spin-triplet nematic superconductivity, we computationally investigate magnetic susceptibility in nematic and chiral superconducting states using the Ginzburg-Landau formalism near its critical temperature. A key observation in this analysis is that the superconducting order parameter shows a non-trivial response to the transverse component of an applied magnetic field, which can result in a paramagnetic response. Moreover, the topology of the Fermi surface exerts a substantial influence on magnetic susceptibility, with a specific Lifshitz transition inducing a transition from the nematic to the chiral phase and leading to the divergence of magnetic susceptibility at this transition point. Notably, the interplay between electron-electron interaction and competing phases of superconductivity is investigated, with results showing that the driving force behind a transition from the nematic to the chiral phase can be the presence of electron-electron interaction in the immediate vicinity of the transition. With regard to the interpretation of experimental findings, the investigation shows that the recently reported results indicating a chiral $p$-wave superconducting ground state in some Bi$_2$Se$_3$ samples can alternatively be accounted for by a spin-triplet nematic superconducting state when due consideration is given to the role of electron-electron interaction in these systems. Providing quality feedback is further constrained by the need to supply demonstrations for multiple state actions at once. To overcome these difficulties, researchers propose an alternative where the teacher can provide corrective feedback in the form of preferences or rewards instead of demonstrations. However, existing algorithms are designed to work with specific types of noisy feedback, limiting their application across various teachers and tasks. To tackle this problem, we suggest a different approach, one where we model a variety of feedback types as different loss functions. Using this approach, we can leverage any online learning algorithm to minimize the combined losses and learn from a diversity of weakly correlated feedback. Our proposed method can handle different forms of feedback by treating the teacher's cost function as latent. By applying a general corrective feedback meta-algorithm that unifies prior work, we can achieve similar regret bounds regardless of the type of feedback. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by successfully learning to perform a complex household navigation task on a robotic platform using a variety of noisy feedback. To facilitate future research, we introduce an open-source framework for evaluating corrective feedback algorithms in robotics and highlight its usefulness with respect to existing methods. Our approach provides a general solution for learning from a diverse range of weakly correlated feedback and can be applied across different types of feedback by using the same underlying online learning algorithm. This solution can be expected to yield positive results in other domains that deal with complex demonstrations and weakly correlated feedback.
