Determining whether bulge growth causes the flattening of the star formation main sequence at the high mass end remains uncertain. To explore the role of bulges in forming the main sequence, a study examined the NUV$-r$ color of 6401 local star-forming galaxies by comparing the central and outer regions of each galaxy. Since NUV$-r$ color serves as a specific indicator of star formation rate, a distinction emerged when analyzing galaxies based on their stellar masses. At stellar masses less than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, there is only a small color difference between the central and outer NUV$-r$. Above this threshold, however, a more significant difference in color becomes apparent, indicating the central bulge in massive galaxies is more mature. Observing the behavior of galaxies based on their S\'ersic index $n$ also provided valuable insights. Those with an index of 2.0 or greater are more likely to exhibit redder NUV$-r$ colors even when considering factors like bulge-to-total mass ratio and stellar mass. This indicates a stronger relationship between star formation within bulges and $n$ (or central mass density) than with the B/T ratio. Notably, a sharp increase in galaxies with an index of 2.0 or greater occurs at stellar masses greater than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$. This pattern is consistent with the downturn observed in the mass-star formation rate relation at the same mass transition point. Therefore, it appears the growing presence of dense bulges with low specific star formation rates in massive galaxies is the key factor contributing to the flattened slope of the mass-star formation rate relation at the high mass end. This behavior is likely a result of bulges becoming dominant enough to influence the overall star formation rate across the mass sequence. In support of this finding, a comparison with previous studies that focused solely on the central color of galaxies revealed similar results. Furthermore, analyzing the fraction of massive star-forming galaxies that contain bulges did not provide a complete picture due to numerous dilution effects, whereas studying the intrinsic properties of these galaxies directly revealed the underlying relationship between bulges and the mass-star formation rate relation. Lastly, incorporating a function representing the fraction of bulges that form at different mass scales allowed for an accurate prediction of the overall specific star formation rate across the mass sequence, thereby demonstrating the profound impact of bulges on the mass-star formation rate relation. We examine a specific nonlinear elliptic equation in R^N, where N is 5 or greater. No studies on the periodicity of its solutions have been done previously, so we explore related issues by making some key assumptions about a given function, Q(y), which is periodic and has a minimum value at zero. We demonstrate that numerous "bubbling solutions" for this equation exist and can be classified in a specific way when these conditions are met, resulting in some of these solutions maintaining the same symmetry as Q(y). Additionally, we find that "bubbling solutions" will not exist under alternative circumstances when Q(y)'s local minimum is zero, specifically in instances when it does not equal zero. Joseph and L. R. Beck, and further on a paper by A. Azzalini and P. A. Ferrari. Real-time anomaly detection in continuous data streams presents difficulties for conventional and advanced methods due to shifting concepts and ongoing learning requirements. Existing approaches, such as using hash functions or nearest neighbors with fixed memory, can struggle to accommodate frequent fluctuations, remove smooth outliers, and adapt to deep neural network architectures. We introduce a new technique for continuous real-time anomaly detection based on quantum measurements, which can process infinite data streams at constant $O(1)$ update complexity and effectively estimate changing densities through random Fourier features and an exponential moving average. This approach was thoroughly evaluated by comparing it to 12 prominent algorithms for real-time anomaly detection on 12 diverse data streams. It consistently outperformed all competitors across all evaluation metrics, demonstrating significant improvements in accuracy, performance, and update efficiency. The implementation of this approach is part of an open-source Anomalous Pattern Learning package that includes multiple real-time anomaly detection methods. Furthermore, we introduced the Open Data Stream Repository, an openly available repository of real-time anomaly detection datasets that can be used for research purposes. This repository includes 12 diverse data streams generated by 3 different data generation models, along with the parameters used to create them. A pivotal question arises when a court possesses information that an individual knows the passcode to a device. To answer this inquiry, we develop a novel approach to an established legal doctrine, drawing on precedents set by the case of Fisher v. US. Our overarching objective is to create a framework that clarifies whether any action taken has already provided implicit evidence accessible to the authorities. Instead of addressing this overarching goal, this paper introduces a framework that identifies specific actions where any implicit evidence effectively becomes a foregone conclusion. At its core, this framework places the onus on the government to prove it is not leveraging the respondent's compliance. Building upon this, we introduce 'demonstrability' as a central concept to describe actions compelled by the authorities. Moreover, we develop a language that discerns whether an action is as efficacious as the government's intended goal. Subsequently, we apply our framework to evaluate the compelled actability of several cryptographic tools, such as decryption, multifactor authentication, and hash functions, and arrive at a novel conclusion about compelled decryption. Finally, we propose a possible reform to the Fisher test and examine how it would impact these tools. Our exploration of our framework is available online at our workshop paper 'Compelling Cryptographic Actions: Examining Fisher v US through a New Lens'.

We have developed a comprehensive model that enables simulation of the measurement-device-independent quantum key distribution (MDI-QKD) process. It can predict real-world observations and outcomes in scenarios involving linear channel loss, including the associated gain levels, error rates in different measurement bases, and final key rates. Our model is versatile and can be applied to various MDI-QKD implementations that employ convex source states or diverse coding techniques. As such, it is an invaluable resource for analyzing and evaluating the performance of different MDI-QKD protocols. Furthermore, we used this model to examine several recently proposed protocols for improving the efficiency of quantum key distribution. Specifically, we investigated the source state protocols proposed by Wang et al. and the multi-channel MDI-QKD protocol suggested by Sheltzer et al. Our simulations revealed how these protocols handle different levels of linear channel loss and the resulting gain levels, error rates, and final key rates. In doing so, we verified that both of these proposed solutions can achieve high key rates even in scenarios with significant channel loss. Our model also enabled us to identify the critical factor that limits the performance of these improved QKD protocols. Fake news has become a pressing concern on social media platforms due to its rapid dissemination and potential to cause harm worldwide. Although machine learning models have been successful in detecting false information, especially when large amounts of labeled data are available, their effectiveness significantly declines when they are applied to emerging events. This limitation creates a significant obstacle for the current methods in detecting false news on unexpected events. Furthermore, the fact that newly emerging events necessitate building a new model from scratch or retraining the existing one, which is often expensive, time-consuming and impractical in real-world settings. To address this challenge, an end-to-end fake news detection system called MetaFEND has been proposed, allowing for the rapid learning to identify false information on unexpected events with limited information from verified sources. This system leverages the strength of both meta-learning and neural process methods, incorporates a module to address label embedding, and employs a hard attention mechanism to enhance the effectiveness by dealing with category information and eliminating unnecessary information. Experiments conducted on large multimedia datasets obtained from Twitter and Weibo demonstrate the effectiveness of the MetaFEND system in detecting false information on previously unseen events and outperforms the current state-of-the-art techniques. Moreover, the system's capacity to handle multiple events with limited data from a single meta-world has been proven. The source code of the proposed method has been made available at https://github.com/ghori13/MetaFEND. The model relies on the meta-learning approach from the paper titled Meta-Learning for Explainable Product Embedding and the neural process method from the paper titled Neural Process Networks for Data Efficient Fake News Detection. Quantum tunneling is an inherent process that lacks a direct analogy in classical physics, and it can rival Coulomb interactions to give rise to intricate phenomena.
In silicon, precise placement of phosphorus dopants is feasible to address the diverse consequences of this interplay, however this approach depends on wave functions related to crystal symmetry, which quantum tunneling inherently affects.
In this study, lattice-aperiodic valley interference patterns were directly visualized in silicon by employing scanning tunneling microscopy to investigate coupled atoms.
The examination reveals the significance of envelope anisotropy, valley interference and the location of the dopants on Heisenberg's spin exchange interaction in silicon.
The findings indicate that exchange interaction becomes immune to valley interference by arranging in-plane dopants in particular directions aligned with the crystallographic orientation, ultimately retrieving vacuum-like characteristics where the exchange interaction maximizes the overlap between donor orbitals, and the variation in pairs is minimized to less than 10-fold.
This robust exchange interaction remains over a considerable distance range, from a high-fidelity quantum computation regime influenced by Coulomb interaction to coupled donor arrays used in quantum simulations in silicon. 
Therefore, this study demonstrates that precise placement of donor dopants can accurately control the exchange interaction to obtain a uniform, tunnel-coupled background for varied applications. 
This breakthrough contributes to the development of robust, accurate, and wide-ranging donor-based quantum computing, coupled to extensive scientific calculations, or used in quantum simulations where the exchange interaction can be manipulated to perform specific tasks. 
Additionally, this advancement paves the way for the production of high-fidelity quantum processors by matching the exchange interaction to the operational principles of the processor by selecting donor pairs with the desired exchange interaction before assembling them. 
Furthermore, this breakthrough enables multiple quantum applications, such as the simultaneous execution of multiple operations, by exchanging the interaction of multiple couples, or the construction of a quantum channel using exchange interaction instead of tunneling. 
The findings of this study also reveal the potential for exchange interaction to be used as a tunable barrier in silicon quantum wells, and the discovery of an unexpected 10-fold variation in exchange interaction in silicon, which may be useful for encoding quantum information. 
The research also uncovers the underlying causes of exchange interaction in silicon, including valley interference, and the location and arrangement of the donor dopants, which can be controlled by modifying the crystal structure, or the inclusion of a layer of diamond or a different oxide, which can reduce the variation in exchange interaction to near uniform.

When capturing panoramic scenes, individuals usually align their cameras parallel to the direction of gravity. Many portable devices, including smartphones and tablets, are fitted with sensors that can accurately track the direction of gravity. Based on this assumption, the axis of cameras in such configurations can be assumed to be aligned or adjusted accordingly, thus reducing the necessary alignment parameters to one dimension. Taking advantage of this assumption, novel simplified approaches to stitching panoramic images from rotating cameras have been developed, focusing on cameras with the same optical centers. Four realistic scenarios, accounting for unknown and varying focal lengths as well as radial distortion, are explored in this context. Comprehensive testing of the proposed methods was conducted using artificially created scenes and over 500k pairs of real images obtained from the Sun360 dataset and from scenes taken with the aid of smartphones equipped with sensors that track the direction of gravity. These methods demonstrate superiority over current techniques in terms of precision and processing speed. The developed approaches also facilitate division of labor, where detecting duplicate frames, feature detection, and radial distortion estimation can be performedally using a combination of existing techniques. The multivariate interpolation operator is traditionally constructed using piecewise linear functions to approximate absolute differences between values. In this study, we develop a novel, transcendental interpolation function derived from the hyperbolic tangent, providing more precise approximations of functions that increase linearly with the distance. Building on the Wu-Schaback quasi-interpolation formula, we adapt this new interpolation function while preserving the original scheme's characteristics, including monotonicity and convexity. It has been mathematically proven that our adaptation converges at a rate of O(h^2), enabling smoother interpolation results. Several numerical experiments are presented to demonstrate the method's efficiency and accuracy. In particular, we find that using this new interpolation function results in more accurate interpolations of monotonic and convex functions, as well as better restoration of the original curve's shape in case of a given set of interpolating points. The method is also applicable to boundary points and achieves a significant improvement in accuracy when compared to the traditional approach. Additionally, we observe that for certain input data, our new interpolation function produces interpolations at a rate of O(h^4). This is further confirmed by a theoretical convergence analysis. In conclusion, we propose a new interpolation function derived from the hyperbolic tangent, which offers a more precise approximation of functions that increase linearly with the distance. This is demonstrated through several numerical experiments, showcasing the method's efficiency and accuracy. The results indicate a significant improvement in the accuracy of interpolations, especially for monotonic and convex functions. Additionally, we investigate the method's performance with respect to continuity and Lipschitz continuity. The obtained interpolations exhibit a continuous behavior, with a Lipschitz constant that increases in proportion to the maximum possible value within the given domain. This is mathematically proven through a convergence analysis. The method achieves a convergence rate of O(h^2) for functions with continuous second derivatives and an increased rate of O(h) for functions with less regularity. Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces classification outputs. When access to the original data is possible, a training sample's resistance to other classes is quantified by measuring the distance between its class and the network's decision boundaries, which is used to assign a soft label to the sample. This allows for the model to be trained via standard knowledge distillation methods. A strong geodetic subset of a graph~$G$ comprises a selection of vertices~$S$, which allows for the coverage of the remaining vertices in~$G$, by establishing unique shortest paths between all pairs of vertices in~$S$. The Strong Geodetic problem (SG) involves determining if a graph~$G$ and an integer~$k$ have a subset of vertices~$S$, with at most~$k$ elements, which is strong geodetic. This problem has been proven to be NP-hard for all graphs. This study introduces the Strong Geodetic Recognition problem (SGR), which requires identifying if a specific vertex subset~$S$ within a graph~$G$ constitutes a strong geodetic subset. SGR is found to be NP-complete. Research into SGR is conducted, and comparisons of computational complexities are made across various graph types, including the derivation of efficient algorithms, NP-completeness proofs, and preliminary results on parameterized complexity, which provide insight into the complexity of SG, particularly in chordal graphs. Moreover, a generalization of SGR, called Multiple Strong Geodetic, is introduced and analyzed. Finally, the scope of further research on the complexity of SG is outlined. For SGR, this involves determining the computational complexity in specific graph types, such as planar graphs, as well as the development of efficient algorithms and NP-completeness proofs. Leveraging existing results on the Minimal Dominating Set problem, which shares some characteristics with SGR, can facilitate such research, by either providing solutions or pinpointing reasons why problems may be difficult to solve. In the case of Multiple Strong Geodetic, further research aims to establish the exact computational complexity of this problem, including identifying potential connections with other problems, such as the 3-Color Problem, especially in the context of chordal graphs. Additionally, this study introduces the Multiple Strong Geodetic for Fission graphs problem, which is defined as the Multiple Strong Geodetic Recognition problem when the graph in question is a fusion of several sub-graphs, characterized as single-component trees, connected by edges between any adjacent two sub-graphs, and referred to as a fission graph. The complexity of this problem is determined as NP-complete, by providing an NP algorithm and a certificate for completeness, and is expected to have a high computational complexity, likely requiring an exponential number of iterations in its solution. The ultimate goal of imitation learning is to develop efficient policies using nearly optimal expert examples. Nonetheless, getting numerous high-quality examples from human experts is very costly. On the other hand, getting vast amounts of low-quality or irrelevant paths in a task can be quite easy, but these paths aren't helpful for imitation. Nonetheless, these suboptimal paths still provide insight into the system dynamics and what actions are feasible within that environment. This study investigates whether these suboptimal paths can be utilized to enhance imitation learning performance using new objectives that learn a factored transition model. The learned model allows us to derive a latent action space, making downstream imitation learning much more efficient by reducing the necessity for extensive expert datasets. This is achieved by leveraging additional non-expert data. For practical applications, we suggest TRAIL, an algorithm that utilizes contrastive learning for energy-based models to derive the action space. The benefits of this approach were verified in experiments on navigation and locomotion tasks, yielding up to a 4x performance improvement compared to baseline imitation learning methods. The code is available at https://github.com/vtargon/trail. The theoretical finding that these suboptimal examples can be utilized to reduce the necessity for expert data by introducing latent structure was also established. This study built upon previous work by introducing contrastive learning over multiple policies, resulting in energy-based models that can be applied to a broader class of games than previously reported. The scope of games that can be played with TRAIL includes action games with multiple possible actions, including multi-agent games, by extending the algorithm to utilize non-expert data from other agents' play. The algorithm's performance was evaluated on a range of physical environments, including a freight transport scenario. The freight transport scenario involved multiple agents, involved multiple possible actions, and involved a complex topology, making it one of the most complex tasks evaluated with TRAIL. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents in an alternating exploration-exploitation process. Although agent experiences may be both beneficial and misleading, our method employs value function expected gain estimation to filter out less useful knowledge. As a result, the agents learn from each other, selectively imitating valuable information and rejecting unnecessary data. Experimentation across multiple scenarios highlights the superiority of our Co-Imitation Learning framework, confirming the benefits of inter-agent knowledge exchange in the absence of external supervision. When using our proposed metric, the PAC code decoding computations are comparable to conventional convolutional codes with sequential decoding. Moreover, our results demonstrate improved error-correction performance for low-rate PAC codes with the proposed metric function. We show that using the polarized cutoff rate as the bias in our metric function reduces the risk of incorrect path selection during decoding, exponentially decreasing as the incorrect path depth increases. We also prove and validate the Pareto distribution of PAC code computation complexity. Additionally, we provide a scaling-bias procedure and guidelines for selecting optimal threshold spacings in search-limited sequential decoding, which significantly improve average decoder computations. For some 128-bit codes, our results indicate that search-limited PAC codes can achieve error-correction performance near that of polar codes under successive cancellation list decoding, with a list size of 64 and a CRC length of 11, at a much lower computation cost. We also demonstrate the efficacy of search-limited decoding for convolutional codes. For some 64-bit codes, our results show that search-limited decoding can achieve error-correction performance near that of polar codes under successive cancellation decoding, at a fraction of the computation cost. We conclude that search-limited decoding is an attractive alternative to CRC-aided decoding and is more efficient than polar codes, especially for high-rate polar codes. Furthermore, as polarization occurs in larger codes, search-limited decoding can be an even more effective method of error correction. We anticipate that this new method will be useful for correcting errors in sequential decoding applications. A novel, markerless extrinsic calibration system is introduced that relies on real-world depth camera data rather than simulation or fiducial markers. Our system leverages machine learning to automatically develop and utilize real-world models for identifying and positioning the end-effector, predicting object rotation, and pinpointing critical points in a single image frame. A mathematical transformation and a keypoint-matching algorithm allow us to accurately estimate end-effector pose based on rotation and keypoint data. Enhanced system robustness is achieved through a combination of advanced algorithms, including the iterative closest point method, multi-frame processing, filtering, and outlier detection. Results show our method's calibration and pose estimation capabilities can be as precise as sub-centimeters and sub-degrees with minimal and unseen test poses; we have also found that incorporating data from just one optimal pose yields comparable accuracy. In real-world testing, our method consistently calibrates and estimates poses within a few seconds for each new object and pose. A demonstration of our system integrating a motion planning algorithm for successful pick-up tasks can be found in the supplementary video. We have also open-sourced our calibration and pose estimation code on GitHub. Due to the variety and endless creation of household objects, we have established a dataset of unannotated depth camera images containing various objects from different poses, which is accessible on the Object-Oriented Recognition and Localization (OOPL) dataset platform. This dataset, combined with our state-of-art calibration and pose estimation methods, paves the way for more robust multi-frame processing, filter applications, and outlier detection strategies. We have obtained outstanding results with our method, surpassing currently available models, particularly in the household domain, as evidenced by the evaluation of our predictions against original annotation in over 3000 keypoints. Overall, our method achieves highly accurate extrinsic calibration and pose estimation using only a single image frame for each object and pose of interest. This method has several significant advantages, including the ability to easily integrate new objects and poses without any modifications to the system, and it can calibrate and estimate poses for previously unseen test poses and objects in a matter of seconds. This study introduces two key concepts, quasi-finitely separating maps and quasiapproximate identities, which form the basis for the definitions of QFS-spaces and quasicontinuous maps. Building upon these definitions, various properties and characteristics of QFS-spaces are investigated. Key findings include: Firstly, any QFS-space is inherently a quasicontinuous space; secondly, closed subspaces, as well as quasicontinuous projection spaces, derived from QFS-spaces are themselves QFS-spaces; thirdly, continuous retracts of QFS-spaces possess the same characteristic and specific types of QFS-space retracts can be constructed; lastly, upper power spaces of continuous QFS-spaces correspond to FS-spaces. Furthermore, investigators offer a broader definition which encompasses QFS-spaces, related maps, and defined points, leading to the generalization of established properties for more comprehensive spaces. This generalized framework is dubbed the QFS-theory. Finally, a distinction is made between two variants of this broader definition, resulting in the derivation of a new concept called defined points of quasicontinuous type which, in turn, facilitates the proof of upper power space theorem for quasicontinuous maps. This proof, in turn, leads to the conclusion that continuous QFS-space correspond to FS-spaces. Additionally, investigators provide an alternative proof for continuous QFS-space topological equivalence to FS-spaces using a different approach. This approach involves the utilization of differential maps to establish connections between the two types of spaces and their maps. This proof is more concise and provides further evidence of the internal consistency of the QFS-theory. Finally, a note is made on a potential generalization of the QFS-theory for (quasi)approximate identities with multiple factors. This potential generalization could lead to a broader exploration of space properties but would also likely result in more complex definitions and greater diversity within the QFS-theory. Research into the Web's influence on polarization has produced several key findings in the past. To build on existing research and gain deeper insights, we've studied browsing habits of thousands of users along with their online interactions with news sources. Our results reveal that users' online exposure to news sources follows distinct ideological patterns where they consistently spend more time browsing news aligned with their own viewpoint. Moreover, we've identified clear partisan groups within the broader online population based on shared browsing habits. Ultimately, we examined the impact of user decision-making on online polarization, and we've uncovered substantial evidence indicating users' deliberate actions can contribute significantly to the amplification of partisan divisions. To achieve this, we present an intuitive benchmark to measure online polarization and a novel user clustering technique that can handle browsing history dynamically. By combining these approaches, we were able to investigate the intricate polarization processes occurring online, revealing that user decision-making plays a prominent role in shaping their browsing habits, which in turn are influenced by various factors, including underlying ideological preferences, active engagement with news sources, and online browsing costs. We also explored the effects of different user groups on online polarization, and we've found that some of these effects can be quite substantial, often exceeding 30%. We experimented with a personalized news feed algorithm that considers users' browsing history and found it to be very effective in reducing online polarization. Our research provides valuable insights that can be useful in informing the design of more adaptable and user-centric algorithms, which can contribute to mitigating the amplification of partisan divisions on the Web. Ultimately, we believe that our results can be applied to other online platforms that involve personalization and group polarization, and we hope to make our data and algorithms available for further research into the Web's polarization processes. We examine the Lehnert and Schweitzer proof that the word problem for Thompson's group V has a non-context-free property. We further prove this word problem to be equivalent to the complement of a combined cyclic variant of several context-free languages, and for some of its generators, the combined cyclic variant of four deterministic context-free languages is sufficient. This relationship reveals that the time complexity of solving V's word problem deterministically is no more than quadratically scaling with input size. Additionally, we demonstrate that V's word problem can be resolved by a deterministic finite automaton with four states, and acknowledge the possibility of a simpler proof existing for this fact. Furthermore, we explore the implications of this relationship on the time complexity of other problems related to V. Specifically, we show that solving the identity problem for V is equivalent to solving its word problem, and that resolving the order problem for V determines its word problem equivalent, but also requires additional information. Finally, we consider the magnitude of exponential growth rates that can be achieved by V, and while it cannot exceed the maximum possible value of 2^n for n-generated V, we are unable to pinpoint a specific exponent within this range. Additionally, we note that V's order problem's resolution can result in languages with a combined cyclic variant of two deterministic context-free languages having an exponential growth rate of 2^n for some n. Lastly, we mention the possibility of further researching the intersection of two V groups with an order problem whose resolution has been determined. This research builds upon previous work by the second author mentioned in the paper, specifically referencing the proof that V's identity problem is undecidable, the conclusion that V's word problem includes the complement of a combined cyclic variant of two deterministic context-free languages, and the examination of two-step group recognition problems. This research expands upon that foundation by introducing a combined cyclic variant of several context-free languages that is equivalent to V's word problem, as well as exploring the implications of this relationship on V's time complexity, other related problems, and its groups. This research expresses appreciation for the input provided by J. Lehnert and S. Schweitzer on previous work related to this research. This research concludes by outlining potential future study on problems related to V. Adding three right-handed neutrinos and a simple QCD axion sector to the Standard Model effectively explains multiple phenomena including neutrino oscillations, dark matter, and baryon asymmetry. In doing so, it also resolves issues with strong CP problems and stabilizes the electroweak vacuum while fitting within observational limits of Higgs inflation. MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented, distributed NoSQL database that allows for three different types of transactions: standalone, replica set, and sharded cluster deployments. Considering the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB transactions in each deployment, we investigated their transactional protocols. However, we found that the documentation for these protocols is unclear, particularly in regards to pseudocode and formal specifications of the consistency guarantees they provide. In our work, we clarified the transactional protocols for each MongoDB deployment, using pseudocode derived from official documentation and source code, and verified that they conform to specific variants of snapshot isolation. Our approach also enables efficient checking of the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB's transaction protocols. To accomplish this, we developed a tool that automatically generates specifications from pseudocode, and employed this tool to verify the transactional protocols for MongoDB's various deployments. Our research demonstrates the value of clear, formally definable transaction protocols, and our approach can be adapted to verify the consistency of other database protocols. Our work has already inspired the development of a similar approach for verifying the transactional protocol of Google Spanner. However, when these datasets contain biases, the models can learn them, compromising their ability to generalize and produce reliable results.  While research exists on developing unbiased models, the problem lies in identifying and mitigating the inherent biases present in medical image datasets.  In an effort to address this issue, we first establish a metric to quantify data intrinsic bias and propose a new framework for detecting biases in medical image datasets.  Our proposed framework, comprising of two primary components, namely KlotskiNet and Bias Discriminant Direction Analysis, aims to identify and quantify the inherent biases present in medical image datasets.  Our experimental results on multiple datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework in accurately identifying biases.  Our research lays the foundation for further development of algorithms capable of detecting and quantifying the inherent biases present in medical image datasets. We present an investigation of Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ (BFTO), a four-layer Aurivillius compound, under the influence of high hydrostatic pressure.  Our X-ray diffraction data does not exhibit a phase transition under pressure but lattice changes suggest a series of structural adaptations as the pressure increases.  Initially, BFTO displays a quasi-tetragonal symmetry but transforms into an orthorhombic structure beyond 8 GPa.  Our Raman spectroscopy analysis reveals local structure alterations at 5.5 GPa, contradicting crystallographic changes, and our Nuclear forward scattering measurements disclose the onset of magnetic order in BFTO above 5K under high pressure conditions, with enhanced magnetic order with increasing pressure.  Conversely, NFS at 6.4GPa and varying temperatures indicates magnetic loss at higher temperatures (20K), with the structural changes potentially influencing this magnetic phenomenon.  We propose that pressure-induced shifts in bond lengths and the reduced tolerance factor may contribute to the appearance of magnetism in BFTO. When the adiabatic index lies between one and approximately 1.16, these solutions consistently occupy all space without gaps, showing close alignment with each other. As the index surpasses this threshold, pressure drops to zero at a finite distance from the origin, and in both scenarios, a spherical void forms. All matter becomes concentrated in a thin layer behind the shock wave's front. This layer's structure, however, changes depending on the index, especially where the inner edge meets a sudden and infinite density at approximately 1.4 in both models, even though the pressure at this edge remains consistently zero. Increasing the index to 1.4 in both models results in an exponential decrease in temperature behind the shock wave's front, contradicting the commonly held assumption of a constant temperature in this region. In 2015, CERN introduced "Emittance Scans," a new fast luminosity separation scanning method at the Large Hadron Collider. These scans were consistently carried out during physics production runs, utilizing full-intensity beams at the CMS experiment's interaction point. The emittance scans allowed for the simultaneous measurement of beam properties and closed orbits at the level of individual bunches, yielding precise insights into long-range beam-beam effects, as predicted by the improved TRAIN code. Furthermore, the scans facilitated differentiation between beam profiles in the horizontal and vertical directions, as observed with the CMS pixel detector. The emittance scans also served as an early warning system for beam quality degradation, informing decisions on beam operation and optimization. The introduction of closed-orbit feedback in 2017 further underscored the value of these scans. With beam parameters changing over time, the emittance scans were repeatedly used as a reference for the comparison of different beam states, revealing that the typical beam quality could be achieved in approximately half the time required before the introduction of this feature. The emittance scans have paved the way for the development of closed-orbit reference scans, which feature full-intensity beams at the level of individual bunches. These advances in beam diagnostics have contributed significantly to the improvement of beam parameters at the Large Hadron Collider. The experience gained from emittance scans will be valuable in guiding the development of future beam diagnostics for future colliders. The progress made in beam diagnostics will be presented, alongside the underlying physics that underpin it, as well as the development of the code used. By harnessing the power of time and frequency-domain measurements, a cutting-edge technique offers unprecedented accuracy (<1%) and precision (0.42%) for determining pressure. Initially demonstrated in a sealed environment over a pressure range (1-1.5 bar), the method effectively captures intricate pressure variations resulting from nitrous gas interacting with a solid surface in various states of flow. Notably, it can also detect very fine-scale pressure differences arising from the conversion of kinetic energy into pressure as well as distinct O2/N2 patterns formed by turbulent mixing processes. These findings are validated through comparative measurements with established methods, including direct pressure sensors and sampling techniques for analyzing gas composition. Overall, this approach paves the way for enhancing spatial resolution and capturing dynamic processes in complex flows through high-resolution pressure mapping. Additionally, it opens up new applications for rotational CARS in the aerospace and automotive industries by providing high-accuracy, non-invasive measurements of pressure and composition in flows. This technology is also being integrated with high-speed flow visualization to give real-time visual feedback, allowing for precise control over the development of turbulent structures and resulting pressure and composition patterns. This combined method could significantly improve our understanding of mass transport processes occurring during the transition from laminar to turbulent flow and may also find use in detecting turbulent patterns associated with disease progression and cancer metastasis. Furthermore, it is possible to adapt this technique to operate with a wider range of pump and Stokes wavelengths, which could enable the simultaneous detection of additional gas species using the same experimental setup. This would provide even greater insights into the complex phenomena involving the transport of heat, mass, and momentum in various environments and could lead to the development of new, high-resolution imaging methods for identifying objects based on their composition. This includes cancer detection, where rotational CARS can be used to take advantage of the unique rotational resonance of molecules in cells and tissues to pinpoint tumors and enhance their contrast in imaging scans. This could further contribute to improving the accuracy of surgical removal by identifying all tumor cells throughout the treatment. Moreover, this technique is also being combined with laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy to detect bone fractures by identifying the unique chemical structure of hemoprotein in blood. This could lead to the non-invasive detection of fractures through analyzing the composition of bone cells, which would be a groundbreaking advancement in medicine, especially in the field of orthopedics.

The catalog of the Milky Way's globular clusters remains incomplete. We have investigated 19 newly proposed globular cluster candidates located in the galaxy's bulge using infrared color-magnitude diagrams and the VVV survey database. We calculated key astrophysical properties including the reduction of light passing through interstellar gas, distance from Earth, total brightness, average cluster movement through space, metal composition, and age. We constructed a catalog of likely cluster members using vector motion diagrams and removed extraneous stars from the observed data. We estimate a broad range of light obstruction and gas reduction across the sample clusters as expected within the galaxy's bulge. We calculated their distances from Earth as being between 6.8 to 11.4 kiloparsecs and consequently determined that the clusters could be anywhere between 0.56 to 3.25 kiloparsecs from the galaxy's center. We compared their motion to typical galaxy bulge movements except for VVV-CL160, whose movement was distinct. We calculated their metallic content and ages, discovering metal contents between minus one and four tenths and ages between 8 to 13 billion years. We calculated total brightness levels both in the infrared K-band and the visual V-band and found a range from minus 3.4 to minus 7.5 in visual brightness levels. We further analyzed the possible presence of RR Lyrae stars found within the proposed cluster regions, basing our findings on positions, motion, metal composition, and ages, and comparing the data with previous research, ultimately classifying nine candidates as confirmed globular clusters, seven others needed further investigation, and the remaining three as open clusters rather than globular ones. High-resolution images from the VMC archive, previously published by Clementini et al. (2015), were used to illustrate the newly identified globular clusters VVV-CL157, VVV-CL160, and VVV-CL162. These new findings contribute to completing the list of Milky Way globular clusters. Additionally, we suggested that two already known globular clusters, 3X1353 and 3X1410, needed further observation due to unlikely light obstruction and gas reduction levels. Furthermore, we proposed that the previously unknown open cluster VVV-CL161, consisting of six RR Lyrae stars, could be used as an internal distance measurement tool for the galaxy's bulge. This particular research centers around the Drell-Yan process and focuses on vector-boson transverse momentum, $q_T$, and beam thrust, $\mathcal T$, to illustrate exclusive observable behavior. Our analysis addresses the various scale relationships in differential distributions ranging from massless $m \ll q_T$ to heavy-quark dominant decoupling limit $q_T \ll m$. To investigate quark-mass dependencies accurately within intermediate regime $m \sim q_T$, it necessitates a consideration of beam and soft functions as mass dependent entities. We examine the techniques of simulating light-matter interactions within tight-binding models that derive from first-principle theory. The conventional method for describing optical properties uses a velocity-based approach tied to the vector potential. An alternative method exists, where a finite system is represented through the electric field, resulting in a dipole-based model inspired by Peierls substitution. This study evaluates the accuracy of both methods in relation to gauge invariance, utilizing TB models constructed from maximally localized Wannier functions and applied to two-dimensional paradigm materials. We calculate the electromagnetic responses under linear and strong excitations, comparing the outcomes to converged first-principle simulations to validate our TB models' accuracy. The results indicate that the dipole-based model yields a more precise description than the velocity-based model. We attribute this to the imperfect compensation of diamagnetic and paramagnetic currents in the velocity-based model. To rectify this shortcoming, we formulated a sum rule that explicitly addresses the compensation issue, allowing the correction of velocity-based models to match dipole-based models and guarantee gauge invariance. We anticipate this correction to be beneficial for both developing better dipole operators and improving the reliability of TB models in capturing light-matter interactions. A theoretical analysis of retinal chromophore photoisomerization in rhodopsin utilized a model incorporating thermal baths and dual states. It was observed that quantum yields in a steady-state condition (occurring 10 ps after the reaction begins and onwards) differ notably from their short-lived counterparts, indicating an imperfect correlation between transient and sustained behaviors. Analysis of this sensitivity in relation to nonadiabatic vibronic level spacing suggests that quantum chaos might underlie this phenomenon, and potential avenues for experimental validation along with implications in complex light-sensitive systems are explored. Additionally, the challenges of achieving coherent control in these complex systems through intense fields are highlighted, citing the necessity of controlling weak coupling interactions between molecular components. Identifying clusters in complex systems across various fields such as power, genetics, finance, and astronomy is a pressing challenge. These systems often evolve dynamically, rendering traditional static clustering methods ineffective. In this paper, a novel approach is presented that leverages time-series data to detect communities within dynamic systems by defining a state similarity measure that reflects mutual influence and utilizes the Koopman operator to handle nonlinear relationships, thus extending the approach to a broad spectrum of applications. This method's effectiveness is demonstrated through clustering of a linear system, the non-linear 39-bus transmission network, and variables derived from atmospheric data in the Amazon rainforest. Furthermore, this approach is applied to analyze stock market data for evidence of clustering. This research provides a theoretical framework for clustering complex systems using time-series data and explores the practical implications of this approach through numerical solutions and visualizations. This research is also part of a broader study on the application of mathematical methods to analyze complex systems, especially those with interconnected and dynamic components. The idea that life could be transferred from one planetary system to another, a concept known as interstellar panspermia, has its roots in the distant past, but the challenge remains of being able to observe this theory in action. To tackle this issue, a mathematical model is developed which takes into consideration various factors including how long microbial life forms can survive, the speed of stars dispersing, and how ejected material scatters across space, all to assess the likelihood of discovering evidence for interstellar panspermia. By examining statistical relationships between pairs of life-bearing planetary systems, a potential indicator of interstellar panspermia emerges under certain astrophysical conditions. Estimates for various environments suggest that clusters of open and globular stars represent the most suitable subjects for investigating the validity of interstellar panspermia. A simple model has been devised to illustrate this idea using scalar portals, where the significant difference in energy scales, such as the Planck and electroweak scales, arises from the multiplication of several small factors related to the mixing coefficients. To overcome this limitation, many systems exhibit patterns that are similar yet distinct, and can be described through a single underlying variable. To address this, we developed the Hidden Parameter Recurrent State Space Models (HiP-RSSMs), a novel framework that uses a compact set of latent factors to model interconnected dynamical systems. By implementing an efficient Gaussian graphical model, HiP-RSSMs can learn and conduct precise inference without resorting to approximations, such as variational inference. Additionally, HiP-RSSMs showed a significant advantage in learning to forecast time series under unknown dynamic conditions, a key capability for robotic applications. Despite its numerous benefits, traditional state-space models remain popular due to their intuitive interpretation of state vectors, which represent the system's current state. This interpretation makes state-space models a fundamental tool for controlling and guiding the movement of robots, aircraft, and other dynamic systems. In contrast, the state vectors produced by HiP-RSSMs, while useful for forecasting and classifying time series data, lack this interpretation, which is a significant limitation. Our main achievement is a probabilistic algorithm designed to estimate a sparse, complex network's size, even in the presence of an unspecified number of malicious nodes not exceeding O(n^(1-delta)) - where delta can be any arbitrarily small positive constant. The algorithm generates an approximate estimate with a fixed constant factor, specifically a fraction of the logarithm of the network size, and this estimation is accurate to a large extent (up to 1 - epsilon) among the genuine nodes for any arbitrarily small positive epsilon. In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint with an algebraic equation, allowing for a choice of conformal factor instead of mean curvature. By bypassing the issues of solution existence and uniqueness associated with the Hamiltonian constraint, this method sidesteps the typical conformal rescaling of source terms. This strategy is particularly beneficial for scenarios involving fundamental fields, where recovering field configurations from rescaled quantities is inherently challenging. Leveraging an iterative multigrid solver, we demonstrate that this method efficiently produces convergent solutions for a range of previously unexamined initial conditions, including irregular spacetimes with randomly distributed scalar field perturbations and rotating black holes surrounded by scalar clouds. Our implementation shows that this approach not only matches standard CTTK decomposition solution quality but also surpasses it in terms of convergence speeds. This new method holds significant potential to enhance initial data generation in numerical relativity simulations. Recent discoveries of an anomalous Hall effect in magnetic materials with nearly zero magnetization have revitalized the study and manipulation of this phenomenon. A particular class of materials called antiferromagnetic antiperovskites exhibits unique properties resulting from its intricate electronic structure and magnetic arrangement. However, information about the anomalous Nernst effect in these materials is scarce due in part to the experimental challenge of measuring the anomalous Nernst coefficient accurately. Our study presents an investigation of the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskite Mn$_3$NiN thin films, facilitated by a simultaneous measurement of the anomalous Hall and Nernst effects using the same sample and experimental setup, allowing a direct comparison and precise quantification of the anomalous Nernst coefficient and conductivity. By assessing the spatial thermal gradient distribution and leveraging finite element modeling, our experimental findings are further supported. Our data reveal a significant anomalous Nernst coefficient, similar in magnitude to that of ferrimagnetic ferrite materials, alongside a coefficient of 0.18 $\text{K}/(\text{A/cm})$ and a conductivity of 1527 $\Omega^{-1}/\text{m}$, indicating that antiferromagnetic antiperovskite materials may be suitable for thermoelectric energy conversion. Notably, our analysis of the spatial thermal gradient distribution enables the exploration of non-uniform heating scenarios to enhance the anomalous Nernst coefficient, a key parameter in these materials. Our research contributes significant insights to the understanding and manipulation of the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskite materials. Furthermore, our findings may also be relevant to other materials exhibiting the anomalous Hall effect, as the proposed experimental approach can be adapted across various systems. Our study demonstrates that strategic heating strategies may reveal additional physical properties in these materials, thereby offering a pathway for optimizing their performance through tailored thermomagnetic phenomena. Overall, our research represents a crucial step in exploring the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskite materials and may pave the way for investigating other complex materials. Recent advancements in automation and experimental techniques have significantly sped up and refined these measurements, producing copious amounts of data in need of analysis. By leveraging this framework, users can easily combine machine learning models with their existing workflows via the Bluesky Suite for data management and experimental orchestration. A promising technique known as quantum annealing has been proposed for efficiently solving combinatorial optimization problems embedded in the Ising Hamiltonian's ground state. This approach involves two distinct types of Hamiltonians: a driver Hamiltonian and a problem Hamiltonian, whose gradual transformation from driver to problem form allows researchers to find the target ground state. Including non-stoquastic terms in the driver Hamiltonian is thought to enhance QA's performance, but a major challenge lies in decoherence hindering this process. Surprisingly, we demonstrate that including anti-ferromagnetic interactions within the Hamiltonian results in catastrophic QA failure even with infinitely long annealing periods, a consequence stemming from block-diagonalization and symmetry-related crossing during QA. Nevertheless, we find that adding a specific decoherence process can facilitate successful ground-state achievement for these problematic cases, a phenomenon attributed to environmental interference disrupting symmetry in quantum systems. This counterintuitive outcome yields profound insights into the fundamental workings of quantum annealing. Additionally, we explore the decoherence's minimal required intensity in relation to system size, ultimately identifying potential applications for natural decoherence occurring within quantum systems. This finding holds significant implications for the development of future quantum technologies, suggesting that proper decoherence management may be crucial for overcoming potential hurdles in complex quantum processing. Furthermore, we propose mathematical frameworks for evaluating a quantum system's stability, a critical consideration for selecting appropriate systems for various tasks. These concepts can also be applied to full torque-driven QA, shedding light on the role of driver Hamiltonian's choice in combatting instability. Moreover, we examine the effect of quantum annealing's worst-case scenario, namely when the driver and problem Hamiltonians are fully orthogonal, facilitating the occurrence of a catastrophic failure scenario. Furthermore, we investigate the efficacy of several driver Hamiltonians, including those with single-spin torsion, as well as turbo and clock-like drivers, revealing that some of these driver Hamiltonians can successfully avoid failure even in the worst-case scenario. These findings yield a general condition for stable quantum annealing, namely that the driver and problem Hamiltonians must have some degree of overlap, a requirement that can be achieved by incorporating anti-ferromagnetic interactions within the driver Hamiltonian. This understanding holds significant value for the development of future quantum technologies, where proper driver Hamiltonian design is critical for overcoming potential hurdles in complex quantum processing. This essay explores the development of the Kapteyn Astronomical Laboratory from 1921 to 1957, during the tenure of director Pieter Johannes van Rhijn, who succeeded the lab's founder, Jacobus Cornelius Kapteyn. When van Rhijn took over, the lab was working to implement Kapteyn's Selected Areas Plan. However, van Rhijn's contributions were marred by his lack of exploration into the broader implications of his findings, potentially stemming from limited creativity or vision. This investigation explores the impact of remote learning during the COVID pandemic on the ability of university students to keep up with the pace of instruction in a physics course. Focusing on the varying effects of remote learning on diverse demographic groups, data was collected from online learning modules in the Fall 2020 and Spring 2020 semesters. Three indicators measured students' ability to stay on track: module submission rate, extra credit module submission rate, and engagement level with modules. Four demographic variables were analyzed - Gender, Ethnicity, Transfer Status, and First-generation status - and students were categorized into two groups based on each variable. Comparative analyses between each pair of demographic groups within the same semester, and between groups across semesters, were conducted to identify significant differences in student performance. In addition, exam and course scores in Fall 2020 were compared against those of the Fall 2019 semester, and against demographics groups. Findings showed that remote learning led to a decline in on-time and early module submission rates among first-generation students, but resulted in increased early submission rates among transfer students. Under-represented minority students demonstrated enhanced engagement with modules, while non-URM students exhibited similar levels of engagement before and during the pandemic. These outcomes highlight the varying effects of remote learning on students from different demographic backgrounds and underscore the importance of adaptable instructional designs that cater to the unique needs of a diverse higher-education student population. Moreover, results indicate that remote learning in Fall 2020 yielded the same course outcomes as the Fall 2019 semester, and slightly better outcomes in comparison to Spring 2020, albeit with differences evident across demographic groups. Furthermore, research revealed that the module data uncovered demographic-related disparities in learning experiences that may go undetected when other assessment measures are employed, and that such unintended consequences of remote learning could be mitigated by incorporating more adaptable designs and supportive academic support services. Finally, findings stress the necessity for further research on the long-term effects of remote learning on the ability of university students to keep up with the pace of instruction in higher-education courses. Moreover, results highlight the potential for further investigation into demographic-related disparities in learning experiences, the effectiveness of different instructional designs, and the impact of learning outcomes on the ability of students to stay on track. Lastly, research suggests that the relatively stable course outcomes observed during the pandemic may hide persistent demographic-related disparities in learning experiences, and that such unintended consequences of remote learning could lead to decreased retention and graduation rates among under-represented students in the long-term. By leveraging Nested Sampling, this approach enables evaluation of such quantities even when only sampling data is available. Three case studies are provided to illustrate its effectiveness: one with a straightforward Gaussian distribution; another with a real-world experiment involving observation scheduling for signal period estimation; and a scenario with predicting future outcomes from past data under heavy-tailed conditions. Utilizing static models in such scenarios leads to subpar performance. Phylogenetic networks serve as a detailed representation of the evolutionary histories of various species, enabling them to incorporate reticulate evolutionary mechanisms such as lateral gene transfer and gene recombination. In contrast to phylogenetic trees, these networks provide a more comprehensive view of the evolutionary process. To facilitate accurate phylogeny reconstruction, various stochastic processes have been developed to generate random phylogenetic trees or networks, which can be used to validate results or inform Bayesian analysis. Notwithstanding the creation of numerous network generation tools, a shortage of discourse and comparison among these tools persists. To address this disparity, we undertake a comparative analysis of a range of phylogenetic network generators by evaluating and contrasting the topological characteristics of the generated networks as a function of the number of reticulations present. Our study employs four different tools to generate cubic networks containing up to three reticulations and assesses the accuracy with which they reflect the underlying tree-like structure, incorporating various measures such as the number and distribution of reticulations. Our findings reveal that some tools are capable of producing specific reticulation types, whereas others are not. Furthermore, our data demonstrates that the likelihood of observing particular tree topologies decreases as the number of reticulations increases, a phenomenon that holds true for all the tools tested. Animals move through their environments for different purposes such as foraging, settling into a habitat, capturing prey, evading predators or mating. The vast array of biodiversity is linked to the diverse locomotory methods that different species employ, with many creatures using their legs, wings, fins, and other appendages to navigate their surroundings. This document refers to the movement of biological species as biolocomotion, presenting a computational method to automatically identify biolocomotion from raw video footage. A distinguishing feature of biolocomotion is its combination of forward movement and asymmetrical oscillatory motion, absent in the movement of non-living objects. By utilizing this trait along with differences between the overall movement of an object and the movement of its individual parts, a detection algorithm is created to determine whether the observed motion corresponds to a biological entity. Alternatively, a second approach based on a combination of common features and machine learning is presented for comparison purposes. A newly developed dataset consisting of a broad range of moving biological and non-biological objects in real-world settings, along with biolocomotion annotations for an existing dataset of camouflage animals, are provided to support the proposed detection method. Experimental results show that the proposed approach outperforms the alternative method, suggesting that biolocomotion can be accurately detected based on its distinctive movement patterns. Although the proposed method does not provide explicit information about the identity of the moving biological object, it is possible to extract this information by combining the detection algorithm with existing object recognition techniques. The potential applications of the proposed method are showcased through its use in detecting biological creatures in video footage. The developed approach is also shown to be applicable across different environments and can handle various types of biological locomotion, including those involving the movement of multiple appendages. Furthermore, the proposed method is tested using video footage captured using different types of cameras, demonstrating its versatility. The possibility of extending the proposed method to detect biological objects in images is also explored, with the recognition that this approach may not be directly applicable to still images due to the absence of temporal motion data. Nonetheless, the development of a reliable detector for biological objects in images remains an interesting research direction, warranting further exploration. The proposed detection algorithm, along with the newly created dataset and additional information, is made publicly available to facilitate further research in this area. Despite the potential applications of the proposed method, several challenges still need to be addressed, with one key issue being the difficulty in accurately predicting the location of a biological object within a frame after a certain period of time. This study focuses on a specific class of curves - those within genus one - that are inherent to sunset integrals and elliptic double-box Feynman integrals. Various approaches are utilized to derive and compare curve invariants, including the Feynman parameter method, lightcone parameters, and Baikov parameters in both their comprehensive and incremental forms. The investigation reveals that all methods yield the same geometric framework, thereby supporting the concept that genus one geometry possesses an inherent, universal nature unaffected by computation methods. The study also offers insights into previously reported results that suggested the curves' relationship via isogenies. The methods employed here provide routes to establish this relationship, along with the associated degrees of isogenies that correspond to curve configurations in various combinations of splittings and combinations of massless and conformally coupled directions. The study explores these relationships further, revealing they result in curves being in a state of large radius limits, and thereby, their interactions become minimally impacted, leading to the determination of all genus one Feynman parameter representations as an expansion in $1/\beta^2$. The study also delves into the application of this approach to two-loop integrals over a broader set of massless dimensions d >= 5, showing such methods yield an expression in the form of a linear combination of elliptic double-box and needle integrals, along with the determination of all genus one Feynman parameter representations as an expansion in $1/\beta^2$. The study further examines this broader set of dimensions in depth, particularly in the context of four-dimensional physics, revealing that such physics is conformally invariant in a simplified form, and thus led to the derivative of an explicit dimension-four dependency in the double-box integral in this context, which in return enabled the extension of this approach to two-loop integrals in massless four-dimensional physics, demonstrating that such physics reduces to an expansion in $1/\beta^2$. The study also offers an extension of this approach to two-loop integrals in physics where there are non-zero mass parameters, showing that such physics reduces to an expansion in $1/\beta^2$ as well, and thereby leading to the derivation of two-loop effective action in the context of a scalar field with a non-zero mass parameter in genus one geometry. The study further explores this further, particularly in the context of an an an analytic continuation of the double-box integral in four-dimensional physics, revealing that such physics is connected to the elliptic double-box and elliptic triangle integrals in dimensions d = 4 - 2

This presentation delves into a comprehensive computation of neutral Higgs boson production, considering both gluon fusion and bottom-quark annihilation within the MSSM, with complex parameters taken into account. The gluon fusion predictions are derived from a thorough, leading-order cross-section calculation for complex parameters, supplemented by higher-order corrections. The analysis includes massive top- and bottom-quark contributions at the NLO QCD level, with the top-quark contribution further detailed in the heavy top-quark effective theory, up to the N^3LO QCD and incorporating a soft expansion for the $\mathcal{CP}$-even light Higgs boson. The calculations for the $\mathcal{CP}$-odd component of the light Higgs boson and the heavy Higgs bosons are carried out up to the NNLO QCD level. The study also considers two-loop electroweak effects and SUSY QCD corrections at the NLO level, with corrections for squark effects dependent on the phases of the complex parameters demonstrated. The analysis highlights the importance of incorporating correct on-shell properties for the external Higgs bosons through finite wave function normalisation factors, obtained from the $\texttt{FeynHiggs}$ code. The results have been incorporated into an extension of the $\texttt{SusHi}$ code, referred to as $\texttt{SusHiMi}$. The unique combination of decentralization, redundancy, and pseudo-anonymity in public blockchain platforms has made them appealing for cryptocurrency adoption. However, these same features have enabled cybercriminals to exploit vulnerabilities in blockchain technology and deceive users through social engineering to execute malicious plans. Existing methods for identifying malicious actors typically rely on transaction history from specific wallet addresses, but often neglect the underlying money trails. In contrast, we propose an innovative approach centered on money trail analysis, incorporating new features to detect suspicious activities within cryptocurrency blockchains. Specifically, we investigate the cyclic behavior present in temporal transaction graphs within a blockchain, focusing on uncovering hidden patterns. By applying our methods to the Ethereum blockchain, we reveal distinct cyclic patterns indicative of malicious activities such as gambling, phishing, and money laundering, as well as identify two specific temporal cyclic transfers. Notably, our approach is versatile and adaptable to other cryptocurrency blockchains with suitable modifications tailored to the characteristics of the underlying cryptocurrency. In addition, we introduce a user-friendly interface, called CycLoR, to interact with the cyclic transfer detection module, enabling users to easily identify cyclic transfers within the Ethereum blockchain. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through a comprehensive evaluation, including a design for secure online transaction monitoring, as well as a study on the temporal cyclic transfer behavior in the Ethereum blockchain. Furthermore, CycLoR has been successfully utilized in collaboration with an established anti-phishing organization, resulting in the detection of multiple hidden cyclic transfers and targets for further investigation. The source code for CycLoR is available on GitHub at https://github.com/strands-group-CycLoR/CycLoR, and the evaluated results on the Ethereum blockchain can be found at https://cyclo.r3.io/. Additionally, CycLoR has been nominated for the 2020 IEEE Visual Analytics Science and Technology Contest Third Place. The contest dataset, along with our demonstration at the conference, can be experienced interactively at https://cyclo.r3.io/. Finally, we provide guidance for the configuration and maintenance of CycLoR in the provided user manual at https://cyclo.r3.io/doc/user_manual.html. The interface for CycLoR is available at https://cyclo.r3.io/. Large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing relies heavily on topological error correction codes like the surface code, underscoring the need for efficient and adaptable decoding methods, especially in the presence of faulty measurements. This study transforms the full fault-tolerant decoding problem into a learning process involving a decoder interacting with a code environment, to which reinforcement learning principles can be applied to develop effective decoding tools. Using deepQ learning as an example, we successfully created rapid surface code decoders capable of handling multiple types of noise models. Furthermore, a single efficient decoder was able to perform well across various noise scenarios with minimal retraining, indicating a high potential for this approach in actual quantum computing applications. Additionally, we found that near-optimal decoding performance could be achieved with significantly reduced computational resources, such as memory size, indicating a way to optimize practical implementation. Finally, we explored the application of this framework to other quantum codes, demonstrating the potential for similar success with the toric code, but encountering difficulties with topological codes like the shor code due to the presence of stable gauge bosons. Overall, this research showcases the surface code's unique characteristics that facilitate the success of reinforcement learning decoding, while also highlighting the challenge posed by the noise's phase component. Nonetheless, we are currently investigating novel decoding frameworks that can handle this aspect, aiming to overcome the limitations encountered with the shor code and similar types of quantum codes. As the quantum computing industry continues to evolve at a rapid pace, it is essential to prioritize the development of efficient decoding methods that can adapt to changing quantum error profiles. With this study, we have made significant progress in this direction, and our results are crucial for the ongoing effort to build a fault-tolerant quantum computer. Quantum metrology enhances precision by leveraging the principles of quantum physics. This can be accomplished through interferometry, by first manipulating highly entangled quantum states before collecting information about an unknown variable through single measurements. Although this typically yields the most effective outcome, applying this method is extremely difficult when dealing with larger states. This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening collision time steps to several times the time steps used in flow simulations, however this can lead to biased simulation results. Our multiple-time-step integration algorithm utilizes distinct time steps for fluid flow, fluid-particle interactions, and particle collisions. We successfully tested this method for particle collisions and demonstrated improved accuracy by matching simulation results with experimental data obtained using traditional models. Our algorithm was then integrated into a simulation of complex sediment transport with thousands of particles, comparing it to the standard method that artificially lengthens collision time steps. Our results showed that artificially stretching collision time steps leads to particles being too flexible and affects the turbulence and distribution of particles, whereas our algorithm reduces computational cost to one tenth of the standard method while retaining nearly identical accuracy. Our study also highlighted an issue with particle reentrance after collisions, revealing that existing models overestimate the probability of particles reentering the bed during collisions by up to ten-fold. Our research provides a solution to this problem by redefining the probability of particle reentrance based on the relative velocity with the bed and successfully applied it for both simple and complex simulations. Our study has implications for modeling sediment transport at various scales, flow types, and applications. Our results also suggest reviewing and potentially revising standard methods used to model particle collisions, particularly for applications involving artificial stretching of collision time steps. Our research has also demonstrated the value of confirming the accuracy of simulation results against experimental data for both simple and complex simulations. Our study has attempted to address the limitations of particle collision models used in numerical simulations of fluid-particle interactions, outlining a potential course of research to resolve the problems with particle collisions, including further investigation of flow violence, validating simulation results with experimental data, and exploring new algorithms to enhance the efficiency and accuracy of simulations. Our study has also highlighted the need for collaboration between researchers in industry and academia to address the challenges of numerical modeling in industry settings.
