A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the uncertainty that arises when robots navigate deformable terrain. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of terrain dynamics caused by ground deformation. Developing efficient and stable control systems for robots moving on soft ground poses an even greater problem. This project focuses on controlling a one-legged hopping robot to jump to a predetermined height. Initially, a simulated environment representing a soft ground was created using a discrete element method (DEM) based on spherical granular material. This simulation was utilized to derive models of ground reaction forces through the resistive force theory (RFT). A feedforward force control system was developed and tested in conjunction with the DEM simulation. To account for discrepancies in the RFT model's predictions of ground reaction forces, a feedback control system was employed. As a result, the robot successfully tracked its intended trajectory, reached the desired height in five hops, and reduced height errors compared to a feedforward control system alone. Furthermore, by increasing the robot's foot area from 1cm^2 to 49cm^2, the feedback controller demonstrated its ability to adapt to changing ground reaction forces, even when the foot size was comparable to the diameter of individual grains. This research provides evidence that advanced control systems can enable stable operation of one-legged robots on soft ground, potentially paving the way for control systems that account for ground reaction forces in multiple-legged robots. In addition, this work highlights the potential of DEM simulations and control system design to produce consistent performance across different robot foot sizes and terrain samples. This research was presented at the 2019 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS). Since then, a video of the associated demonstration was released on the Yale Robotics YouTube channel. It demands that models infer the implications of negated statements within passages, collected from a diverse set of paragraphs featuring varied negation cues. Additionally, human evaluators asked questions regarding the implications of these negations and performed a series of challenging tasks: paraphrasing negated statements, altering the scope of negation, and reversing the negation, resulting in distinct groups of question-answer pairs that current models struggle to tackle without resorting to workarounds. Our CONDAQA dataset comprises 14,182 challenging question-answer pairs, encompassing over 200 unique negation cues and proves particularly demanding for leading NLP models. Notably, even the best-performing model (UnifiedQA-v2-3b) managed only 42% accuracy according to our consistency metric, significantly lagging behind the 81% achieved by human evaluators. In a bid to fuel further NLP innovations, we publicly release our dataset, along with comprehensive evaluations involving fully-finetuned, few-shot, and zero-shot scenarios. Our aims align with those of prominent datasets like NaturalLogicMars or AristoMultigenre, which have greatly contributed to the development of comprehensive NLP models capable of navigating complex situations. Like them, we anticipate that CONDAQA will play a pivotal role in the creation of flexible, commonsense reasoning models. Ultimately, such models are crucial for empowering natural language processors to efficiently process a wide range of everyday texts that often incorporate negations as a normal part of constructed sentences. In contrast, models lacking such capacity have been shown to fall prey to misconceptions and inaccuracies when presented with negated statements, as evidenced by recent studies. Therefore, we consider the construction of highly effective NLP models to be dependent on the availability of specialized datasets like CONDAQA, which provide the necessary tools for continuously advancing the field's ability to process negation effectively. Moreover, our work highlights the considerable differences that exist between human intuition and the actual performance of cutting-edge NLP models. In particular, our evaluation highlights the significant disparity between the ease with which humans can comprehend the implications of negations when stated orally, as opposed to in written form. Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, yet the automatic generation methods available today don't account for the interconnections in modern information networks. Presently, most techniques represent topics as abstract probabilities rather than tangible components of the underlying network, and many lack the scalability needed for web-based applications. In contrast, we propose a novel approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), utilizing a non-parametric distributed processing model that effectively extracts meaningful hierarchies from large networks, even at a massive data scale, as evidenced by our experiments using three smaller datasets and Wikipedia's full content. HDTM's results were found to be prunable for topic interpretation without sacrificing coherence, and its scalability was demonstrated by applying the model to massive datasets. Furthermore, we show that HDTM-generated hierarchies are coherent and readable, and our implementation's efficiency is showcased by its application to Wikipedia. Our code is openly accessible on GitHub. Leveraging a web crawler and reducing Wikipedia to its core, we generated a hierarchy with 12 topics having over 10 million associated document pairs, and this has been made available on Wikipedia's research page. In addition to presenting our approach, we explore how to effectively visualize multi-level hierarchies, and our innovations have already been utilized in two external projects. Our research provides a scalable solution for extracting meaningful organizational structures from large information networks and offers a suitable alternative to current topic modeling techniques. As such, we believe it to be a significant improvement over previous methods. Additionally, our approach has already been applied in practical applications, and we hope our findings will be built upon by other researchers in the field. Two specific applications of our approach are described in Sections 4 and 5 of the paper, and its performance is examined in detail in Section 6. This study investigates the interconnection between the two scenarios and reveals that the minimal point of the annealing gap, a critical obstacle in quantum annealing algorithms, can be determined from a dynamical quench parameter that defines the quantum state following the quench. When combined with statistical tools, such as neural network training, this relationship between quench and annealing dynamics can be utilized to accurately reproduce the annealing gap's functional behavior based solely on the quench data. As such, partial or full understanding of the annealing gap, obtained in this manner, can be employed to devise optimized quantum annealing protocols, leading to a tangible improvement in solution-finding efficiency. These findings stem from simulations of random Ising Hamiltonians that model complex, intractable instances of the exact cover problem. Furthermore, the representation of the annealing gap's function through quench data holds significant theoretical value, as it implies the existence of a quantifiable, universal gap dynamics that underlies all quantum annealing processes. This universal gap dynamics can be probed experimentally using the same quench dynamics, thereby providing valuable insights into the process. Overall, this research demonstrates the usefulness of quench studies in the optimization context and sheds light on the underlying dynamics of quantum annealing. Additionally, it highlights the potential for overlap between quantum annealing's problem-solving and our understanding of quench and annealing dynamics. Finally, this study proves that the description of the annealing gap through quench data can be experimentally verified, which paves the way for the investigation of other theoretical gap dynamics in various quantum annealing scenarios. extent to which it can be reduced to a simplified one-band Hubbard model. 
Screening of the $s$-like orbital's influence is a critical factor here. 
Without screening, an isolated highly-correlated band yields an
antiferromagnetic ground state. For mild screening, strong correlations cause
the more freely moving $s$-electrons to shift to the $d$-band and the nickelate
then becomes a half-filled, highly insulating state. This case is notably
distinct from high-$T_c$ cuprates, with $s$-wave symmetry being a more
expected phenomenon. 
On the other hand, strong screening leads to a mixture of filled and weakly
coupled $s$ and $d_{x^2-y^2}$ bands and results in self-doped $d$ orbital and
$d$-wave pairing tendencies emerging. 
Interestingly, strong screening allows for another one-band physics approximation,
this time incorporating significant weight transfer when an extra filled $s$-band
is included, exhibiting both one-band physics and Kondo-lattice-like behavior,
which arises solely from this single model.

essential to describe the inherent complexity of infinite layered nickelates.

mutually exclusive.

An anti Tai mapping, defined as the subset $M$ of $V_1\times V_2$, excludes any node pairs $(x,y)$ and $(x',y')$ that would conflict with each other's ancestral hierarchy, given that $x<x'$ indicates $x$ is an ancestor of $x'$. This research addresses the challenge of protecting machine learning (ML) model outputs from an untrusted client and a semi-reliable server. The goal is for the client to obtain the inference output while the server learns nothing. Although initial studies by Lehmkuhl and Chandran have shown significant advancements, there remains a considerable gap between current solutions and practical implementations. To address this issue, our proposal SIMC 2.0 maintains the foundation of Chandran's work while improving the efficiency of linear and non-linear layers within the ML model. Key innovations include a customized coding technique for matrix and vector operations that reduces expensive rotation computations. Furthermore, SIMC 2.0 reduces the size of garbled circuits used for non-linear calculations and introduces an alternative lightweight protocol. As a result, our experiments demonstrate substantial performance gains for linear computations (up to 17.4 times faster), reduced computation and communication overhead in non-linear layers (by at least 1.3 times), and improved overall runtime by 2.3 to 4.3 times. Additionally, SIMC 2.0 exhibits competitive security attributes on par with state-of-the-art solutions like Leonidas and Hexayou. To facilitate reproducibility and exploration of various cryptographic components, our implementation includes modular protocol stacks that enable experimentation with distinct security parameters. Our results demonstrate the efficiency and practicality of SIMC 2.0 for securing real-world ML models. To this end, we introduce a benchmark that evaluates the performance of ML models based on multiple criteria, including model size, computation intensity, and overall runtime. Using this benchmark, we find SIMC 2.0 capable of securely supporting up to 450 linear calculations, 40 non-linear calculations, and multiple real-world ML models, including convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and reinforcement learning models. To further improve the scalability of SIMC 2.0, we introduce two novel protocols, SIMC-HLS and SIMC-GLV, that leverage hardware accelerators for improved performance. Experimentation with actual hardware demonstrates that these protocols achieve enhanced security and near native performance for specific application domains. Finally, we conclude that our proposal SIMC 2.0 represents a well-rounded solution meeting both high performance and security standards for securing ML inference against malicious clients. To facilitate exploration of future research directions, we provide a comprehensive evaluation framework that assesses the performance of different secure ML protocols. Using this framework, we identify several opportunities for further improvement, including the development of more efficient customized coding techniques and lighter-weight rotation protocols.

Our team employed photonic technology to revolutionize the conventional method of spectroscopy, enabling on-device spectral cross-correlation using a template spectrum. This was achieved by designing photonic devices with intricately modulated transmission spectra, thus performing cross-correlation without the need for dispersion. Consequently, our device simplifies the apparatus while reducing its overall cost, enabling precise detection of atomic/molecular substances as well as accurate radial velocity measurements of astrophysical objects.

We outline two innovative design approaches based on distinct photonic platforms, silicon and fibre-based photonics. Silicon-based photonic technology incorporates thermally modulated ring resonators for spectral cross-correlation, whereas fibre-based photonics utilize strain-modulated customized fibre Bragg gratings. Both approaches successfully detected molecular gas in a laboratory setting and are currently undergoing field testing.

Furthermore, our research has far-reaching implications as these photonic devices may pave the way for developing low-cost, custom-built spectrographic instruments capable of simultaneously analyzing multiple objects or providing high-resolution field spectra. This technology has immense potential to contribute to groundbreaking research in stellar radial velocity measurements and exoplanet discoveries.

In the context of a Parameter Server, learning a model from distributed data on a graph is a challenging task, especially when it comes to Federated Learning. A significant obstacle in this process is the substantial communication required between nodes and the server. A common strategy used to address this issue involves each node making several local model updates before sharing the updated model with the server. Although this method reduces communication costs, it introduces statistical disparities among the nodes' data sets, leading to slower model convergence and biases. This paper explores the application of random walk learning algorithms to tackle these issues by exploiting existing connections between nodes, as they typically require less communication with the server. A random walk is proposed where a node shares the updated model with a neighbor, with the aim of visiting more informative nodes more frequently. This goal is framed as a sleeping multi-armed bandit problem to devise an efficient node sampling strategy that generates variance-reduced gradient estimates. A novel adaptive random walk learning algorithm is introduced and proven to converge theoretically. Moreover, our results demonstrate its superior performance compared to other random walk algorithms. Notably, our proposed algorithm outperforms existing methods in terms of model accuracy on real-world datasets. Additionally, the energy savings achieved by random walk learning are substantial, amounting to up to $17\%$ in energy consumption. As the field of Federated Learning continues to evolve, the potential applications of random walk learning algorithms will expand, making them essential for addressing the challenges of large-scale FL deployments. Nonetheless, there are instances where random walk learning may not yield substantial energy reductions, such as (1) large models requiring less communication, (2) nodes with large, diverse data sets, or (3) sparse, uniform graph connections. In these scenarios, the benefits of random walk learning might be marginal, resulting in only slight improvements in energy efficiency. Consequently, more significant advantages in energy savings, up to $17\%$ in our experiments, will motivate the fusion of machine learning and optical transport technologies to achieve multi-layer transport protocols, leading to potential energy reductions of up to $48\%$. As a result, future large-scale FL deployments will need to consider more sophisticated multi-layer transport architectures, leading to increased cooperation between ML and OT researchers. This, in turn, may give rise to innovative new data transfer protocols, such as those utilizing the principles of entropy from information theory, such as relative entropy, Kullback-Leibler divergence, or Jensen-Shannon entropy, leading to even more substantial energy reductions of up to $48\%$. Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health disorders.  An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 1994 and 2009 examined how court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation affects an offender's chances of returning to the justice system.  The research focuses on offenders who were sentenced to probation and assesses those who were required to undergo mental health treatment against those who were not.  It discovered that receiving mental health treatment as part of their sentence lowered the odds of recidivism within a three-year time frame by 17 percent or 5.6 percentage points.  The data suggests mental health treatment reduces future violent and property crimes more significantly and that this reduction in crimes increases with time since the original conviction.  An initial financial analysis of these results indicates the decrease in future crime could cover and exceed the expenses associated with providing treatment.  However, the study also discovered a closed loop where offenders with greater mental health needs are more likely to be given ineffective and short-term treatment as part of their sentence, suggesting an opportunity to improve the effectiveness of mental health services within the criminal justice system.  To address potential selection issues, the study employed statistical matching and identified key differences between offenders who received mental health treatment and those who did not, including greater mental health needs, more severe previous crimes, and higher rates of previous justice system encounters.  Notably, offenders with the greatest mental health disorders saw the most significant reduction in future crime, a finding that could result from either improved treatment outcomes or a self-selection effect where those with the greatest needs are more likely to engage with the treatment process. This enhancement includes upgrading the Level 1 trigger based on calorimeter data to utilize finer details of the data, courtesy of the Feature EXtractors (FEX) system. Specifically, the jet FEX (jFEX) system aims to enhance jet identification and calculate global variables within an extremely tight latency constraint of under 400 nanoseconds. This will involve six distinct modules, where each module on an ATCA board contains four high-end Xilinx FPGAs to process the data at an astonishing 3.6 terabytes per second rate. This ATCA board utilizes an array of components such as electrical-optical devices and multi-gigabit transceivers for data transfer, as well as a custom 24-layer PCB to minimize interference while maintaining high signal integrity. This project has successfully overcome design hurdles and has demonstrated its performance capabilities with the fully assembled final prototype having achieved up to 12.8 gigabits per second during in-house and CERN integrated testing. With production scheduled for completion by the end of 2018, the full jFEX system will be ready for deployment before the LHC's anticipated 2021 restart. This project serves as a landmark example for the feasibility and viability of implementing complex digital trigger systems in particle physics. It does this by leveraging the capabilities of modern digital technology, such as FPGAs and high-speed serial interfaces, to process vast amounts of data at incredible speeds. This work also highlights the importance of close collaboration between hardware designers, physicists, and system engineers in achieving such complex digital systems. This will be particularly relevant during the ongoing and future detector system upgrades in the context of the HEP community's evolving needs. It is essential to note that this work has incorporated industry-standard digital technology widely employed in numerous industrial applications beyond particle physics. This includes the use of FPGAs, such as the Xilinx Ultrascale+ family, along with optical connections such as the XAUI interface, and multi-gigabit transceivers like the K28-5 interface. This paper provides a technical overview of the jFEX system, its associated logic using FPGAs, as well as the resulting data transfer using optical connections and multiple gigabit interfaces. This involves describing the design of the feature extractor using FPGAs, its associated data path using multi-gigabit interfaces, and the resulting data transfer using optical connections.

A floating raft made of particles offers a clear model for observing material breakdown. Due to the slow timescales, both how the particles move back to a more stable configuration and the formation of cracks within the raft can be measured precisely. When we extend a raft made of particles by expanding its surface of support, we see that its breaking pattern changes constantly based on the rate at which we are stretching it. This effect is caused by the ongoing competition between two speed factors: the rate at which the particles reassemble, which is influenced by forces like viscosity and surface tension, and the rate at which neighboring particles move apart due to the expansion of the surrounding fluid. This balance of forces ultimately decides the length of clusters within the raft. A theoretical model that takes this competition into account successfully predicts the breakdown patterns we see in our experiments. This model also reveals that the clusters within the raft act as isolated units, a phenomenon we observed in another setting where we stretched a raft that had already broken apart. This paper introduces a novel form of leakage in modern encrypted databases, specifically 'update pattern leakage'. A formalized definition and security framework for DP-Sync are presented, leveraging differential privacy through 'DP update patterns'. A proposed framework, DP-Sync, builds upon existing database schemes by incorporating differential privacy-protected update patterns, ensuring the entire update history of outsourced data remains confidential. DP-Sync is demonstrated through two efficient, near-optimal constructions, one based on CP-ABE and another on searchable encryption, both of which provide update pattern privacy with minimal additional storage and low update pattern costs. Nevertheless, enhanced datasets are expected to yield statistically significant evidence in the future. This study endeavors to eliminate sampling bias in data analysis. By examining various configurations of nested samplers and traditional Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods, we aim to identify the time efficiency and consistency of these sampling techniques on pulsar timing array data. Despite producing consistent parameter results across methods, our research suggests the implementation of two robust sampling methods for cross-validation and realistic run times in future analyses. This involves employing two different nested sampler configurations: 50 and 500 walkers, which we found to be sufficient for accurate results while minimizing time expenditure. We also introduce a comprehensive package, PTABayes, incorporating an extensive dataset interface and multiple sampling methods for ease of use and reproducibility. This updated package provides the fully usable code employed in our analysis and is available for users to execute the same results. Additionally, PTABayes includes custom visualization tools to compare the results obtained using different sampling methods. This study is a significant contribution to the evolution of Bayesian analysis for pulsar timing array data and a vital step before the discovery of a nano-Hertz gravitational wave background signal. Furthermore, PTABayes is poised to become an essential tool in the statistical analysis of such data. This study underscores the importance of employing time-efficient Bayesian methods on the large datasets expected from future radio telescope observations. Using lattice QCD, a thorough investigation of correlation functions of two quark currents within a pion is conducted, yielding clear signals for nearly all significant combinations of quark field contractions except one. The results are further examined to determine how they vary with the mass of quarks and whether correlations between the quark and the corresponding antiquark play a significant role in the pion's properties. Our lattice findings are compared with theoretical predictions made through the application of chiral perturbation theory. For a pion at rest, the sum of the correlations is shown to be consistent with zero, as expected. However, the magnitude of the correlations is observed to be significantly higher than predicted by the theoretical model. Additionally, chiral perturbation theory fails to accurately explain how these correlations change as the quark mass increases, which has implications for our understanding of the pion's structure. Furthermore, the results raise interesting questions about the nature of the pion's wave function and whether it holds insights into the phenomenon of quark confinement. Ultimately, this study underscores the importance of exploring quark correlations inside hadrons to gain a more comprehensive picture of their internal structure. Despite the complexity, a straightforward interpretation of the data is presented through a numerical analysis that reveals the correlations' magnitude and how they are influenced by quark mass. This study lays the ground for more in-depth investigations of quark correlations inside other hadrons, such as vector mesons, where higher-dimensional quark field contractions arise, further complicating the analysis. Nevertheless, this research demonstrates that lattice QCD is capable of handling such complexity, making it an ideal tool for exploring the intricacies of quark structures within hadrons. In the case of the pion, lattice simulations reveal that the correlations between the quark and the corresponding antiquark are an essential aspect of its composition, with lattice QCD being an effective means of examining these relationships in depth. We gather responses from a group of participants, who consider various scenarios in which good luck can affect worker outcomes. The results show that participants generally want to reduce the gap in earnings, but are less motivated to do so and react differently to circumstances where luck has an impact on job success rather than overall income. These findings have implications for research aiming to model people's opinions on income inequality and the apparent disparity between laboratory research and real-world inequality trends in the US. Further research is needed to fully understand the underlying reasons for these differences. In the context of the current study, we identify how the diversity of participants' opinions is reflected in the variety of thought processes they use, as has been observed in previous research on the dual nature of human thinking. Additionally, we find that the variety of thought processes is linked to the degree of diversity in participants' backgrounds, with less diverse groups producing more uniform results. The range of thought processes observed in this study includes two main types: a straightforward analysis of circumstances and a more complex consideration of multiple factors, each contributing to overall income levels. When participants consider scenarios where luck affects job success rather than overall income, a larger proportion of them employ the more complex consideration of multiple factors in their analysis. This interpretation is supported by additional findings from a follow-up study, which showed that a larger subset of participants who used the complex consideration of multiple factors in the initial study, also employed a causal chain of thought, linking chance to job success and subsequent effects on income. Additionally, increasing the temperature or changing the wavelength of the light also lead to additional, valuable insights into these phenomena. Furthermore, it is shown that implementing a quantum description for interacting atoms, while resulting in more complex calculations, is ultimately justifiable as it yields accurate measurements even with loosely coupled atoms. Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
practical applications involving multiple interacting entities. Yet, offline learning often encounters issues due to differing levels of effectiveness among the agents' learned behavior. Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests lasting merely a day rather than weeks or even months. As a test of the simulation's validity, we employed deep learning agents to play both the original and accelerated versions of the games, finding that the former can learn effective strategies significantly faster than the latter. Despite the time difference, the performance of the agents on both versions was remarkably similar. We believe that TextWorldExpress offers a better balance between realistic testing and the need for large datasets, and it is available online for public use. Additionally, we include statistics on the performance of multiple state-of-the-art games agents on both TextWorldExpress and the original games. Unfortunately, many of these agents crashed during their attempts to complete the original games due to their slow speed and limited memory allocation. We hope that TextWorldExpress will serve as a more reliable and efficient platform for evaluating the full potential of virtual agents. As part of our research, we also present a general framework that can be used to optimize the performance of similar text-based games, and this framework is comprised of five key components. Finally, we acknowledge the expertise and guidance provided to us by Geoffrey James, and we offer him our heartfelt appreciation. Additionally, we would like to express our gratitude to the individuals who contributed valuable feedback to our research, particularly the team at Google AI. Finally, we would like to reiterate that TextWorldExpress is an open-source platform that is freely available for download. Deep learning models such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) have been highly effective in various sequence analysis tasks but suffer from limitations in their practical application due to their size. This problem is particularly pronounced in video recognition, which involves high-dimensional data. In an attempt to overcome these constraints and unlock the full potential of LSTMs, this research proposes an integrated design of algorithms and hardware to achieve high-performance, energy-efficient LSTM networks. At the algorithmic level, a new LSTM structure called FDHT-LSTM is developed, which significantly reduces model complexity without sacrificing accuracy. In addition to this optimized algorithm, a customized hardware platform is also designed to efficiently execute the FDHT-LSTM model by incorporating a sophisticated memory access scheme that minimizes data conflicts and allows for real-time matrix transformations. Experimental results indicate that the compact FDHT-LSTM models and the hardware accelerator exhibit high performance, outperforming existing compressed LSTM models by an order of magnitude in terms of model size while also demonstrating substantial improvements in accuracy across multiple video recognition datasets. Furthermore, the proposed FDHT-LSTM architecture is found to excel over a leading tensor decomposed hardware model called TIE in terms of throughput, area efficiency, and energy efficiency in various benchmark tests. In particular, on the HMDB51 dataset, the FDHT-LSTM model achieves an accuracy of 61.4%, a model size of 83.5KB, and requires 1.3 million logic gates to implement, along with a 32-bit binary hardware accelerator that can process approximately 43 frames per second with an energy consumption of 1.5 millijoules per frame. Overall, this research demonstrates the potential for high-performance video recognition using LSTMs through a combined algorithmic and hardware approach. Furthermore, this work's decomposed memory structure, dynamic memory access scheme, and matrix transformation unit may also find applications in other deep learning models and signal processing workflows. In addition to video recognition, this research's findings may equally be applied to speech recognition and other time-series recognition tasks involving LSTMs. In fact, this integrated design approach is particularly well-suited to handling a type of data that is becoming increasingly popular in machine learning known as multivariate time-series data. As deep learning models continue to evolve to handle increasingly complex data sets, this research's findings may prove particularly relevant in unlocking the full potential of models like LSTMs for a wider range of applications and data sets. With that in mind, this research's findings may also attract the interest of a wider range of fields beyond

Significant advancements in NLP have been observed in the last decade thanks to neural models and substantial labeled datasets. However, NLP models are often hindered by a reliance on extensive data availability, hindering their application to resource-constrained settings and unique tasks necessitating large-scale labeling. As a means of enhancing NLP data efficiency, data augmentation techniques have been investigated in recent years. A systematic examination of data augmentation in NLP under low-labeled data settings has been lacking until now, resulting in difficulty in comprehending the efficacy of diverse methods in various contexts. This study provides a comprehensive survey of data augmentation in NLP under low-labeled data settings, encompassing an overview of methods such as token-level and sentence-level augmentations, along with experiments conducted on 11 datasets across topics/news classification, inference, paraphrasing, and single-sentence tasks. Our research enables the formulation of recommendations to guide practitioners in selecting suitable augmentations tailored to different settings and highlights the current limitations and potential future pathways for NLP under low-labeled data settings. The survey also concludes with implications for further research on NLP models that are both highly parallelizable and efficient in low-resource settings, as well as the integration of domain knowledge in multi-task NLP settings. Our work is accompanied by an online repository containing reproducible experiments and actionable results. In the realm of NLP under low-labeled data settings, our study marks a significant empirical survey on data augmentation techniques. Furthermore, both theoretical and practical aspects of neural back translation are re-examined in this study, along with the exploration of novel applications for established models such as multi-task learning and universal sentence encoders. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of neural back translation in multiple settings, alongside the utility of pre-trained universal sentence encoders in reducing the requirements for labeled data. Additionally, our study highlights the challenges faced by token-level augmentations when processing topics characterized by a high proportion of out-of-vocabulary words. In the realm of NLP under low-labeled data settings, our study paves the way for the investigation of additional data augmentation techniques, as well as the exploration of novel applications for both single-sentence and paragraph-level models. Our work is accompanied by an online repository containing reproducible experiments and actionable results. Moreover, both explicit and implicit labeling methods are being continuously developed to handle increasingly complex NLP tasks that require large-scale labeling. As a result of continuously advancing in both directions, the field of NLP under low-labeled data settings is on the verge of significant breakthroughs in the near future

To stabilize the estimation of ground and excited states on a quantum computer, we modify the quantum imaginary time evolution (QITE) to utilize the model space. This model-space QITE method iteratively expands the model space while maintaining its orthogonality, enabling simultaneous description of multiple states. We enhance model-space QITE by integrating the quantum Lanczos algorithm, which boosts its convergence rate. In simulations, our approach outperforms both standard quantum Lanczos and the folded-spectrum QITE in calculating excited states. We show that spin contamination can be mitigated through an imaginary time propagator shift, efficiently obtaining excited states with specific spin properties without descending into lower-energy states with mixed spins. Additionally, we examine how the degree of unitary approximation within MSQITE influences its results. Our findings suggest that, despite unitary approximation errors, MSQITE can effectively produce multiple-state wavefunctions with a small to moderate number of unitary steps. We believe that this model-space QITE scheme has the potential to efficiently address multi-configurational problems on near-term quantum computers. Furthermore, we discuss how imaginary time propagation can be applied to tackle problematic unitary dynamics in the simulation of certain many-body systems. For instance, the challenging tunneling process in Heisenberg microscopy can be overcome by using short imaginary time evolution followed by a unitary transformation. We expect that our proposed MSQITE circuit will serve as a viable option for the development of quantum algorithms capable of resolving complex, intra-molecular processes. Nonetheless, further research is necessary to fully explore the capabilities and potential of this approach. Given a Noetherian local ring with a specific prime characteristic and its primary ideal in terms of an $\mathfrak{m}$-primary parameter, we establish criteria for $F$-rationality based on the tight Hilbert function of that ideal. These criteria make use of a specific polynomial and its coefficient. Additionally, we provide a lower bound for the tight Hilbert function that extends a previous result from Goto and Nakamura, which specifically holds true in equidimensional excellent local rings. If the ring has a specific dimension, we demonstrate the connection between the tight Hilbert function and its lower bound, achieving this condition implies that the ring is $F$-rational. However, this condition does not hold without further constraints, as evident from constructed examples. Based on the ring's properties and test elements, we find formulas to compute various coefficients, which are in turn used to establish the relationship between $F$-rationality and these coefficients, ultimately leading to the condition for $F$-rationality as depth $R \geq 2$ and a specific equality of these coefficients. Finally, we explore connections between these results and previous work, particularly focusing on the results of many authors, including Kodai, Nakamura, Sato, Takayama, and Tanaka, whose proofs often relied on the results and techniques established in this paper. Finally, we offer an open question related to the tight Hilbert function in the context of $F$-rationality. Thanks to the feedback from the audience, especially Takayama and Tanaka, the paper now includes more clear definitions, a clearer presentation of the main results, and the open question has been accurately reflected. The rapid transformation of the electricity sector necessitates innovative ancillary services that guarantee the stability and dependability of the electricity network. Unfortunately, evaluations and policy advice concerning ancillary services and market structures lack methods for examining the intricate interplay between markets and services. Consequently, this study presents an open-source agent-based model to evaluate design options for ancillary services and electricity markets. The Ancillary Services Acquisition Model integrates the MESA agent-based modeling framework with the PyPSA Python toolset for Power System Analysis. This model offers adjustable market parameters, agent-specific tactics, and thorough clearing algorithms for the day-ahead market, continuous intra-day trading, redispatch, and imbalance management. Furthermore, the model includes multiple policy performance indicators, including a novel pricing multiplier and new redispatch performance indicators. The results from a stylized simulation scenario validated the model and explored a redispatch design issue, revealing several key implications. The findings indicate that, when implementing order types in multi-period redispatch markets, the following effects are produced: the risk is minimized for market participants due to complete order fulfillment, but this may lead to increased trading of imbalances during intra-day and dispatch ramp risks, resulting from large orders; meanwhile, the grid operator over-procures redispatch during peak periods when all-or-none design is employed, which can also lead to induced imbalances due to inadequate redispatch activation. The research concluded that, when evaluating market designs and policy options for ancillary services and electricity markets, models need to consider the intricate interplay between markets and services. The model proposed is suitable for this purpose and is an valuable tool for policy design. The model is applicable to highly decentralized and peer-to-peer oriented electricity markets, and it is also an appropriate method for evaluating design options for frequency response and reserve markets. The study recommends employing multi-method policy analysis, involving the integration of theoretical models, empirical data, and case studies, for an in-depth evaluation of market designs and policy options. The model is an important step in developing a unified framework for evaluating design options in electricity markets and it has the potential to be applied to other complex economic systems. The study is an example of the benefits of collaboration between researchers and policy designers, and it demonstrates the effectiveness of model-based policy analysis in influencing policy decisions in the electricity policy domain. R.W.K. Odoni initially established the connection between the Galois group of an iterated polynomial and the symmetric group in fields of characteristic zero. A generalization to fields of positive characteristic was achieved by Juul. Building on these findings, we explore a scenario involving an irreducible polynomial F over the algebraic closure of a finite field k(t) with algebraic and separable coefficients. When a generic monic polynomial Phi is composed with F, resulting in a new polynomial with coefficients (a0, a1,...), we identify the Galois group of the composite polynomial's mth iterate. The structure of this Galois group mirrors the (m-folded) iterated wreath product of the symmetric group S_(nd) for n > 0, where n represents the polynomial's degree. In the case of large finite fields, the application of this discovery aligns with analogous theories, including the polynomial equivalent of the Bateman-Horn conjecture, the Chowla's conjecture regarding autocorrelation, and the Chebotarev density theorem over function fields. These findings are validated through composed polynomials related to elliptic curves and modular forms. The article also explores the novel properties of composed polynomials, particularly those with prime values, and provides supporting numerical data. The associated software, comprising the Mathematica package GaloisCompositional, is designed to handle these complex computations and generate prime output for composed polynomials up to a certain degree and prime count. The package is available for download at the website of the first author. The study on composed polynomials with prime values raises several open questions regarding their behavior, especially in regards to the Bateman-Horn conjecture, and we include a section dedicated to these unsolved problems. The article concludes with the description of a new project, the Galois census, which aims to gather comprehensive information on composed polynomials for all possible coefficient values. The goals of this project are notable in the context of the broader theory of composed polynomials and Galois orbits. The article provides a clear overview of the objectives of the Galois census and outlines the initial strategies for achieving these goals. Furthermore, it includes a supporting section that provides the historical background necessary to understand the context of the project, including the contributions of previous researchers. The article also includes a section dedicated to the format and structure of the data related to composed polynomials, which is integral to the success of the Galois census. The section is followed by a description of the available resources and the team behind the Galois census

Specifically, our analysis focuses on final states with two leptons and assesses the effectiveness of separating signal and background for experimental conditions representative of the ATLAS and CMS experiments during LHC Run 2, leveraging the DELPHES simulation package. As a result, we were able to achieve a $0.26\%$ top quark pair background suppression, corresponding to a $35\%$ Higgs boson pair signal efficiency. Furthermore, our findings indicate that with more stringent cuts, the Higgs boson pair signal efficiency can be enhanced up to $48\%$, achieved by applying a relative efficiency threshold of $10^{-4}$ to the $s$-discriminant value. This study provides valuable insights for developing efficient event selection procedures to identify the $\textrm{HH} \to \textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ channel at the LHC in future experiments. Moreover, we highlight that the distinction between signal and background based on the $s$-discriminant value or related variables can be cross-verified by actual LHC data, eliminating any systematic uncertainty associated with this procedure. In addition, we outline additional research needed to fully explore the potential of the matrix element method for Higgs boson pair production studies. Moreover, with the expected outcomes of this research, we will be able to accurately assess the reach of future LHC studies in HH production, also considering other relevant processes such as $\textrm{ZZ}$ and $\textrm{WW}$ production. Saturn's polar atmosphere is characterized by seasonal variations of large warm whirlpools north of 75 degrees latitude. The strongest of these appear during Saturn's summer and disappear in the winter. The extensive exploration of the Saturn system enabled by the Cassini spacecraft has facilitated a comprehensive study of the formation of the North Polar Stratospheric Vortex through the application of infrared spectroscopy. By analyzing this phenomenon, researchers were able to identify the rates of formation and dissolution of these polar vortices in both hemispheres. The vortex in the north began forming in the late spring, but it took until the end of the summer for it to exhibit the temperature and chemical contrasts seen in the southern hemisphere during its own summer. The vortex in the north was found to be surrounded by a strengthening temperature gradient at 78 degrees latitude and displayed a hexagonal shape. This indicates that a particular type of atmospheric wave, previously thought to influence temperatures deep in the planet's atmosphere, has the ability to impact temperatures as high as 300 km above the clouds. The formation of the North Polar Stratospheric Vortex is thought to occur when the increasing solar insulation on the North Pole becomes strong enough to overcome the planetary rotation's dissolving effect on the forming whirlpool, and it may serve as a crucial test for the theories explaining why certain large-scale waves fail to overcome the planet's rotation in various atmospheres. The vortex in the north is also providing a unique opportunity to study the Saturnian equivalent of the Earth's polar jet stream, which was previously unknown to exist. This paper investigates solutions to the Schrödinger equation under the influence of a focusing nonlinearity with mass-supercritical properties, in a domain exterior to a compact convex obstacle in a higher-dimensional space. We demonstrate that solutions with negative energy will inevitably collapse within a finite time period. Additionally, under the assumption that the nonlinearity is not too strongly energy-dependent and given specific symmetry conditions, we establish the same optimal blow-up criterion found by Holmer and Roudenko for solutions in an infinite domain. A previously established approach, derived by Glassey through the concavity of variance, is not applicable in this context due to the appearance of boundary terms of undesirable sign in the second derivative of variance. Our primary argument introduces a new, modified variance measure, bounded from below and concave in a way that is relevant for solutions in this particular scenario. This approach relies on the specific properties of the Schrödinger equation and its conservation laws, particularly the mass and momentum laws, which facilitate the derivation of a relevant inequality via the concavity of the new variance measure. This inequality, in turn, enables the establishment of the blow-up criterion. We also explore additional properties of this method's applications and adaptations. Furthermore, we identify a condition on the nonlinearity that is both sufficient and necessary for this approach to be effective. It should be noted that this condition can be interpreted as a definition of the "subcritical mass" of a nonlinearity. We derive a new generalization for damped systems and a related result for wave equations, both of which rely on this new approach. It is essential to mention that the main limitations of this method's applicability are tied to the specific properties of the Schrödinger equation and its associated conservation laws. Therefore, it is likely that this approach could be expanded to accommodate other types of differential equations with similar properties. Additionally, we highlight a striking phenomenon associated with boundary layers in this context, which may have broader implications within the field of differential equations. We also explore potential connections with the Dirac equation in curved spacetime, specifically in contexts where dilation fields are present, which could lead to further insights into the blow-up of solutions in those scenarios. Although the technical details required to address these broader mathematical questions related to the Dirac equation are too elaborate to be tackled within this paper's scope, they do represent an interesting area for potential future research. We provide a novel proof that local characteristic-zero, semi-parametric embeddings for a polynomial variety defined over the integers have an equivalent form to local positive-characteristic reductions of the variety for nearly all prime numbers. This result is demonstrated using the geometric Langlands correspondence and Chaberts' discovery about geometric representations. Additionally, we offer a new characterization of varieties with this property, using the geometry of Bala-Mathieu and Chaberts. This involves showing that a local characteristic-zero, semi-parametric embedding for a polynomial variety defined over the integers can be transformed into local positive-characteristic reductions of the variety for infinitely many prime numbers. This characterization holds when the variety's algebraic group is simply-connected. We extend this proof to varieties whose algebraic group is not simply-connected, using the properties of central squashes. This involves showing that local characteristic-zero, semi-parametric embeddings for these varieties have an equivalent form to local positive-characteristic reductions of the variety for a specific set of prime numbers that becomes infinite when scalar extension is performed. This result holds when the base field's algebraic dimension is higher than the variety's dimension. We offer a generalization of this proof, using the geometry of Bala-Mathieu and Chaberts, for local characteristic-zero, semi-parametric embeddings for a specific type of geometric object called a smooth twisted conjugacy class. This involves showing that local positive-characteristic reductions of these geometric objects have an equivalent form to local characteristic-zero, semi-parametric embeddings for these objects for nearly all prime numbers. Furthermore, we provide a novel characterization of local positive-characteristic reductions of these geometric objects when the variety's algebraic group is simply-connected. This characterization holds when the base field's algebraic dimension is higher than the variety's dimension. The manner in which the surface of materials is terminated has significant implications for their physical characteristics. Investigating the metal-insulator transition in V$_2$O$_3$ films necessitates a deep comprehension of the effect of surface termination.  Our studies achieved varying surface terminations in V$_2$O$_3$ films using low energy electron diffraction and photoemission spectroscopy, which led us to a key finding - depending on the terminations, the metal-insulator transition may be significantly impeded or totally hindered near the surface due to distinct variations in electron distribution at different layers and altered screening length as compared to the bulk.  A considerable reorganization of spectral weight across the metal-insulator transition has also been observed, with an observable transfer of spectral weight across the entire energy scale from the high-binding energy regime to the low-binding energy regime, in contrast to our findings of unconserved total spectral weight across the metal-insulator transition, which indicates a failure in applying'sum rules of spectral weight',  a hallmark of systems with strong correlations.  Our data suggest that changes in hybridization, effective carrier density, lattice volume, and spin degrees of freedom, possibly all interlinked with the change in electron correlations across the metal-insulator transition, are responsible for such a shift in spectral weight.  Furthermore, our research demonstrates that in V$_2$O$_3$, the metal-insulator transition is fundamentally driven by correlation between electrons, with the effect of these interactions playing a pivotal role in determining the transition's occurrence.  Our studies also offer a greater insight into understanding the electronic structure of systems with strong correlations, underscoring the significance of factoring in surface-related effects while interpreting experimental data collected through surface-sensitive techniques such as resistivity measurement, as this has significant implications for comprehending physical characteristics.  Furthermore, our research highlights the importance of choosing appropriate reference systems in the interpretation of ARPES data, particularly in situations where the effect of variation in electron distribution across the metal-insulator transition is concerned, with special emphasis on the impact of hybridization, carrier density, volume of lattice, and spin degrees of freedom, all of which have a substantial influence on the distribution of electrons as observed through photoemission, ultimately affecting the interpretation of results.  Lastly, our studies demonstrate that in V$_2$O$_3$, the effect of variations in electron correlations across the metal-insulator transition on the absorption of photons, holds the key to a better comprehension of systems with strong correlations, with a noteworthy dispersion of spectral weight

Our study uncovers new features of non-equilibrium behavior in quantum double dark-soliton states for one-dimensional repulsive boson gases. We find a specific scaling of Bose-Einstein condensation fractions in ground states that can be used to analyze quasi-condensation in weakly coupled quantum double dark-soliton states. We first demonstrate the precise time-dependent density profile of a quantum double dark-soliton state via the Bethe ansatz method. Next, we derive an effective macroscopic wave function for these states by calculating the amplitude and phase of field operator matrix elements. In the weak-coupling regime, these profiles resemble those of dark solitons. We then precisely examine the interaction between two notches in quantum double dark-soliton states. Observations suggest that quasi-condensation may play a significant role in quantum double dark-soliton dynamics, and that states with high condensate fractions should be well-represented by a quasi-condensation state that follows a mean-field model. Conversely, states with low condensate fractions may be more complex, involving unstable modes that could be influenced by quasi-condensation. We also propose a new finite-size scaling for Bose-Einstein condensation in isolated quantum double dark-soliton states, and predict that a critical point will shift with system size in proportion to L^-4. Additionally, we identify a critical exponent for a phase separation line in the quantum double dark-soliton phase diagram. This new scaling will be useful in identifying and distinguishing between quasi-condensation and BEC in future experimental studies. We compare our results to those obtained from a weak-coupling theory, and find that while the two approaches converge in the weak-coupling limit, they produce distinct predictions for quasi-condensation and BEC in the strong-coupling regime. Furthermore, we propose that future experimental studies should focus on observing the interaction between two notches in quantum double dark-soliton states, and that accurate measurements of these interactions will be crucial in fully understanding the behavior of quantum double dark-soliton states. We also examine the possibility of observing quasi-condensation in quantum double dark-soliton states, and predict that future experimental studies should be able to distinguish between quasi-condensation and BEC using our proposed finite-size scaling. The interaction between light and matter is used in various spectroscopic techniques to extract details about a sample's molecular, atomic, or nuclear components. Although scattered light conveys both amplitude and phase information, this phase information is frequently lost during standard intensity measurements, yet it is crucial for reconstructing essential details of a target, as evident from applications like coherent x-ray imaging. A new algorithm is introduced that allows for retrieving phase information from two-dimensional time- and energy-resolved spectra, a feature we demonstrate with x-ray scattering off M\"ossbauer nuclei using a synchrotron radiation source. The knowledge gained through phase information also leads to accurate reconstruction of energy spectra from experimental data, a level of precision that cannot be achieved with other methods. Our approach provides a useful data analysis tool, offering a beneficial impact on x-ray quantum optics and M\"ossbauer spectroscopy that employs synchrotron radiation. Furthermore, this method may be adapted for application in wide-ranging fields including chemical physics, biology, and medical science. The data analyzed in this study are publicly available and can be freely downloaded from https://doi.org/10.20379/nibis/vtqz-0f47. Additionally, the associated xrayHR.org entry can be found at https://doi.org/10.20379/nibis/vtqw-0f46. The new algorithm introduced in this research has been successfully applied to experimental data obtained from the ID21 beamline at the ESRF. The expertise and knowledge shared in this study are also currently being used in another ongoing research project at the ID21 beamline. The research described in this study was supported by the European Union's Horizon 2020 Research and Innovation Programme under grant agreement number 65420100005 and 691156, the German Research Foundation (DFG) under grant agreement number CH 710/4-1, the Austrian Science Fund (FWF) under grant agreement number I 4350-G, and the X-FEL National Laboratory Program of Japan. The authors would like to show their appreciation to the ID21 beamline staff at the ESRF for their support during the experiment. Furthermore, we would like to extend our gratitude to the members of the X-ray Quantum Optics group led by J. V. Krsti\'c for their valuable input and suggestions. Finally, we would like to express our gratitude to the members of the M\"ossbauer Spectroscopy group led by T. Kr\"amer for their valuable input and suggestions.

By linking quantum error correcting codes to models of disordered classical statistical mechanics and examining the phase diagram of these models, researchers have found a valuable tool for studying how these codes resist errors under various noise conditions. This study expands this mapping to account for realistic faulty quantum circuits when describing quantum error correcting codes. First, based on a detailed circuit noise model, we develop a strongly correlated classical spin model corresponding to each circuit noise scenario. This approach is illustrated using the quantum repetition code, where we simulate the impact of periodically malfunctioning stabilizer readout circuits. We utilize Monte Carlo simulations to investigate the phase diagram resulting from these interactions, and our findings are compared with the performance of a minimum-weight perfect matching decoder. This research provides a method for assessing the fundamental error thresholds of quantum error correcting codes, independently of any specific decoding strategies, and could help inform the design of near-term quantum computing hardware. Additionally, this framework may facilitate the exploration of novel quantum error threshold results arising from faulty circuit designs that cannot be understood through solo study of the code's decoding mechanisms.

We introduce a novel mixed finite element approach for single-phase Darcy flow within a fractured porous media, incorporating two types of fractures. These fractures can be viewed as interfaces within a $d$-dimensional space, where $d$ equals either $2$ or $3$. A significant distinction is drawn between fractures with notably high and low permeability compared to their surrounding medium, categorized as conductive and blocking fractures respectively. Our proposed method uses traditional hybrid-dimensional techniques to model conductive fractures and a more recent Dirac-$\delta$ function approach for blocking fractures. This results in our numerical scheme being compatible with nonconforming meshes in regards to the blocking fractures. A major advancement of our approach, the method also achieves conservative and symmetric results with regards to pressure. This methodology's effectiveness is demonstrated through the execution of numerous test cases across both two and three-dimensional settings. Our numerical data indicates that our approach offers highly comparable performance to existing literature methods. Furthermore, our scheme allows for easy implementation of varying fracture geometries without significant alterations to the method itself. This includes the incorporation of infinitely long fractures in a $2$-dimensional setting. Our proposed approach has the potential to be expanded to account for nonlinear fluid transport and specific types of porous media phase change. This includes the incorporation of inner obstacles within a $3$-dimensional setting, making our method a robust and versatile numerical solution for a broad range of single-phase Darcy flow applications. This work is also presented as a part of the recent joint research project with the Center for Computational Science and Engineering at Nanyang Technological University. This involvement has provided valuable opportunities for collaboration with fellow researchers and staff at the university. This project is an essential component of the Singaporean Ministry of Education's Multi-disciplinary Domain Research Project. This project's primary objective involves developing an adaptable and highly accurate numerical solution for a wide range of flow problems within porous media across various dimensions and geometries. Hypothesis evaluation plays a significant role in cognitive science, where Bayes factors can compare and contrast competing theories by assessing their consistency with available data. However, implementing Bayes factor analysis is often complicated and heavily dependent on the accuracy of computational methods, as well as assumptions related to the model and data. We aim to investigate these challenges in cognitive science using Bayes factor analysis, focusing on the underlying statistical concepts and the need for objective utility functions to make informed decisions. We explore various issues with Bayes factor estimates, including their tendency to err and the reliability of bridge sampling, especially when analyzing complex scenarios. To tackle these challenges, we develop a simulation-based approach for validating the accuracy of Bayes factor estimates and examine the stability of Bayes factors in relation to different Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) draws. We also investigate the variability of Bayes factor estimates and the effectiveness of utility functions in making informed decisions. To facilitate the assessment of Bayes factor reliability, we outline a step-by-step workflow that researchers can use to evaluate the performance of Bayes factor analysis for their individual studies, including an illustrative example from the cognitive sciences. We anticipate that this research will contribute to the development of a robust methodology for evaluating scientific hypotheses based on Bayes factor analysis, along with reproducible code available online. Additionally, we discuss various strategies, including utility functions and multiple comparison methods, that can be employed in conjunction with the proposed workflow. The use of these techniques can help enhance the credibility of cognitive science findings by ensuring the robustness of Bayes factor analyses. In turn, this, in turn, can provide a more reliable framework for evaluating hypotheses in the cognitive sciences. To this end, we propose the term "reproducible hypothesis evaluation" (RHE) to capture the workflow's key aspects, including utility functions, multiple comparison methods, and variability assessment, among others. Furthermore, we explore potential extensions to the proposed workflow, considering factors such as the choice of prior distributions, model selection, and the use of cross-validation, which researchers can adapt to their specific needs. Discourse indicators such as "by contrast" and "happily" facilitate the identification of connections between sentences. To improve the effectiveness of sentence representations in classification tasks, research has been done on predicting these indicators between sentences. This work diverges from this approach by using a trained model to forecast suitable indicators between sentences that have an established semantic connection, based on existing datasets used for classification tasks. These predictions enable researchers to investigate the relationship between discourse indicators and the annotated semantic relations. Existing studies have established correlations between indicators and discourse relationships but are limited to specific instances and categories. On the other hand, numerous discourse indicators convey diverse relations and a universally accepted classification system does not exist. To rectify this, an automatic prediction method is applied to pre-existing semantically annotated datasets, leading to a novel characterization of discourse indicators in the English language, and a resulting dataset named DiscSense which is available for public use. This dataset is distinct from datasets used in classification tasks that rely on predicting indicators between sentences, rather than using the specific indicators provided in such tasks' training data. Consequently, it provides a more comprehensive understanding of the English language's discourse indicators and their capabilities to express diverse relations. This characterization is also verified through a user study involving language users from various linguistic backgrounds. In contrast to previous studies on English discourse indicators, researchers do not have a basis for comparison as there is a lack of research on the topic. To verify the characterization's general applicability, the model and technique are applied to a dataset from a different language, specifically French, and a resulting dataset named DiscSense-Fr is created. This process leads to a groundbreaking insight that discourse indicators' diversity is inherent to a language rather than a feature of specific relationships or instances, which is visually represented through a novel visualization technique. This insight is further validated by analyzing the statistical differences between two datasets, DiscSense and DiscSense-Fr, using two types of discourse indicators: those that are inherent to a language and those that are not. The characterization of English discourse indicators and the resulting datasets, including DiscSense and DiscSense-Fr, achieve a significant milestone in the field by providing a general framework for describing discourse indicators' diversity, their diversity's source, and a novel approach to studying the semantics of indicators through an automated method. This enables a deeper understanding of discourse indicators' diversity and their diversity's origin, which is valuable for developing more effective methods for predicting semantic relations and classification tasks. We investigate the properties of a negatively charged nitrogen-vacancy center in diamond under high-temperature and vacuum conditions.  By combining optical detection of magnetic resonance (ODMR) and optical spectroscopy, we studied the spin resonances and radiative transitions at high temperatures.  Our findings indicate that increasing temperature leads to a reduction in the intensity of visible and infrared light emitted from the diamond, as well as a decrease in the frequencies of ODMR resonance and a shift in the emission line towards longer wavelengths.  By comparing our measured data to theoretical predictions, specifically from the Mott-Seitz model, we estimated that a significant nonradiative energy barrier has a height of approximately 0.24 electron volts.  This barrier contributes to a nonradiative decay mechanism, and we were able to use it to explain the observed decrease in emitted intensity at high temperatures.  Furthermore, we found that a substantial amount of the decrease in ODMR frequency with increasing temperature cannot be accounted for by this barrier alone, suggesting that other factors contribute to this phenomenon.  In regards to the shift in emitted light towards longer wavelengths, we proposed an explanation based on a temperature-induced shift in the energy levels of the diamond rather than a change in its environment.  Our research provides valuable insights into the properties of a key quantum system under conditions similar to those found in high-temperature superconducting materials.  Although further study is needed to fully understand this phenomenon, our findings suggest that the nitrogen-vacancy center in diamond may still be a suitable quantum probe for studying the physics of these materials.  To this end, we propose identifying and isolating specific nitrogen-vacancy centers within the diamond before using it to study the physics of these materials.  Additionally, we found that a higher 532-nanometer laser power than previously reported is required to achieve saturation in this type of center, and this could have implications for other research using this configuration.  Our team discovered a similar relationship between this power and the frequency of the ODMR resonance, and we found that it is necessary to control this power closely in order to accurately determine the ODMR frequency.  Finally, we propose that further research should focus on resolving the underlying causes of the decrease in ODMR frequency with increasing temperature, as well as developing techniques for controlling the environment around specific nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond. This presents an insurmountable challenge to modeling brain function accurately. A new algorithm developed for two-layer networks overcomes this hurdle by doing away with explicit error calculation and backpropagation altogether. This algorithm remarkably translates to a neural network that closely mimics the brain's connectivity pattern and learning processes, and experiments show it rivals the performance of backpropagation across various datasets. The underlying mechanism of this algorithm suggests it could potentially facilitate the efficient training of neural networks with diverse structures. A variation of this algorithm, suited for networks with multiple local layers, has also been devised and proven to be a more practical learning approach. The new algorithm and its variants offer promising solutions for building models of the brain's learning processes and provide a stepping stone for further research into neural networks inspired by the brain. These algorithms may also be the next breakthrough in developing artificial neural networks in the image and speech recognition fields. A new implementation of the Hartree-Fock (HF) method has been developed to efficiently achieve robust convergence for well-behaved central potentials. The method converts HF equations into a generalized eigenvalue problem by using a B-spline basis in a finite-size box and incrementally increases the strength of electron-electron interactions. The accuracy and performance of this implementation were verified through a series of benchmark tests, involving calculations of atoms and ions with central Coulomb potentials, electron gas confined by harmonic and uniform potentials, and alkali-metal clusters modeled by the jellium model. The results were compared to established methods, showing good agreement in terms of convergence patterns and energies for atoms and ions, electron energy and density for harmonic confinement, and dipole polarizabilities for sodium clusters, aligning closely with theoretical and experimental expectations. Notably, this method was found to be superior to traditional techniques in terms of convergence speed and total computational cost. The code is written in C and is designed for portability, with plans to optimize performance through the use of parallel processing. The full source code has been made available upon request. We investigate a general matrix optimization problem subject to a fixed-rank positive semidefinite constraint and perform the Burer-Monteiro factorization to analyze its landscape under a particular Riemannian quotient geometry. Assuming standard strong convexity and smoothness properties for the objective function f, we find that its factorized version exhibits distinct behaviors in three regions: (1) near the target parameter of interest, it is geodesically strongly convex and smooth; (2) it has neighborhoods of strict saddle points; and (3) it has large gradients in remaining areas. We contribute a global landscape analysis under the Riemannian quotient geometry for the first time and provide a geometric explanation for the effectiveness of vanilla gradient descent in this setting. When f satisfies a weaker convexity property, we discover a geodesically convex neighborhood around local minimizers. To achieve these results, we analyze a matrix factorization problem with a least squares objective, providing a critical connection, and also establish an independent result regarding the convexity of geodesic balls under the Riemannian quotient geometry. Finally, we incorporate an adaptive gradient descent method, which exhibits state-of-the-the-art performance in synthetic and real-world experiments. The implementation of this method is available online. We answer an open question regarding the landscape of nonconvex matrix factorization by showing that, when the target parameter has an exact factorization, it lies within a geodesically convex neighborhood accessible to an exploratory gradient descent method. The theoretical results are backed by an empirical study of the sparsity of local minimizers in a matrix factorization setting. The work provides an extension to a previous study on the landscape of matrix factorization under a standard Euclidean geometry. The results are relevant to other fixed-rank optimization problems, such as low-rank least squares and matrix regression, and can be applied to a broader class of convex and nonconvex optimization problems with constraints defined by matrix trigonometric functions. The work paves the way for further studies on the landscape of more complex matrix optimization problems subject to constraints defined by matrix trigonometric functions. Current constraints from Big-Bang Nucleosynthesis already set a strict limit on their lifespan, at under 0.1 seconds. Next-generation gravitational wave detectors have the potential to drastically improve these limits to the point where their lifespan could be constrained to as short as 10^-16 seconds. This could be possible if these particles once controlled the universe's energy density and led to a transition to a matter-dominated period before decaying in time for Big-Bang Nucleosynthesis to occur. As a result of such an early history of the universe, we could detect unique signatures in gravitational wave backgrounds that originated from primordial sources.
