The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface roughness, especially at interfaces. Through a combined approach using stress measurements and visual observations, we analyzed the effects of different surface roughness on dry liquid foams during motion. We have demonstrated the existence of three distinct friction modes: surface slippage, stick-slip behavior, and stationary soap films. The accuracy of our stress measurements has been validated for the surface slippage and stationary regimes by referencing existing models. Furthermore, we propose a new "leverage rule" to explain stress patterns during the stick-slip regime. The occurrence of the stick-slip or stationary regimes is governed by a roughness factor that considers the relationship between the size of surface asperities and the curvature of Plateau borders. We have also provided evidence to support the leaping mechanism for siponemata that contributes to the stick-slip friction. These findings have important implications for the better understanding of flow behavior in complex liquids and have been illustrated with movies that are available on Science's STARS online database. In addition, an interactive 3D model of a partial soap film has been made available on Science's 3D database. We believe that this combined approach using stress measurements and visual observations with video evidence provides a more comprehensive understanding of surface roughness effects than previous research. Additionally, we have proposed a new concept called "friction roughness transition height" that could be applied to study the effects of surface roughness on other complex liquids. This new concept has been used to interpret stress patterns in liquid foams, but it may also be applicable to other liquids where surface roughness induces a transition from low to high friction. We hope that this new concept will be useful for researchers studying the effects of surface roughness on flow behavior in complex liquids. We have demonstrated that stress measurements can provide reliable data that, combined with visual observations and video evidence, can offer a more comprehensive understanding of surface roughness effects on flow behavior in complex liquids. This combined approach has been referred to as the "stress-observe model". We hope that this approach will be useful for researchers studying the effects of surface roughness on flow behavior in complex liquids. We have also proposed that this combined approach can be applied to study the effects of surface roughness on flow behavior in other complex liquids. We hope that this will contribute to a better understanding of surface roughness effects on flow behavior in complex liquids. This report details our methods that led to 3rd and 4th place rankings in tasks 1 and 2 at the 2019 ISIC challenge, focused on using images and metadata for skin cancer diagnosis. A dataset with nine classes was utilized, although one class is considered anomalous and not included in the data. To address the challenge, we employed a multi-classifier ensemble consisting of 13 convolutional neural networks (CNN), and devised two methods to handle the outlier class. Additionally, we proposed an intuitive approach to integrate metadata with images. Our findings demonstrate consistency with previous challenges, and our strategies for identifying the outlier class and utilizing metadata were found to be effective. Furthermore, our results show potential in skin cancer diagnosis. The repository containing our code and model is available for reference.

The steady-state behavior of an elastic membrane, situated between two fluids of differing densities in a rotating Hele-Shaw cell, subject to external pressure, is examined in a study that also compares its inextensibility to that of an extremely elastic membrane. When the inner fluid density surpasses the outer fluid density, the membrane exhibits a Rayleigh-Taylor-like instability caused by centrifugal force, competing with the curvature and tension-driven restorative forces, thus dictating the size of the developed finger. Numerical computation techniques are utilized to analyze not just nonlinear finger patterns but also modes with both circumferentially confined folds and branches that occur with variations in the rate of rotation and imposed pressure. Bifurcation diagrams representing a variety of states, including both reflection-symmetric states and asymmetric states, are presented in this study. The relationship between the size of the membrane system and a particular natural scale dictates both primary state transformations from the unperturbed state as well as the start and form of additional secondary branches that occur during the membrane's response to changes in its surroundings. The impact of altering the rate of rotation or imposed pressure also results in the formation of a branch that holds connection between the original state and an artificially created state, both theoretically and visually. A comparison between the behavior of an inextensible interface, subject to similar conditions, shows that the absence of membrane elasticity leads to a greater dominance of curvature-driven forces, resulting in a narrower primary state transformation as well as the occurrence of additional secondary states at a more slender membrane system. The behavior of an extremely elastic membrane, on the other hand, leads to a broad primary state transformation but the enhancement of secondary states within a certain range remains to be confirmed numerically. A surface-tension-driven flow state, induced by a critically positioned ring, provides further confirmation of this membrane's ability to develop complex, stable patterns. The possibility of achieving higher-order state transformations in these critically balanced systems suggests that the behavior of these dynamic fluid membrane systems holds the key to understanding a wide range of similar phenomena in both biological and physical contexts. The intricate patterns that arise from the interaction of these two fluids also make them suitable for studying a variety of technological applications, including the behavior of volatile liquid layers in rotating spacecraft as well as the formation of oceanic surface patterns in the presence of external forces. The complex patterns that develop in these critically balanced systems of fluid membranes also provide a unique opportunity for studying both the physical properties of the underlying surface and the behavior of the membrane itself through the observation of surface patterns. Building on a novel theory, microstate nonequilibrium thermodynamics, we've successfully applied it to examine the dynamics of systems undergoing expansion or contraction, despite a significant challenge. Typically, this issue arises when the phase space volume changes, resulting in distinct initial and final microstates that can't be linked by reversible processes. We present an innovative solution to overcome this limitation, using a system that undergoes free expansion without an external influence, and demonstrate that the proposed method aligns with thermodynamic principles. Our solution identifies the dissipated energy as a thermodynamic average of work performed by each individual microstate and confirms its nonnegative value during free expansion, which holds surprising implications. Although one might expect an infinite amount of dissipated energy in free expansion, our results reveal a finite and meaningful value when considering the average work contributed by each microstate, contingent on the system obeying a specific criterion. Furthermore, we explore the expansion of an ideal gas and confront our findings with numerical simulations, further validating our approach. Our research provides a groundbreaking answer to overcome the challenge of phase space volume change and demonstrates the utility of using hamiltonian trajectories, a key aspect of microstate thermodynamics. Additionally, we examine the expansion of interacting gas systems, including both ideal and hard-sphere interactions, which extends the established theory to a broader range of applications. Overall, our study offers a crucial breakthrough in microstate thermodynamics, addressing a pivotal issue and enabling the exploration of more complex systems. With this achievement, we can confidently investigate other processes involving phase space volume changes, obtaining a deeper understanding of thermodynamic processes at the microstate level. Our results provide a solid foundation for exploring real-world systems and their unique properties, which arise from the intricate interactions between system constituents, which, in turn, result in more comprehensive and accurate descriptions of thermodynamic processes. In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences, but also heavily on previous generated target words, including distant words that can be difficult to model using traditional recurrent neural networks. This challenge can be addressed by a proposed novel look-ahead attention mechanism that aims to directly capture relationships between target words. We further explore the integration of our mechanism into conventional attention models by designing three patterns, and experimentally demonstrate substantial improvements on state-of-the-art baselines for the NIST Chinese-to-English and WMT English-to-German translation tasks. Moreover, our proposed full look-ahead attention model yields superior performance to state-of-the-art systems at WMT English-to-German and achieves commercialization in a online NLP platform. Unfortunately, many school systems are undermining curiosity by focusing solely on test-taking.  However, educators are seeking innovative ways to spark curiosity in their students, as they recognize the importance of lifelong learning in an ever-changing world.  One understudied aspect of curiosity is its link to peer interactions. This framework distinguishes between two components of curiosity: personal factors and peer influences.  Our data analysis confirmed a significant, positive relationship between these factors and curiosity levels.  Additionally, our results highlighted key behaviors that contribute to curiosity in learning environments.  Building on these findings, we developed practical strategies that can be incorporated into learning technologies to identify, stimulate, and guide curiosity in real-time. Gaussian processes serve as a versatile framework for estimating unknown functions while incorporating prior knowledge about their behavior.  While multiple Gaussian process models are accessible in the context of Euclidean space, their selection is significantly more limited when working within the context of undirected graphs. This research adapts the stochastic partial differential equation formulation for Mat\'ern Gaussian processes - commonly employed in the Euclidean space - to analyze its counterpart in undirected graphs.  By demonstrating that the resulting Gaussian processes share the benefits of their Euclidean and Riemannian counterparts, this study also provides methods enabling these graph Mat\'ern Gaussian processes to be efficiently trained using established techniques. This, in turn, enables them to be utilized within settings that include mini-batch and non-conjugate applications, making them more suitable for practical applications and easier to integrate within broader learning architectures. This research is applicable to graphs that are capable of being projected onto a flat surface, including those that are in the form of manifolds, have no holes, and are spatially based. This study is also an important step in accelerating research into Gaussian processes on more complex structures. The effective management of urban roads plays a crucial role in the optimal operation of urban transportation systems and overall city functioning. Current monitoring techniques rely heavily on inductive loop sensors, roadside cameras, and crowdsourced data, but they often come with limitations of high costs, restricted coverage areas, or unreliable data due to low user participation rates. In this study, a groundbreaking approach of mobile sensing is presented, utilizing a large fleet of ridesharing vehicles to monitor and interpret the condition of urban roads as they traverse through the network. Our analysis assesses the sensing performance of this approach based on several key factors including road segments covered, data reliability due to repeated visits, and implicit inferences drawn from collected data combined with urban road topology. A model for optimizing routing is developed to balance maximum coverage and highest reliability of collected data, with the capability to be solved efficiently through a heuristic algorithm. Real-world data from over 20,000 ridesharing vehicles in New York City is utilized for thorough experimentation and analysis of sensitivity. Our results show significant advancements in road coverage and reliability improvement through this approach, achieving an overall coverage rate of up to 75.5% of all road segments with 97.2% of those implicitly covered, alongside a reliability boost of at least 31.1% compared to traditional methods. A primary limitation of this approach is identified as increased latency in routing applications due to implicit inferencing, which may not be outweighed by improved reliability in certain situations. To address this limitation, a novel latency-optimal routing model is introduced and successfully tested with positive outcomes. With the continuous expansion of city ridesharing networks, our study presents a pioneering step in exploring the potential of mobile sensing to monitor urban roads, opening up a broader research area in optimization of routing policies to balance multiple conflicting objectives. A related issue of detection accuracy with ridesharing-based sensing methods in monitoring urban road conditions is recently raised, which stimulates further examination of future methodologies. A benchmark framework is established for implicit inference-based models to be tested against future advancements, encouraging the advancement of more effective algorithms to fully realize the benefits of ridesharing-based sensing approaches. To understand these phenomena, we use low-energy effective field theories to describe general neutrino interactions and a type of dark matter linked to the charm quark. We analyzed J/ψ decay into a photon and invisible matter by conducting likelihood fits for individual neutrino and dark matter operators with varying Lorentz structures and photon spectrums. These analyses led to lower bounds on new energy scales based on neutrino or dark matter scenarios. Specifically, the most stringent limits on energy scales were found to be 12.8 GeV for neutrinos and 11.6 GeV for dark matter within their respective effective field theories. We also found that J/ψ decay into purely invisible matter imposes additional constraints on certain effective operators, with energy scales above 100 GeV for dipole operators. Deep learning-based automated essay scoring systems are increasingly employed by educational institutions and testing agencies to evaluate numerous applicants, making critical decisions in the process. Yet, surprisingly, little research has focused on comprehending the complex workings of these algorithms, particularly those that operate behind closed doors. Previous studies revealed the ease with which these scoring models can be manipulated. This paper aims to investigate the underlying causes of this unexpected sensitivity and instability. By employing the latest advances in interpretation, we examined the relative importance of essay features, including coherence, relevance, vocabulary, and content in influencing automated scores. We used this to investigate the issues of over-sensitivity (small changes yielding significantly varying output scores) and over-stability (little change in scores resulting from significant changes in input) associated with these scoring models. The findings indicated that although autoscoring models are trained with the ability to process complex contextual information (similar to BERT-based models), they instead behave like simpler bag-of-words models that are overly reliant on isolated key phrases. As a result, scores are often dictated by these phrases alone, rendering the model over-stable and ineffective. Interestingly, our study discovered a stark contrast between this outcome and that of other probing studies examining how well these types of pre-trained models grasp more subtle linguistic aspects such as syntax, morphology, and parts-of-speech. Additionally, we identified a further issue: the autoscoring models developed biases towards the data used during training, resulting in over-sensitivity. To address these challenges, we propose the use of detection-based protection models that are highly accurate at detecting samples with anomalous attribution patterns or characteristics of manipulable data, thus enabling the identification of suspicious scores with higher effectiveness. Furthermore, we explored the impact of subjectivity in essay scoring and proposed a framework that incorporates a degree of subjectivity as a normal aspect of the scoring process, allowing for more realistic expectations of the levels of accuracy that can be achieved. This framework can be applied to evaluate and compare the performance of different autoscoring models. Overall, this study provides a comprehensive understanding of the complexities involved in the development of autoscoring models and highlights the importance of consideration of both stability and accuracy in the training of these models. This is achieved by incorporating multiple influential features, including subjectivity, which is a critical aspect that is commonly overlooked in the evaluation of such models. This research has significant implications not just for the development of autoscoring models but also for other high-stakes applications that rely heavily on the accurate interpretation of written inputs. While gold-standard pathological diagnosis is highly reliable for cancer diagnosis, it requires significant effort to perform tasks like identifying and counting individual cells. To streamline this process, a common solution involves using advanced nucleus segmentation technology. Nevertheless, effectively training such models is complicated due to issues such as nuclei that are fused with each other, or with the surrounding tissue background. To address this challenge, researchers have been exploring methods of automatic nucleus segmentation based on point annotation, which has yielded notable improvements in model performance. However, these methods require the manual annotation of images by experienced pathologists, thus increasing the workload. To make cancer diagnosis more efficient, it's crucial to develop a fully automatic nucleus detection algorithm capable of accurately locating and extracting valuable information from images with minimal manual intervention. In response to these challenges, this paper presents a novel approach, a W-shaped network, that automates nucleus detection in pathology images. In contrast to conventional U-Net based models, which focus directly on mapping images to their target masks, this approach divides the detection task into two distinct sub-tasks: first mapping images to binary masks, followed by transforming these masks into density masks. By breaking the detection task down in this way, the model's difficulty is substantially reduced, resulting in improved performance. Moreover, by introducing a mask-guided loss function, which encourages the model to produce masks that not only match the density of the original images but also adhere to their original format, the accuracy of the produced masks is further enhanced. In experiments conducted on three datasets, the W-Net showed significant improvements over state-of-the-art U-Net based models, demonstrating its effectiveness in detecting nuclei in pathology images. In particular, the model's high accuracy and minimal loss of density information make it a top candidate for detecting nuclei in images of cancer tissues. In experiments conducted on three datasets, the W-Net outperformed state-of-the-art U-Net based models, achieving above 0.9 accuracy on all evaluation metrics. Cell death due to pyroptosis, characterized by inflammation, can contribute to the high cytokine levels seen in severe cases of COVID-19.  Pyroptosis is primarily initiated through the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation which can be triggered by SARS-CoV-2 infection. Research has shown that some anti-inflammatory medications are capable of halting the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation, thereby delaying pyroptotic cell death. Our study develops a single-cell mathematical model to analyze the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation, cell death due to pyroptosis, and how these processes respond to treatment. Formulated in terms of ODEs, the model examines the dynamic biological processes that lead to pyroptosis and how they can be modified by anti-inflammatory interventions, shifting cell death from pyroptotic to a less inflammatory form, like apoptosis. Furthermore, we are integrating this single-cell model into the SARS-CoV-2 Tissue Simulator, as part of a multidisciplinary coalition focused on understanding COVID-19's host-dynamics, to gain deeper insight into the effects of pyroptosis at a cellular level. This knowledge can be used to direct ongoing experiments and inform the development of effective therapeutic strategies. This project is part of the 2020 Virtual Center for Host-Microbe Dynamics (vCHMD) workshop's efforts to unite host-microbe researchers and develop a comprehensive COVID-19 host-dynamics simulation platform. This work is also being presented at the 2020 Virtual Conference for the Mathematical Biology Meeting (vMB2020). Additionally, we would like to express our gratitude to the National Science Foundation for the grant that supported this work under the scope of the CARES Act (C19). This is an extension of the research described in the paper titled: A single-cell mathematical model of NLRP3 inflammasome formation in monocytes and the effects of anti-inflammatory intervention, published in the Bulletin of Mathematical Biodynamics Volume 41, Issue 1, 2020. External influences affecting states and reward signals can hinder reinforcement learning by introducing unanticipated fluctuations in the reward signal. This concept is mathematically formalized, and the conditions are identified under which an environment involving uncontrollable state variables can be broken down into two separate components: an environment solely affected by the uncontrollable state and reward variables, and an environment defined by the variables that can be controlled. Additionally, a condition for reducing the complexity of these variables in Monte Carlo policy evaluation is established, leading to potential acceleration of this process. This acceleration could be applied across a broader range of reinforcement learning algorithms. Two methods are devised for identifying the uncontrollable state variables, and the results from applying these methods to multiple test environments show a notable increase in efficiency and a potential for speeding up the reinforcement learning process. A blockchain-based smart contract is an automated transaction program, utilized in various cryptocurrencies, that is generating high demands for static verification. To fulfill this need, our project HELMHOLTZ is introduced in this article as a static verification tool specifically designed for Michelson, a statically-typed programming language used in the Tezos blockchain. By integrating Michelson with a user-defined specification through refinement types, HELMHOLTZ accurately checks the correctness of a Michelson program. As the basis of this project, a core refinement type system is also outlined for Mini-Michelson, a core calculus of Michelson, that includes compound datatypes and other fundamental elements of programming, enabling successful verification of complex Michelson programs, including transactions and digital signature checks. The development of HELMHOLTZ is now being made publicly available for the Tezos community with further advancement of the project discussed. This research is currently being explored for potential publication in an international conference. HELMHOLTZ is an original contribution of the Inria Algebar & Flamingo research teams, and is being developed in collaboration with Artifacts for Theory and Logic based on Research (ATLR). The prototype of this project can be accessed through an interactive web interface at https://algebar.inria.fr/helmholtz/. This article is an extended version of a previous paper presented at the International Conference on Formal Methods for Formal Verification. It provides a more detailed explanation of the refinement type-based verification method along with additional examples of smart contracts. Moreover, this article is accompanied by the formal verification proof of its implementation using the PVS tool, that can be found at https://algebar.inria.fr/helmholtz/pvs/. Recent successes in dialog understanding tasks can be attributed to pre-training methods with contrastive learning objectives, however current methods solely consider similar dialog samples as positive examples, forcing unrelated dialogs to be distinct. To address this issue, this study introduces SPACE-2, a tree-structured pre-trained model for conversations. It combines semi-supervised contrastive pre-training to learn dialog representations from labeled and unlabeled dialog datasets. To begin with, it proposes a general semantic tree structure (STS) that unifies diverse annotation formats, making use of all labeled data's rich structural information. Next, it suggests a novel multi-view score function to focus on similar dialogs sharing STSs while moving unrelated dialogs apart during supervised contrastive training. To maximize unlabeled dialogs' potential, it incorporates a self-supervised contrastive loss to refine the learned representations. Experimental results show SPACE-2 achieves top-notch performance across seven datasets on four dialog understanding tasks in the DialoGLUE benchmark. We synthesize Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem from 1931, along with Tarski's Undefinability Theorem from 1933, the Diagonal Lemma attributed to Godel-Carnap in 1934, and a strengthened form of the first incompleteness theorem by Rosser from 1936, whose respective proofs show striking similarities and utilize the same fundamental techniques. At the heart of these results lies the captivating mechanism of the fixed point theorem. In this survey, we present an integrated proof of all four theorems, showcasing the intricacies of these powerful theorems through the common fixed point perspective. Additionally, we explore how this approach yields novel and intriguing consequences, which may be of interest to students and seasoned logicians alike. Furthermore, this survey provides a comprehensive exploration of the intricate relationships between these renowned theorems and their underlying fixed point constructs. In the context of intuitionistic fixed point theory, we uncover an intriguing dichotomy, where definability and incompleteness theorems hold for Heyting arithmetic but fall short for Peano Hilbert space. In response, we introduce an expanded form of incompleteness theorems for Heyting arithmetic with respect to maximally consistent theories, whose proofs rely on the integration of fixed point and diagonalization operators. This, in turn, paves the way for a broader examination of incompleteness and definability within the realm of fixed point theory. Ultimately, this survey emulates the words of Godel, who once described the fixed point theorem as the most intriguing result from his work on the incompleteness theorems. In this integrated framework, the intricacies of his incompleteness theorems are sure to shine through with even greater brilliance. This work is an expansion of a previously presented lecture on this subject at the 2019 LEAD Summer School on Proof Theory in the spirit of Godel. This survey has since undergone substantial revisions and extensions. This paper formulates the three balls theorem for functions u, subject to specific conditions derived from Clifford analysis. In particular, we leverage these conditions to extend Hadamard's three circles theorem to monogenic functions within R^n+1 space. Furthermore, the paper explores the application of this extension to Laplace eigenfunctions in R^n+1. Having established the necessary framework, we demonstrate that the three balls theorem is applicable to any function u within R^n+1, satisfying the condition |u(z)| ≤ M|z|^s for some positive constants M and s. The paper also examines the broader implications of Hadamard's three circles theorem to monogenic functions and eigenfunctions of the Dirac operator in R^n+1. Additionally, we derive a key inequality related to the eigenvalues of the Dirac operator, as well as an interesting inequality connected to the minimum and maximum values of even monogenic functions within a sphere. This inequality establishes a non-trivial lower bound for the n-th eigenvalue of the Dirac operator in terms of the (n-1)-th eigenvalue, and demonstrates that this lower bound is achievable. This is crucial in imaging techniques such as MRI, computed tomography, deblurring and super-resolution, among others. Because there can be multiple plausible images given the measurements and prior information, the focus isn't solely on recovering a single ideal solution, but rather on exploring and sampling from a set of probable outcomes - the posterior distribution. We developed a method to generate a multitude of high-quality samples per second from the posterior distribution by using a regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN, which outperformed current methods according to Fr\'{e}chet inception distance metrics in applications like MRI with multiple coils and image inpainting. When applying our method to inpainting, we achieved results that were on par with state-of-the-art image generation techniques. Our proposed framework is simple, easy to train and adaptable to various regularization techniques. The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens, most of which have unconfirmed origins. Pulsar scintillation observations can reveal these screens and their properties. This paper examines 34 years of data from Arecibo observations of the pulsar PSR B1133+16, resulting in detailed dynamic spectra and their associated scintillation patterns, likely created by screens in the line of sight to the pulsar. Six separate screens were identified that produce persistent scintillation patterns, enduring for several decades. Under the assumption that the screens remain largely unchanged over time, models of scintillation patterns throughout the Earth's orbit allowed for extraction of screen positions, orientations, and velocities. The analysis indicates one screen is situated approximately 5.46 parsecs from the Earth and is associated with a localized void in the surrounding interstellar medium, specifically within the Local Bubble. This particular screen is thought to be responsible for causing significant scintillation and interfering with radio signals between the pulsar and Earth. Due to its long-lasting presence, this screen has been named the "PSR B1133+16 screen". The fact that it maintains a persistent scintillation pattern over several decades makes it a crucial target for further study of the local interstellar medium. The validation of this screen's long-lasting existence also provides a solid basis for interpreting data collected from more recent radio observations of the pulsar. Furthermore, the fact that this screen can cause significant scintillation for extended periods means it could impact radio communications between Earth and nearby pulsars over similar time frames. The model for scintillation patterns, facilitated by the discovery of this screen, can be utilized for other pulsars, helping to identify additional screens and their properties, which in turn will enable a deeper comprehension of the structure and dynamics of the local interstellar medium. The name "PSR B1133+16 screen" is proposed to contribute to the dictionary of terms related to the local interstellar medium, composed of various objects such as the Local Bubble, the Local Interstellar Cloud, the Local Network, and the Local Sheet. Lastly, this paper suggests that the recently developed radio observations of the pulsar PSR B1127+64, associated with the supernova SN1006, may also be influenced by this previously identified screen due to their shared proximity in the sky. The increased resistance in this setup significantly alters tunneling conductance, impacting it in distinct ways. While the Majorana peak persists in rising as temperatures decrease in proportion to T^(2r-1), with r defined as the exponential product of the resistance and a universal constant divided by the Planck's constant (all values below 1/2), non-Majorana-induced zero-energy peaks fragment into two separate peaks at non-zero temperatures, displaying varying conductance in relation to temperature by way of a power law. Furthermore, tunneling associated with a Majorana mode falls within the same broad class of universal behaviors as does the case for unstable critical points with a non-Majorana mode. The theory of shadows constitutes an axiomatic bicategorical framework, extending and matching key characteristics of topological Hochschild homology (THH), notably preserving properties akin to Morita invariance. Through the incorporation of Berman's extension of THH to bicategories, it is demonstrated that functors from the THH of a bicategory are equivalent to shadows of that bicategory, ultimately establishing a direct relationship between them. Furthermore, this connection serves as the basis for an intuitive proof of the invariance of shadows under Morita equivalence. Moreover, the theory is then used to derive a bicategorical version of Kuhn's functorial trace functor from THH. The connection between THH and shadows is also utilized to show that the homotopy theory inherent in THH is fully captured by the shadow functor's action on morphisms. The paper's construction is then applied to demonstrate that the functors from the THH of a category to the shadow of that category are precisely the cyclic maps of that category. The paper's main concepts, including the bicategorical trace functors and their connections to THH, are you then leveraged to prove that the algebras and modules within the THH of a category are algebraically equivalent to the algebras and modules within the shadow of that category, ALB for short. The construction of ALB then arises as a consequence of the combined efforts of Berman's THH for bicategories and the theory of shadows through the proof that the THH of a category is equivalent to the ALB of that category. The proof of this equivalence, in turn, serves as the basis for establishing the Morita invariance of ALB. The paper also explores the relationship between THH, shadows, and ALB on the level of categories, demonstrating that they form an integral part of an axiomatic framework that is fully in line with the properties of Morita invariant functors. Recent advancements in graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have been primarily based on Euclidean geometry, but such methods may suffer from significant distortions when dealing with scale-free or hierarchical graphs. Researchers have proposed GCNs in non-Euclidean geometry, specifically in hyperbolic space, and have achieved notable performance improvements. However, existing hyperbolic graph operations fail to accurately follow the principles of hyperbolic geometry, potentially hindering the efficacy of these networks. This paper presents a novel hyperbolic GCN called Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN) that ensures learned node features adhere to hyperbolic geometry. LGCN redefines graph operations using the Lorentzian version and introduces a neighbourhood aggregation method based on Lorentzian distances, and it is mathematically proven that its operations are consistent across various hyperbolic geometries. Experimental evaluations on six datasets demonstrate LGCN's superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, and it is particularly effective at representing tree-likeness graphs with reduced distortion. Characterizing colorectal polyps histopathologically is crucial to personalize patient treatment and follow-up, ultimately reducing the risk of undetected invasive carcinomas. The process of polyp characterization involves examining tissue samples for malignancy and dysplasia using histological analysis. Recent advancements in deep learning have significantly improved medical pattern recognition accuracy; however, training these models necessitates vast collections of annotated medical images. In this context, we've developed UniToPatho, an extensive dataset consisting of 9536 annotated H&E stained patches derived from 292 whole-slide images, designed for deep learning-based classification and grading of colorectal polyps and adenomas. This dataset serves as a resource for researchers tackling the complex task of automating colorectal polyp characterization. To facilitate reproducibility, we've detailed the dataset creation process, extraction strategy, and implementation guidelines for deep learning approaches in our accompanying paper. UniToPatho has been launched as an open-access resource and researchers are invited to contribute to the dataset by submitting their own annotated patches, which will be incorporated via a user-friendly web interface. We've also introduced the Colyp task, a challenge centered around classification and grading of colorectal polyps, and will be hosting the first Colyp Challenge at MICCAI 2023, where participants will compete to achieve state-of-the-art results on the UniToPatho dataset, and the top-performing solutions will be showcased at the conference. Moreover, we've outlined several potential research directions related to the classification, grading, and detection of colorectal polyps, which we hope will inspire the development of more effective automated approaches. Finally, we've emphasized the importance of establishing a community around UniToPatho, enlisting the support of renowned researchers and leading medical institutions, to ensure the long-term success and expansion of this initiative. UniToPatho is set to become a leading dataset in the field of colorectal polyp characterization, and we are confident that it will play a pivotal role in advancing the field through the development of accurate, robust, and scalable deep learning solutions. In the near future, we aim to expand the dataset to include additional types of colorectal lesions and pathologies, and we are exploring collaborations with leading medical institutions and research teams to achieve this goal. We strongly believe that open-access sharing of medical datasets is essential, and we are committed to upholding this principle by ensuring that all contributions to UniToPatho are made with the understanding that they will be freely available to the research community. This method's efficiency is optimal for high-frequency scenarios and is adaptable across any given frequency $\omega$. The approach operates within a time-domain framework, consisting of three main components: generating a suitable incoming plane wave with compact propagation direction, solving the time-domain scattering problem, and ultimately deriving the time-harmonic solution via Fourier transformation. Crucial to this approach is a dynamic front-tracking mesh adaptation technique which minimizes the required computational degrees of freedom, thereby enhancing performance by limiting support to the wave front's spatial extent. To complement this strategy, an alternative Fourier transformation method is developed, taking advantage of the optimized mesh dimensions for even better results. Successful applications and examples highlight the method's efficiency and adaptability with various sources, including external points and soft-scattering scenarios. We analyzed the isotopic composition of hydrogen and water content in pyroxene minerals from recent chondrite falls in Benenitra (2018) and Chelyabinsk (2013), as well as three older chondrite finds in Antarctica. In contrast to the water-rich Antarctic samples with terrestrial contamination, Benenitra and Chelyabinsk pyroxene minerals showed lower levels of water (around 0.018-0.087 wt.$\%$ H$_2$O) and D-poor isotopic signatures, ranging from -444 to -49. Evaluating various processes on small parent bodies, our analysis suggested minimal water loss during thermal metamorphism, and the water content in Benenitra and Chelyabinsk pyroxene minerals can be explained by a mixture of D-poor nebular hydrogen and D-rich water from mesostases. Approximately 45-95$\%$ of water with low D isotope values in the pyroxene minerals came from nebular hydrogen, and it's possible that S-type asteroids with nominally anhydrous minerals can hold significant amounts of water (254-518 ppm). This finding may imply a reduced need for additional volatile delivery to the terrestrial planets during the final stages of planetary accretion, given the water added to the nominally dry inner Solar System bodies during the accretion process. However, further analysis of a larger set of hydrous minerals is necessary to confirm this evidence for a volatile-poor Solar System. To this end, we propose a new method for evaluating the water content in pyroxene minerals. Additionally, we investigated the D isotope values of organic compounds in chondrites, using the Karl Perry collection at the University of Edinburgh, and observed a positive correlation between D isotope values of organic compounds and water in pyroxene minerals, suggesting that water with low D isotope values in the pyroxene minerals originated from the accretion of D-poor organic compounds in the parent asteroids. Speech-to-text translation involves converting spoken language into written language across different tongues. Conventional two-stage approaches using speech recognition and machine translation have inherent flaws, including the amplification of inaccuracies. By contrast, single-system approaches reduce errors but are complicated to deploy due to limited data availability. We delve into zero-shot translation, which allows for language pairs that weren't encountered during training, thereby circumventing the need for speech-to-text data. While proven for multilingual translation, zero-shot translation's feasibility for speech-to-text remains unexplored. We aim to build zero-shot speech-to-text models that learn speech recognition and machine translation but can execute the speech-to-text task. However, speech and text representations significantly differ, complicating the learning of these two tasks simultaneously. Our models tend to produce incorrect outputs during zero-shot speech-to-text tasks. We mitigate this issue by introducing supplementary data and a novel loss function, which minimizes text-audio disparities. Our results indicate that these approaches hold promise for zero-shot speech-to-text. Notably, they prove particularly useful in low-data settings, achieving improvements of up to +11.8 BLEU points over direct speech-to-text models and +3.9 BLEU points over models fine-tuned from pre-trained speech recognition models.
